chapters.n: This heading introduces the whole book. Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem for roughly forty years, under four kings of Judah, during the rise of the Assyrian Empire (about 740–700 BC).

f.g: Hebrew ḥazon — a revelation seen by a prophet; here a title for his whole collection of prophecies.

chapters.n: Like a lawyer calling witnesses, Isaiah summons heaven and earth to hear the Lord’s case. God is a loving Father who raised His children, yet they rebelled against Him.

f.w: Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth
I have nourished and brought up children

chapters.n: Even farm animals know who feeds them, but Israel does not recognize or think about the God who cares for them. Their forgetfulness is worse than an animal’s.

f.g: Feeding trough or manger.
Understand or pay attention.

chapters.n: Isaiah mourns over a nation weighed down by sin. They have abandoned the Lord and turned their backs on Him. “Holy One of Israel” is Isaiah’s favorite title for God.

f.g: Used about 25 times in Isaiah and often in the Book of Mormon (e.g. 2 Nephi 9:41).
Turned away; become estranged.

chapters.n: Why keep rebelling and getting hurt? The nation is like a body sick from head to heart. Their punishments haven’t brought them back.

f.g: Struck, punished.
Sick, weak.

chapters.n: The nation is covered in untreated wounds from head to foot. No one has cleaned, bandaged, or soothed them — a picture of a people who refuse healing.

f.g: Fresh, open wounds.
Softened or soothed.

chapters.n: Isaiah describes the land devastated by foreign invaders. Many scholars connect this with Assyria’s invasion of Judah under Sennacherib in 701 BC, when many towns were destroyed.
Jerusalem is left alone like a flimsy watchman’s hut in a field after harvest — isolated and vulnerable, surrounded by enemies.

f.g: A poetic name for Jerusalem and its people.
A temporary shelter for a field watchman.

chapters.n: If the Lord had not spared a small remnant, Judah would have been wiped out like Sodom and Gomorrah. The idea of a faithful remnant runs through Isaiah.

f.g: Jehovah of armies — Lord over the hosts of heaven and earth.

chapters.n: The Lord now speaks, shockingly calling Judah’s leaders and people “Sodom” and “Gomorrah” because of their wickedness.

f.g: Hebrew torah — instruction or teaching.

chapters.n: God says He is sick of their many sacrifices. He did not reject sacrifice itself, but sacrifice offered without repentance and righteous living.

f.g: What good is it?

chapters.n: Who asked them to trample through the temple courts with empty worship? Coming to the temple without changed hearts is mere trespassing.

f.g: Trample the temple courtyards.

chapters.n: Stop bringing meaningless offerings. Even holy days and gatherings become offensive when mixed with wickedness.

f.g: Empty, worthless offerings.
I cannot endure or put up with.

chapters.n: God says their festivals have become a burden He is tired of carrying. Ritual without righteousness wearies Him.

f.g: Monthly festivals at the start of each lunar month (Numbers 28:11).

chapters.n: When they raise their hands to pray, God will not listen, because their hands are stained with violence and injustice.

f.g: The ancient posture of prayer, with palms lifted up.

chapters.n: The cure begins here: wash, become clean, and stop doing evil. These verses outline repentance.
Repentance includes actively doing good: seeking justice, helping the oppressed, defending orphans and widows. Religion must reach the vulnerable.

f.g: Defend the cause of the orphan.

chapters.n: One of scripture’s most beloved invitations: the Lord invites His people to come and settle the matter with Him. Even the deepest-stained sins can be made pure through His mercy, which Latter-day Saints understand as the Atonement of Jesus Christ.

f.g: Settle the case together, as in a court.
A deep red dye that was almost impossible to wash out.

chapters.n: Those who are willing and obedient will enjoy the blessings of the land. Both desire and action matter.
But those who refuse and rebel will fall by the sword. The choice and its consequences are theirs.

f.w: the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it

chapters.n: Isaiah laments that Jerusalem, once faithful like a loyal wife, has become unfaithful like a prostitute. Where justice once lived, now there are murderers.

f.g: A common prophetic image for spiritual unfaithfulness to God (Jeremiah 3:1; Hosea 2).

chapters.n: Their silver has become worthless slag and their wine watered down. What was once pure is now corrupted and diluted.

f.g: The impurities skimmed off when refining metal.

chapters.n: Judah’s leaders are rebels who partner with thieves and love bribes. They ignore orphans and widows instead of protecting them.

f.g: Loves bribes.

chapters.n: God, using three solemn titles, announces He will deal with His enemies — here, the wicked among His own people.

f.g: A title echoing Jacob’s blessing (Genesis 49:24).
Get relief from; settle accounts with.

chapters.n: Like a refiner, God will purify Jerusalem, melting away its impurities. His judgment is meant to cleanse, not merely destroy.

f.g: An alloy or impurity mixed with silver.

chapters.n: Afterward God will restore honest judges and counselors, and Jerusalem will again be called the city of righteousness. Latter-day Saints also see a latter-day fulfillment in a redeemed Zion.
Zion will be redeemed through justice, and those who return to God through righteousness.

f.g: Those who return or repent.

chapters.n: But rebels and sinners who abandon the Lord will be destroyed together.
They will be ashamed of the sacred oak groves and gardens where they worshiped idols. Pagan fertility worship was often held in such places.

f.g: Sacred trees used in idol worship (Hosea 4:13).
Put to shame.

chapters.n: The idolaters will become like the very things they trusted — a withering oak and a dried-up garden.
The “strong” who trust in themselves will be like dry kindling, their own deeds the spark that ignites them. Sin carries the seeds of its own destruction.

f.g: Flax fibers that burn instantly.
Better “his work” — his own deeds set him on fire.

chapters.n: A new heading begins Isaiah’s next prophecy (chapters 2–4). Isaiah 2–14 is quoted almost entirely by Nephi in 2 Nephi 12–24, with some meaningful differences.

f.w: The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw

chapters.n: In the last days the Lord’s temple will be raised up like the highest mountain, and people from every nation will stream to it. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in the gathering to temples and in the Salt Lake Temple set among the Rocky Mountains.

f.w: the mountain of the LORD's house
f.g: The temple; mountains were seen as meeting places between God and people (Exodus 19:20).
Stream like a river — but uphill, a miracle of gathering.

chapters.n: People invite one another to go to the Lord’s house to learn His ways and walk in His paths. Latter-day prophets have taught that God’s word will go forth from two centers, Zion and Jerusalem.

f.w: he will teach us of his ways
out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem

chapters.n: When the Lord reigns, He will settle disputes among nations, and people will turn weapons into farming tools. This describes the peace of the Millennium.

f.g: The cutting blades of plows.
Knives for trimming vines.

f.w: neither shall they learn war any more

chapters.n: Isaiah invites his own people, Israel, to walk in God’s light now. 2 Nephi 12:5 adds: “yea, come, for ye have all gone astray, every one to his wicked ways.”

f.w: walk in the light of the LORD

chapters.n: Isaiah turns to present problems: God has let His people go because they have filled the land with eastern fortune-telling and Philistine-style magic and made alliances with foreigners.

f.g: Filled with customs and divination from the east (Syria, Mesopotamia).
Fortune-tellers, diviners — forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10-12.

f.w: please themselves in the children of strangers
f.g: Strike hands (make deals) with foreigners.

chapters.n: Judah has grown wealthy and militarily strong under kings like Uzziah. But the law warned kings not to trust in gold or horses.
Their land is also full of idols. People bow to things their own hands made — the irony Isaiah mocks again later (44:9-20).

f.g: Hebrew elilim — “nothings,” worthless things.

chapters.n: Everyone, common and important alike, bows to idols. The KJV reads that people bow down; 2 Nephi 12:9 reads that the mean man “boweth not down” and the great man “humbleth himself not” — they will not humble themselves before God.

f.g: Common, ordinary person.

chapters.n: Isaiah tells them to hide among the rocks out of fear of the Lord’s glorious majesty. The Book of Mormon version begins, “O ye wicked ones,” making clear who must hide.
Proud human looks will be brought low, and the Lord alone will be lifted up on that day. This refrain repeats in verse 17.

f.g: A phrase pointing to the day of the Lord — His judgment and Second Coming.

chapters.n: The day of the Lord will come against everything proud and lofty. 2 Nephi 12:12 adds that this day “soon cometh upon all nations,” widening its scope.
Even the tallest cedars of Lebanon and the mighty oaks of Bashan — symbols of proud strength — will be humbled.

f.g: Fertile land east of the Sea of Galilee, famous for oaks and cattle.

chapters.n: High mountains and hills, symbols of human pride, will be brought low. 2 Nephi adds “upon all the nations which are lifted up, and upon every people.”
Every tall tower and fortified wall — things people trust for safety — will fall.

f.g: Fortified city wall.

chapters.n: Even great trading ships and beautiful luxury goods will be humbled. 2 Nephi 12:16 reads “upon all the ships of the sea, and upon all the ships of Tarshish” — the first phrase matches the ancient Greek Septuagint, and the second the Hebrew.

f.g: Large ocean-going merchant ships; Tarshish was a distant port, possibly in Spain.
Beautiful crafts or luxury vessels.

chapters.n: The refrain returns: human pride will be bowed down and the Lord alone exalted.

f.w: the LORD alone shall be exalted

chapters.n: God will completely wipe out idols. This short verse stands alone for emphasis.
People will flee into caves and holes in the rocks when the Lord rises to shake the earth. The Second Coming is described with great earthquakes in latter-day scripture.
In that day people will throw their silver and gold idols to the moles and bats — creatures of darkness — because they will see how worthless idols are.

f.w: to the moles and to the bats
f.g: Unclean creatures living in dark holes — the idols are tossed into the dirt.

chapters.n: They will hide in cracks of rocks and on jagged cliffs, terrified of the Lord’s majesty as He shakes the earth.

f.g: Rugged cliffs.

chapters.n: Stop trusting in mere mortals whose life is only a breath. Why rely on someone so fragile instead of God?

f.w: whose breath is in his nostrils

f.g: Valued, esteemed.

chapters.n: The Lord will remove every support Jerusalem leans on — food, water, and leadership. This likely points to sieges and exile, especially the later Babylonian conquest.

f.g: Every kind of support — props and crutches.

chapters.n: Soldiers, judges, prophets, wise people, and elders will all be taken away. When Babylon conquered Judah, it deported its leaders.

f.g: Here, a diviner — someone consulted for guidance.
Elder.

chapters.n: Military officers, nobles, advisers, skilled craftsmen, and speakers will also disappear, leaving society without capable leaders.

f.g: A military officer over fifty men.
Skilled craftsman.

chapters.n: Immature and inexperienced people will rule over them. Without wise leaders, the nation will be governed by the foolish.
Society will break down: neighbors will oppress one another, and the young will disrespect the old, the lowly the honorable.

f.g: Low, worthless person.

chapters.n: Things will be so bad that someone will beg a relative to be ruler just because he still owns a coat. 2 Nephi 13:6 reads “let not this ruin come under thy hand.”

f.w: let this ruin be under thy hand

chapters.n: But the relative will refuse, saying he has no food or clothing and can’t heal the nation’s wounds.

f.g: Literally “binder up” of wounds.

chapters.n: Jerusalem is ruined because its words and deeds defy the Lord, insulting His glorious presence.

f.w: provoke the eyes of his glory
f.g: Defy God openly, right before His face.

chapters.n: Their very faces show their guilt. Like Sodom, they flaunt their sins openly. 2 Nephi 13:9 says “they cannot hide it.”

f.g: Their facial expression; the look on their faces.

chapters.n: Assure the righteous that all will be well with them; they will enjoy the results of their good deeds.

f.w: eat the fruit of their doings

chapters.n: But woe to the wicked; they will receive what their actions deserve. 2 Nephi 13:11 adds plainly, “for they shall perish.”
Immature and weak leaders oppress the people. Those who should guide Israel are leading them astray and hiding the right path.

f.w: they which lead thee cause thee to err

chapters.n: The Lord stands up like a lawyer and a judge to bring His case against the people.

f.g: Argue a legal case.

chapters.n: God puts the elders and princes on trial. They have devoured His vineyard — Israel — and filled their homes with goods stolen from the poor.

f.g: Plunder, stolen goods.

chapters.n: “What do you mean by crushing My people and grinding the faces of the poor?” God takes the abuse of the poor personally.

f.w: grind the faces of the poor
f.g: Crush them as with a millstone — oppress them mercilessly.

chapters.n: God now turns to Jerusalem’s proud upper-class women, who parade with heads held high and flirting eyes, mincing along with jingling ankle bracelets.

f.g: Heads held high in pride.
Walking with small, affected steps.
Ankle bracelets jingling as they walk.

chapters.n: Their pride will be humbled: disease and shame will replace their beauty. Captives were often stripped and shaved.

f.g: Scabs or sores; possibly baldness.
Uncover; expose to shame.

chapters.n: The Lord will strip away their jewelry. Verses 18–23 list about 21 fashion items of the day.

f.g: Finery, splendor.
Headbands or hairnets.
Crescent-shaped ornaments.

chapters.n: Necklaces, bracelets, and veils will be removed.

f.g: Veils.

chapters.n: Headdresses, ankle chains, sashes, perfume bottles, and charms will be taken.

f.g: Headdresses or turbans.
Perfume boxes.
Possibly amulets or charms.

chapters.n: Signet rings and nose rings will be gone.
Fine festival clothing, cloaks, shawls, and purses will be lost.

f.g: Festive robes kept for special occasions.
Shawls.
Purses or handbags.

chapters.n: Even mirrors, fine linen, turbans, and veils will be taken away. Isaiah isn’t condemning beauty but pride and luxury built while the poor suffered.

f.g: Polished metal mirrors.
Linen undergarments.

chapters.n: Everything will be reversed: stench instead of perfume, a rope instead of a sash, baldness instead of styled hair, sackcloth instead of fine robes, branding instead of beauty — the fate of captives.

f.g: A rope, used to lead captives.
A rich robe.
Branding, as was done to slaves.

chapters.n: Their husbands and warriors will die in battle.

f.w: Thy men shall fall by the sword

chapters.n: Jerusalem’s gates — where people once gathered — will mourn, and the city, like a widow, will sit desolate on the ground.

f.g: A posture of mourning (Lamentations 2:10).

chapters.n: This verse concludes chapter 3: so many men will die in war that seven women will beg one man to marry them, not for support but to remove the shame of being unmarried and childless.

f.w: seven women shall take hold of one man

f.g: Disgrace — in Israel, being unmarried or childless was considered a deep shame.

chapters.n: After the judgment, the “branch of the Lord” will flourish in beauty and glory for the survivors of Israel. Many read the Branch as a title for the Messiah, Jesus Christ.

f.g: The survivors; the remnant.

chapters.n: Those who remain in Zion and Jerusalem will be called holy — everyone whose name is recorded among the living. God keeps a record of His people.
This will happen once the Lord has washed away Zion’s moral filth and Jerusalem’s bloodguilt with a cleansing spirit of judgment and burning.

The Lord will place over every home and gathering in Zion a cloud by day and fire by night — like the pillar that guided Israel out of Egypt. His glory will be their canopy. 2 Nephi 14:5 reads “upon all the glory of Zion.”

f.w: a cloud and smoke by day

f.g: A canopy or covering, like a wedding canopy (Hebrew ḥuppah).

chapters.n: It will also be a shelter: shade from the heat and a refuge from storms. Latter-day Saints often link this with the stakes of Zion as places of defense and refuge.

f.g: A booth or shelter.
Hiding place, shelter.

chapters.n: Isaiah begins like a singer at a harvest festival, offering a love song about his friend’s vineyard. The “wellbeloved” is the Lord, and the vineyard is Israel.

f.g: Dear friend; here the Lord Himself.

chapters.n: The owner did everything right: he dug and cleared the land, planted the best vines, built a watchtower and a winepress. But it produced only sour, wild grapes.

f.g: A watchtower to guard against thieves and animals.
Literally “stinking things” — sour, worthless grapes.

chapters.n: Isaiah asks the people of Jerusalem and Judah to judge between the owner and his vineyard — not realizing they are judging themselves.
What more could the owner have done? Why did it produce bad fruit? Compare the Lord of the vineyard’s same question in Zenos’s allegory.

f.w: What could have been done more to my vineyard

chapters.n: So he will remove the hedge and wall, letting animals eat and trample it. Without God’s protection, Israel will be overrun.

f.g: Come now.
A thorny protective fence.

chapters.n: He will let it go wild: no pruning or hoeing, only briers and thorns. He will even command the clouds not to rain on it — showing the owner is God.

f.g: Hoed or cultivated.

chapters.n: The meaning is revealed: the vineyard is Israel and Judah. God looked for justice but found bloodshed, for righteousness but heard cries of the oppressed. In Hebrew these are striking wordplays.

f.g: Wordplay: mishpat (justice) / mispaḥ (bloodshed).
Wordplay: tsedaqah (righteousness) / tse‘aqah (outcry).

chapters.n: The first of six woes: against wealthy landowners who buy up house after house and field after field, pushing out the poor until they live alone in the land.
The Lord swore to Isaiah that these great mansions will stand empty. 2 Nephi 15:9 reads “great and fair cities without inhabitant.”
The land will barely produce: ten acres of vineyard will yield only about six gallons of wine, and planted seed will produce a tenth of what was sown.

f.g: A liquid measure of about 6 gallons (22 liters).
A dry measure, about 10 ephahs — so the harvest is one-tenth of the seed.
Literally “ten yoke” — what ten teams of oxen could plow in a day.

chapters.n: The second woe: against those who start drinking early in the morning and continue late into the night until they are inflamed with wine.

f.g: Beer or other intoxicating beverage.

f.w: Woe unto them that rise up early

chapters.n: Their parties have music and wine, but they pay no attention to what the Lord is doing. Pleasure has made them spiritually blind.

f.g: A stringed instrument like a lyre.
Tambourine or hand drum.

chapters.n: Because they lack knowledge of God, the people will go into captivity. Both nobles and common people will suffer hunger and thirst.
The grave opens its mouth wide to swallow Jerusalem’s proud and partying crowds. Death is pictured as a hungry monster.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the world of the dead.

chapters.n: Both common people and the powerful will be humbled, and the proud brought low.
Through righteous judgment, the Lord will show Himself exalted and holy.

f.g: Shown to be holy.

chapters.n: Lambs will graze in the ruins of the rich, and strangers will eat in the deserted estates. The land grabbed by the greedy returns to pasture.

f.g: The wealthy; or fattened animals.

chapters.n: The third woe: against those who drag their sins along behind them like a cart pulled with ropes. They are bound to their sins and keep hauling them.

f.g: Ropes of falsehood or emptiness.

chapters.n: They mock God’s warnings, daring Him to hurry up and carry out His plan so they can see it. Scoffers often demand proof.
The fourth woe: against those who flip moral values, calling evil good and good evil. This warning feels especially relevant today.

f.w: call evil good, and good evil

chapters.n: The fifth woe: against those who think they are wiser than God.
The sixth woe: against those whose only “heroic” talent is drinking and mixing liquor. Isaiah mocks their false strength.

f.g: Sarcasm — “champions” at drinking.

chapters.n: These same people take bribes to declare the guilty innocent and deny justice to the innocent.
Like fire burning straw, their roots will rot and their blossoms blow away as dust, because they have rejected the Lord’s law and despised His word.

f.g: Dry stalks left in a field after harvest.

chapters.n: The Lord’s anger has struck His people, yet His hand is still stretched out. In context this means continued judgment; Latter-day Saints also find hope in the phrase, since His hand remains extended to those who repent.

f.w: his hand is stretched out still

chapters.n: The Lord will raise a banner for distant nations and whistle for them. Historically this summoned Assyria against Israel; Latter-day Saints also see the ensign as the restored gospel gathering Israel from afar.

f.g: A flag or signal pole raised on a hill to rally people.
Whistle, as a beekeeper or shepherd calls.

chapters.n: Those who come will be tireless, never stumbling, sleeping, or loosening their belts or sandal straps — always ready. Some Latter-day Saints see in this the energy of the latter-day gathering.

f.g: Belt; tightening it meant being ready to move.
Sandal strap.

chapters.n: Their arrows are sharp and bows ready; their horses’ hooves are hard as flint and their chariot wheels spin like a whirlwind.

f.g: Strung and ready to shoot.

chapters.n: They roar like lions seizing prey and carrying it off with no one able to rescue it — a picture of Assyria’s unstoppable armies.
In that day they will roar like the sea, and the land will be covered in darkness and distress, even the sky darkened.

Isaiah describes his call as a prophet. In the year King Uzziah died (around 740 BC), Isaiah saw the Lord enthroned in glory, His robe filling the temple. John later says Isaiah saw the glory of Jesus (John 12:41); Nephi testifies that Isaiah saw the Redeemer.

f.g: The hem or flowing skirts of a royal robe.

chapters.n: Above Him stood seraphim, each with six wings: two to cover their faces in reverence, two to cover their feet in humility, and two to fly in service.

f.g: “Burning ones” — heavenly beings in God’s presence. (Seraphim is already plural; the KJV adds an extra -s.)
Two.

chapters.n: The seraphim call to each other, “Holy, holy, holy” — the strongest way in Hebrew to say God is supremely holy. His glory fills the whole earth.

f.w: the whole earth is full of his glory

chapters.n: The doorframes shook at their voices and the temple filled with smoke — signs of God’s presence, as at Mount Sinai.
Overwhelmed, Isaiah cries out that he is ruined. Seeing God’s holiness makes him painfully aware of his own sins and his people’s.

f.g: Ruined, destroyed; or “silenced.”
Lips stained by sin — fitting for a man called to speak God’s word.

f.w: mine eyes have seen the King

chapters.n: One of the seraphim flies to him holding a burning coal taken from the temple altar with tongs.

f.g: A glowing ember from the altar where sacrifices were offered.

chapters.n: The seraph touches Isaiah’s lips with the coal and declares his guilt removed and his sin forgiven. The coal from the altar of sacrifice points to cleansing through the Savior’s Atonement.

f.g: Hebrew kipper — atoned for, covered.

chapters.n: Now cleansed, Isaiah hears the Lord ask who will go as His messenger. Isaiah volunteers immediately: “Here am I; send me” — echoing the premortal Savior’s words in the Council in Heaven.

f.g: “Us” suggests the heavenly council (compare Genesis 1:26).

chapters.n: God warns Isaiah that many will hear but not understand, see but not perceive. Jesus quoted this to explain why He taught in parables. 2 Nephi 16:9 reads “but they understood not … but they perceived not,” describing the people rather than commanding them.

f.w: Hear ye indeed, but understand not

chapters.n: This is ironic: Isaiah’s preaching will make hard hearts harder, because the people refuse to listen. God isn’t wishing them unhealed; He is describing what rejection of His word will do.

f.w: Make the heart of this people fat
f.g: Make it dull and insensitive.

chapters.n: Isaiah asks how long this will last. The answer: until the cities are ruined and the land desolate — fulfilled in the Assyrian and Babylonian conquests.
The people will be carried far away into exile, and the land left largely abandoned.
Yet a tenth will remain. Like a felled tree whose stump still lives, Israel will be cut down, but a “holy seed” — a righteous remnant — will sprout again.

f.g: A terebinth, a large tree that can sprout again from its stump.
A small remnant.

chapters.n: Around 734 BC, the kings of Syria (Aram) and northern Israel joined forces to attack Jerusalem, wanting to force Judah into their alliance against Assyria. This is called the Syro-Ephraimite War.

f.g: King of Aram (Syria), capital at Damascus.

chapters.n: When the royal family heard that Syria had allied with Israel, King Ahaz and his people trembled like trees shaking in the wind.

f.g: The leading tribe of the northern kingdom; a name for the whole kingdom of Israel.
Allied.

chapters.n: The Lord sends Isaiah to meet Ahaz at the water channel outside the city, where the king was likely inspecting Jerusalem’s water supply for the siege. Isaiah brings his son, whose name is itself a message.

f.g: “A remnant shall return” — a name of both warning and hope.
Where cloth was washed and bleached.

chapters.n: Isaiah tells Ahaz to stay calm and not fear these two kings, who are just smoldering stubs of firewood — almost burned out.

f.g: Charred sticks with only smoke left — enemies nearly finished.

chapters.n: Syria and Israel have plotted against Judah.

f.g: A wicked plan.

chapters.n: Their plan: invade Judah, break it open, and set up a puppet king, the son of Tabeal, in place of David’s line.

f.g: Terrify or harass.
An otherwise unknown man, likely an Aramean ally.

chapters.n: The Lord declares their plan will fail.

These kingdoms are led only by men — Damascus by Rezin. Within sixty-five years, Ephraim will be shattered as a people. Assyria conquered Samaria in 722 BC, and later resettlement completed Israel’s scattering.

f.g: Sixty-five years.

chapters.n: Samaria is led by Pekah, mere “Remaliah’s son.” Isaiah’s challenge to Ahaz: if you do not stand firm in faith, you will not stand at all — a Hebrew wordplay.

f.w: If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established
f.g: Wordplay on the Hebrew root ’aman (believe/be firm): “No firm faith, no firm footing.”

chapters.n: The Lord speaks again to Ahaz through Isaiah.
God generously invites Ahaz to ask for any sign at all, as deep as the underworld or as high as heaven, to strengthen his faith.

f.w: in the depth, or in the height
f.g: Anything from the depths below to the heavens above.

chapters.n: Ahaz refuses, sounding pious: he won’t “test” God. But he had already decided to seek help from Assyria instead of trusting the Lord.

f.g: Test.

chapters.n: Isaiah rebukes the royal house: is it not enough to try the patience of people? Must they try God’s patience too?

f.g: The royal dynasty — the prophecy concerns David’s line.

chapters.n: So the Lord will give a sign Himself: a young woman — a virgin — will conceive and bear a son named Immanuel, “God with us.” It had meaning in Ahaz’s day, and Matthew declares its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, born of the virgin Mary.

f.g: Hebrew ‘almah — a young woman of marriageable age; the Greek Septuagint reads parthenos, “virgin.”
“God is with us.”

chapters.n: The child will eat curds and honey — simple food of a land returned to pasture — by the time he is old enough to know right from wrong.

f.g: Curds or thick yogurt.

chapters.n: Before the child is old enough to choose good over evil, the two kings Ahaz fears will be gone. Assyria killed Rezin around 732 BC, and Pekah was assassinated about the same time.
But because Ahaz trusted Assyria rather than God, the Lord will bring Assyria itself upon Judah — the worst days since the kingdom split after Solomon.
The Lord will whistle for Egypt’s armies like flies and Assyria’s like bees. Judah would be caught between these two superpowers.

f.g: Whistle or call.

chapters.n: These invaders will swarm everywhere — in valleys, rock crevices, thornbushes, and pastures. No place will be untouched.
The Lord will use Assyria, the “razor” Ahaz himself hired, to shave Judah completely — head, beard, and body. Shaving a man was a deep humiliation.

f.g: Ahaz paid Assyria for help (2 Kings 16:8); now that hired razor will turn on Judah.
East of the Euphrates — Assyria.

chapters.n: So few people will be left that a man will keep only one young cow and two sheep.
With so few people, the animals will give plenty of milk, and survivors will live on curds and wild honey — the simple diet of an empty land.
Rich vineyards worth a fortune will be overgrown with briers and thorns.

f.g: Shekels of silver — a thousand vines worth a thousand shekels.

chapters.n: The land will become so wild that people will go there only to hunt with bows and arrows.
Even hillsides once carefully hoed will become pasture for cattle and sheep because no one will farm them.

f.g: A digging tool like a hoe or pickaxe.
Sheep and goats.

chapters.n: The Lord tells Isaiah to write a strange name in large, ordinary letters on a big tablet, so everyone could read it publicly. The name is a prophecy in itself.

f.g: A large tablet or writing surface.
Ordinary, common lettering anyone could read.
“Swift is the spoil, speedy is the plunder.”

chapters.n: Isaiah calls two reliable witnesses to confirm the writing, so that when the prophecy came true no one could say it was written afterward.
Isaiah’s wife, called “the prophetess,” gives birth to a son, and God tells Isaiah to give him that same name.

f.g: Isaiah’s wife — possibly a prophetess herself, or so called as a prophet’s wife.

chapters.n: Before the baby can say “Daddy” or “Mommy,” Assyria will plunder Damascus and Samaria. Damascus fell in 732 BC, and much of northern Israel was stripped soon after.
The Lord speaks to Isaiah again.
The people have rejected the gentle, quiet waters of Shiloah — Jerusalem’s small water channel, a picture of God’s quiet care — and instead delight in the two invading kings.

f.g: A gently flowing channel feeding Jerusalem’s pool (later Siloam, John 9:7).
Flow gently.

chapters.n: So instead of a gentle stream, God will bring the mighty flood of “the river” — the Euphrates, meaning Assyria — overflowing all its banks.

f.g: The Euphrates, the great river of Mesopotamia.

chapters.n: The Assyrian flood will sweep through Judah up to the neck — nearly drowning it, but not quite. Its outspread wings cover the land of Immanuel, reminding that God is still with His people.

f.g: Assyria nearly took Judah but stopped at Jerusalem (Isaiah 36–37).

chapters.n: Isaiah taunts the nations: band together and arm yourselves if you like — you will still be shattered. The triple repetition makes it certain.

f.g: Prepare for battle.

chapters.n: Make your plans, give your orders; they will fail, “for God is with us” — which in Hebrew is “Immanuel.”

f.g: Hebrew ‘immanu ’el — the name Immanuel.

chapters.n: The Lord gripped Isaiah firmly and warned him not to follow the fearful ways of the people around him.

f.g: With powerful inspiration; urgently.

chapters.n: Don’t call everything a conspiracy as the frightened people do, and don’t share their panic.

f.g: Conspiracy or political alliance.

chapters.n: Instead, treat the Lord as holy. He alone should be the one you reverence and fear — not kings or armies.

f.w: Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself

chapters.n: To those who trust Him, the Lord will be a sanctuary. To those who reject Him, He will be a stone they trip over. The New Testament applies this to Jesus Christ.

f.g: A trap or snare.

chapters.n: Many will trip on that stone and fall, be broken, and be caught.
Isaiah is told to tie up and seal his testimony and teaching among his disciples, preserving it for a later time when it will be needed.

f.w: Bind up the testimony, seal the law

chapters.n: Isaiah will wait patiently for the Lord and hope in Him, even while God seems to hide His face from Israel.
Isaiah and his children, with their symbolic names, are living signs from God to Israel. Hebrews applies this verse to Christ and His followers.

f.w: I and the children whom the LORD hath given me

chapters.n: When people urge you to consult mediums and fortune-tellers who whisper and mutter, ask: shouldn’t a people seek their God? Why ask the dead about the living? 2 Nephi 18:19 reads “for the living to hear from the dead?”

f.g: Spirits of the dead supposedly contacted by mediums (Leviticus 19:31).
Chirp, whisper — imitating spirit voices.

f.w: for the living to the dead?

chapters.n: Turn to God’s law and testimony. Anyone whose words don’t agree with them has no light — no truth or dawn — in them.

f.w: To the law and to the testimony

f.g: Literally “no dawn” — no hope ahead.

chapters.n: Those who reject God will wander the land distressed and starving. In anger they will curse their king and their God, looking up for help that does not come.

f.g: Hard-pressed, in great distress.
Become enraged.

chapters.n: Looking down at the earth, they will see only trouble and gloom and be thrust into darkness. Chapter 9 answers this darkness with a great light.
The gloom will not last. The northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali around Galilee, the first conquered by Assyria (732 BC), will later be honored. 2 Nephi 19:1 reads “by the way of the Red Sea.”

f.g: “Circle of the Gentiles” — a region with many non-Israelites.

f.w: by the way of the sea

chapters.n: People walking in darkness see a great light. Matthew tells us this was fulfilled when Jesus began His ministry in Galilee.

f.w: The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light

f.g: Deep darkness.

chapters.n: God has made the nation grow and filled it with joy like harvest festivals or soldiers dividing the spoils of victory. KJV reads “not increased the joy,” but 2 Nephi 19:3 reads “and increased the joy,” which fits the context and an alternate Hebrew reading.

f.g: The Hebrew lo can mean “not” or (spelled differently) “to it”; many modern translations agree with the Book of Mormon.

chapters.n: God has broken the yoke and rod of the oppressor, just as He did when Gideon’s small band defeated Midian. The Book of Mormon version omits “as in the day of Midian.”

f.g: A wooden bar on the neck of a work animal — a symbol of slavery.

chapters.n: Every soldier’s boot and blood-soaked garment will be burned as fuel. War itself will end.

f.g: Better “the boot of the tramping warrior.”

chapters.n: The heart of the chapter: a child will be born who will rule, with names describing His divine nature. Christians, including Latter-day Saints, see this fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

f.w: unto us a child is born

f.g: Possibly one title: “Wonderful Counselor” — a planner of marvels.

chapters.n: His rule and peace will keep growing without end. He will reign on David’s throne with justice forever, and the Lord’s zeal will make it happen.

f.g: Passionate commitment.

chapters.n: Isaiah returns to the present: the Lord has sent a message of judgment against Jacob, and it has landed on Israel — the northern kingdom.

f.g: Here the northern kingdom of Israel.

chapters.n: All Ephraim and Samaria will learn, even though they speak in proud defiance.

f.g: Arrogance, stubbornness.

chapters.n: They boast: “The bricks fell? We’ll rebuild with stone. The cheap sycamores were cut down? We’ll replace them with cedar.” They refuse to see disaster as a call to repent.

f.g: Common fig-mulberry trees, used for cheap lumber.
Expensive cut stone.

chapters.n: So the Lord will raise up Rezin’s enemies against Israel and stir up its foes.
Syria from the east and the Philistines from the west will devour Israel. Yet God’s anger isn’t finished, and His hand remains stretched out — a refrain repeated four times.

f.w: his hand is stretched out still

chapters.n: Despite being struck, the people still don’t turn back to the God who disciplines them.
So the Lord will cut off Israel’s leaders and followers alike in a single day — head and tail, palm branch and reed.

f.g: Palm branch and reed — the high and the low.

chapters.n: The “head” is the elders and nobles; the “tail” is the false prophets who teach lies.
The leaders mislead the people, and those who follow them are ruined.
So wicked has the nation become that even its young men, orphans, and widows — usually objects of God’s special mercy — are caught up in hypocrisy and foolish speech. Still His hand is stretched out.

f.g: Godless or profane person.

chapters.n: Wickedness itself spreads like a wildfire through brush and forest, rising in clouds of smoke. Sin destroys from within.
Under God’s judgment the land is scorched, the people become fuel for the fire, and no one spares even his brother.
In a famine of the soul and body, people grab on every side but are never satisfied, and turn on one another — even their own kin.

f.w: the flesh of his own arm
f.g: Perhaps “his neighbor” — they devour their own people.

chapters.n: Brother tribes Manasseh and Ephraim fight each other, then unite only to attack Judah. Civil war tore Israel apart in its final years. Still His hand is stretched out.

f.g: The two tribes descended from Joseph’s sons (Genesis 48).

chapters.n: This verse completes the woes of chapter 9: woe to lawmakers who write unjust laws and officials who issue oppressive rulings.

f.g: Oppression, trouble.

chapters.n: Their laws deny justice to the needy, rob the poor of their rights, and make widows and orphans their prey. God watches over the vulnerable.

f.w: turn aside the needy from judgment

chapters.n: What will they do when God comes to judge and disaster arrives from afar? Where will they run and where will they hide their riches?

f.g: The day God comes to judge.
Wealth or honor.

chapters.n: Without God, they will crouch among prisoners or fall among the dead. And still His hand is stretched out — the fourth and final time this refrain appears.

f.w: his hand is stretched out still

chapters.n: Now God addresses Assyria as His “rod” — a tool He uses to discipline His people. 2 Nephi 20:5 reads “their indignation.”

f.g: The empire based in northern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), dominant from about 745 to 612 BC.

chapters.n: God sends Assyria against godless Israel to plunder it and trample it like mud in the streets.

f.g: Godless, profane.
Mud.

chapters.n: But Assyria doesn’t know it is God’s tool. Its king only wants to conquer and destroy as many nations as possible.
The Assyrian king boasts that even his commanders are as great as kings. Assyrian rulers called themselves “king of kings.”
He lists cities he has conquered — Calno, Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad, Damascus, Samaria — all fell to Assyria in the 700s BC. Jerusalem, he thinks, will be next.

f.g: A major city on the Euphrates, taken by Assyria in 717 BC.
A Syrian city on the Orontes River, conquered 738 and 720 BC.

chapters.n: He reasons that he has defeated kingdoms with even more impressive idols than Jerusalem’s or Samaria’s. 2 Nephi 20:10 reads “hath founded.”

f.g: Carved idols.

chapters.n: Since he destroyed Samaria and its idols, he’s sure he can do the same to Jerusalem. He thinks the Lord is just another idol.

f.w: as I have done unto Samaria

chapters.n: But once the Lord finishes using Assyria to discipline Jerusalem, He will punish the proud Assyrian king for his arrogance.

f.g: Proud, arrogant heart.

chapters.n: The king boasts that his own strength and cleverness did it all. He erased borders, stole treasures, and toppled kings.

f.w: By the strength of my hand

f.g: Erased national borders — Assyria deported whole populations.

chapters.n: He bragged that he gathered the nations’ wealth as easily as a boy collecting eggs from an abandoned nest — no one even flapped a wing or chirped.

f.g: Chirped.

chapters.n: Can an axe brag against the person who swings it? Assyria is only a tool in God’s hand, yet acts as if it were in charge.
So the Lord will send a wasting disease among Assyria’s strong warriors and kindle a fire under its glory.

f.g: Stout, well-fed warriors.
Wasting sickness.

chapters.n: Israel’s Light — the Lord — will become a fire, and the Holy One a flame, burning Assyria’s army like thorns and briers in a single day. This was fulfilled when 185,000 Assyrians died in one night.
The splendor of Assyria’s “forest” and “fields” — its armies and power — will be wiped out completely, like a sick man wasting away.

f.g: Possibly “as when a sick man wastes away.”

chapters.n: So few “trees” will be left that a child could count and write them down.
In that day the surviving remnant of Israel will no longer lean on Assyria, who struck them, but will lean truly on the Lord, the Holy One of Israel.

f.g: Lean on; rely on.

chapters.n: A remnant will return to the mighty God. This echoes the name of Isaiah’s son Shear-jashub and the title “mighty God” in 9:6.
Though Israel be as many as the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return. The destruction is decreed, but it will overflow with righteousness — justice and redemption together.

f.w: as the sand of the sea

f.g: Complete destruction; a full end.

chapters.n: The Lord has decided to bring this destruction across the land.

f.g: Decided, decreed.

chapters.n: Therefore God tells His people in Zion not to fear Assyria. It will strike them, as Egypt once oppressed Israel, but not forever.

f.w: be not afraid of the Assyrian

chapters.n: In a very short while God’s anger toward His people will end and turn against their destroyers.
The Lord will lash Assyria as He did Midian at the rock of Oreb, and raise His rod over the sea as He did at the Red Sea for Moses.

f.w: his rod was upon the sea

chapters.n: In that day Assyria’s burden will fall from their shoulders and its yoke from their necks. The yoke will break “because of the anointing” — Latter-day Saints and others see a hint of the Anointed One, the Messiah.

f.g: Hebrew obscure — possibly “because of fatness” (the ox grows too strong for the yoke) or “because of the oil.”

f.w: his yoke from off thy neck

chapters.n: Isaiah pictures an army marching south toward Jerusalem through towns just north of the city — Aiath, Migron, Michmash — where it stores its baggage.

f.g: Ai, about 10 miles north of Jerusalem.
Baggage, supplies.

chapters.n: They cross the ravine pass and camp at Geba. Nearby Ramah trembles and Gibeah, Saul’s hometown, flees. 2 Nephi 20:29 spells it “Ramath.”

f.g: The pass at Michmash.

chapters.n: The villages cry out in alarm — Gallim, Laish, and poor Anathoth, later Jeremiah’s hometown.
Madmenah’s people flee and Gebim’s residents run for safety.

f.g: Fled.

chapters.n: The invader halts at Nob, within sight of Jerusalem, and shakes his fist at Mount Zion. But that is as far as he gets.

f.g: A town on a hill overlooking Jerusalem (1 Samuel 21:1).
Make a threatening gesture.

chapters.n: Then the Lord, like a forester, will lop off the branches with terrifying power and cut down the tallest trees — the proud Assyrian leaders.

f.g: Cut off the branches.

chapters.n: He will chop down the thickets with an axe, and mighty Lebanon — Assyria’s forest-like army — will fall to the Mighty One. Chapter 11 then contrasts this with a new shoot sprouting from Jesse’s stump.

After the proud “forest” of Assyria is cut down (10:33-34), a new shoot will sprout from the stump of Jesse, King David’s father. D&C 113 explains that the “stem of Jesse” is Christ and the “rod” is a servant in His hands, a descendant of Jesse and Ephraim. Moroni quoted this chapter to Joseph Smith, saying it was about to be fulfilled.

f.g: A shoot or twig sprouting from a stump.

chapters.n: The Spirit of the Lord will rest on Him, giving perfect wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, and reverence for God. This describes the Messiah’s divine endowment.

f.w: the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him

f.g: Reverent awe and devotion toward God.

chapters.n: He will delight in revering the Lord. He won’t judge by appearances or rumors, but will see the truth of every heart.

f.g: Literally “his delight” or “his scent” — keen discernment.

f.w: not judge after the sight of his eyes

chapters.n: He will judge the poor fairly and defend the humble. His word alone will strike the earth, and His breath will destroy the wicked — fulfilled fully at His Second Coming.

f.g: Fairness.

chapters.n: Righteousness and faithfulness will be like the belt He wears — always part of who He is, wrapped around Him.

f.g: Waist or inner being.
Belt — what holds a person ready for action.

chapters.n: A famous picture of millennial peace: predators and prey live together, and a little child can lead them. The enmity in nature will end.

f.w: The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb

f.g: Young goat.
A fattened calf.

chapters.n: Cows and bears will graze together, their young lying side by side, and lions will eat straw like oxen. Even animal nature will change.

f.w: the lion shall eat straw like the ox

chapters.n: A nursing baby will play safely near a cobra’s hole, and a toddler will reach into a viper’s nest unharmed.

f.g: A cobra.
An old word for a poisonous snake, perhaps a viper.

chapters.n: Nothing will harm or destroy in God’s holy mountain, because the earth will be filled with knowledge of the Lord as water fills the sea.

f.w: the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD

chapters.n: In that day the “root of Jesse” will stand as a banner for the peoples, and the Gentiles will seek Him. D&C 113:5-6 identifies this root as a latter-day descendant of Jesse and Joseph holding priesthood keys; Paul applies the verse to Christ.

f.g: A banner or rallying flag.
His resting place or dwelling.

chapters.n: The Lord will reach out a second time to gather His scattered people from every land. The first great gathering was the return from Babylon; Latter-day Saints see the second as the latter-day gathering begun with the Restoration.

f.g: Upper (southern) Egypt.
Ethiopia/Nubia, south of Egypt.
Babylonia (Genesis 11:2).

chapters.n: He will raise a banner to the nations and gather the outcasts of Israel and the scattered of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
The old rivalry between Ephraim (the northern tribes) and Judah will end. They will no longer be jealous of or hostile toward each other — a hope for unity in the gathered house of Israel.
United, Israel will swoop down on its old enemies — the Philistines to the west, and peoples to the east like Edom, Moab, and Ammon. The imagery is of triumph, not literal conquest today.

f.g: Neighbors southeast and east of the Dead Sea, longtime foes of Israel.

chapters.n: The Lord will dry up the gulf of the Egyptian sea and divide the great river into seven streams so His people can cross on foot — a new Exodus.

f.w: the tongue of the Egyptian sea
f.g: The Gulf of Suez, an arm of the Red Sea.
The Euphrates.
With dry sandals — without getting wet.

chapters.n: There will be a highway for the returning remnant from Assyria, just as there was when Israel came out of Egypt. God’s past deliverances promise future ones.
This short chapter is a hymn the gathered people will sing “in that day.” Though the Lord was angry, His anger has turned to comfort — the pattern of discipline followed by mercy.

God is my salvation; I will trust Him and not be afraid. The Lord Jehovah is my strength and my song. These words echo Moses’ song after crossing the Red Sea. Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah as the premortal Jesus Christ.

f.w: the LORD JEHOVAH is my strength and my song

f.g: Hebrew yeshu‘ah — closely related to the name Jesus (Yeshua).

chapters.n: With joy they will draw water from the wells of salvation. At the Feast of Tabernacles, water was poured out at the temple, and Jesus there offered “living water.”
Then they will praise the Lord, call on His name, and tell the nations what He has done. Gratitude naturally leads to sharing.

f.w: declare his doings among the people

chapters.n: Sing to the Lord, for He has done wonderful things known throughout the earth.
People of Zion are told to shout for joy, because the great Holy One of Israel lives among them. The chapter closes the Book of Mormon’s first long Isaiah section (2 Nephi 12–22).

f.w: Holy One of Israel in the midst of thee

chapters.n: A new section (chapters 13–23) contains “burdens” — prophecies against foreign nations. It begins with Babylon, which in Isaiah’s day was still under Assyria but would later conquer Judah. In latter-day scripture Babylon also symbolizes the wicked world.

f.g: Hebrew massa’ — a heavy message or oracle, usually of judgment.

chapters.n: Raise a signal flag on a bare hill, shout, and wave the troops forward to storm the gates of Babylon’s nobles.

f.g: Wave the hand as a signal.

chapters.n: God has summoned His “sanctified ones” — warriors set apart for His purpose — to carry out His judgment. 2 Nephi 23:3 reads “for mine anger is not upon them that rejoice in my highness,” assuring the faithful they are not the target.

f.g: Those consecrated for a task — here, soldiers set apart for holy war.

f.w: even them that rejoice in my highness

chapters.n: A roar rises from the mountains — the noise of nations gathering. The Lord of hosts is mustering an army.

f.g: Assembles and inspects troops.

chapters.n: They come from far away, from the ends of the earth — the Lord and the weapons of His wrath — to destroy the whole land.

f.g: The far horizon.

chapters.n: Wail, for the day of the Lord is near, coming as destruction from the Almighty. In Hebrew, “destruction” (shod) and “Almighty” (Shaddai) sound alike.

f.w: the day of the LORD is at hand

f.g: Hebrew Shaddai.

chapters.n: Everyone’s hands will go limp and every heart melt in fear.
Terror and anguish will grip them like a woman in labor. They will stare at each other in shock, faces burning. 2 Nephi 23:8 omits the comparison to a woman in labor.

f.g: Stunned, astonished.

chapters.n: The day of the Lord comes with fierce anger to make the land desolate and remove the sinners from it.

f.w: the day of the LORD cometh

chapters.n: Stars, sun, and moon will go dark. These cosmic signs describe Babylon’s fall and also the signs before the Second Coming.

f.g: Literally “Orions” — the great star patterns.

chapters.n: God will punish the world for its evil and end the arrogance of the proud and ruthless.
So many will die that people will be rarer than the purest gold of Ophir.

f.g: A distant land famous for fine gold (1 Kings 9:28).
Ingot or bar.

chapters.n: The heavens will tremble and the earth shake from its place in the Lord’s fierce anger.
Foreigners in Babylon will scatter like a hunted gazelle or sheep without a shepherd, each fleeing to his own land.

f.g: A hunted gazelle.

chapters.n: Anyone caught will be killed. 2 Nephi 23:15 reads “Every one that is proud … every one that is joined to the wicked,” focusing judgment on the wicked.

f.g: Stabbed, pierced.

chapters.n: Isaiah describes the horrors of ancient conquest: children killed, houses plundered, women violated. War’s cruelty is the bitter harvest of Babylon’s own violence.

f.g: Plundered.

chapters.n: God will stir up the Medes, who cannot be bribed with silver or gold. The Medes and Persians conquered Babylon in 539 BC.

f.g: A people of ancient Iran, allied with Persia under Cyrus.

chapters.n: Their archers will be merciless, sparing not even the young.

f.g: Children.

chapters.n: Babylon — the jewel of kingdoms and pride of the Chaldeans — will be overthrown as completely as Sodom and Gomorrah.

f.g: Chaldeans, the people who ruled Babylon in its last great era.

chapters.n: It will never again be inhabited; even nomads and shepherds will avoid it. Babylon declined over centuries and today lies in ruins in Iraq.
Desert animals will live in its ruins — howling creatures, owls, and wild goats dancing among the rubble.

f.g: Howling animals, perhaps jackals.
Wild goats, or goat-demons of folklore.

chapters.n: Hyenas and jackals will howl in its palaces. Babylon’s time is near. 2 Nephi 23:22 adds: “For I will destroy her speedily; yea, for I will be merciful unto my people, but the wicked shall perish.”

f.g: Jackals.

f.w: her days shall not be prolonged

chapters.n: After Babylon’s fall, the Lord will again show mercy to Israel, bring them back to their land, and foreigners will join them. This was partly fulfilled in the return from exile and points to the latter-day gathering.

f.w: the strangers shall be joined with them

chapters.n: Other nations will help bring Israel home, and the former captives will rule over their oppressors. 2 Nephi 24:2 adds “yea, from far unto the ends of the earth; and they shall return to their lands of promise,” widening it to a worldwide gathering.

f.g: Female servants.

chapters.n: When the Lord gives Israel rest from sorrow, fear, and hard slavery…
…they will sing a mocking song against the king of Babylon: “How the oppressor has stopped! The golden city is finished!”

f.g: Hebrew mashal — here a taunt-song.
Possibly “insolent fury”; the Hebrew word is uncertain.

chapters.n: The Lord has broken the club and scepter of wicked rulers.

f.g: A ruler’s staff, symbol of authority.

chapters.n: The tyrant who struck nations with endless blows and ruled in rage is now chased down himself, and no one comes to his rescue.

f.g: No one holds back his attackers.

chapters.n: With the tyrant gone, the whole earth rests in peace and bursts into song.
Even the trees celebrate! Since the king fell, no woodcutter comes to chop down Lebanon’s forests. Mesopotamian kings boasted of cutting cedars for their palaces.

f.g: Woodcutter.

chapters.n: The underworld is stirred to meet him. The ghosts of dead kings rise from their thrones to greet the newcomer.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the realm of the dead.
Literally “he-goats” — leaders of the flock.

chapters.n: They mock him: “So now you’re as weak as we are!” Death levels all human power.
His splendor and music have gone down to the grave. Maggots are his mattress and worms his blanket.

f.g: Harps or stringed instruments.

chapters.n: The famous lament: “How you have fallen from heaven, shining one, son of the dawn!” Though aimed at Babylon’s king, Latter-day Saints, with scripture, see here the fall of Satan, who rebelled in the premortal world.

f.g: Latin “light-bearer,” translating Hebrew helel — “shining one,” the morning star.

f.w: How art thou fallen from heaven

chapters.n: He said in his heart, “I will climb to heaven and set my throne above God’s stars, on the mountain where the gods assemble.” The repeated “I will” shows his pride.

f.g: The mountain of assembly — in ancient myths, where the gods met.
The far north, the legendary divine mountain.

chapters.n: “I will rise above the clouds; I will be like the Most High.” Lucifer sought God’s honor and power for himself.

f.w: I will be like the most High

chapters.n: Instead, he will be brought down to the depths of the pit. Pride leads to the lowest fall.

f.g: The deepest part of the grave or underworld.

chapters.n: People will stare at him and ask, “Is this the one who shook the earth and made kingdoms tremble?”

f.g: Stare intently.

chapters.n: “Is this the one who turned the world into a wasteland, destroyed cities, and never let his prisoners go home?”

f.w: opened not the house of his prisoners
f.g: Never released captives — Babylon held Judah captive.

chapters.n: Other kings rest in honor, each in his own grand tomb.
But this king is thrown out of his grave like a rejected branch, covered with the slain, trampled like a corpse. Being unburied was the ultimate disgrace.

f.g: A loathed, rejected shoot.

f.w: the raiment of those that are slain

chapters.n: He will not be buried with other kings, because he ruined his own land and killed his own people. His descendants will never be honored.
His sons will be killed for their fathers’ sins, so that they never rise to rule and fill the earth with cities again.
The Lord declares He will cut off Babylon’s name, survivors, and descendants.

f.g: Descendant, posterity.

chapters.n: Babylon will become a swamp for wild birds, swept away by God’s broom of destruction.

f.g: A marsh bird, or possibly a hedgehog.
A broom.

chapters.n: The Lord has sworn an oath: what He has planned will certainly happen.

f.w: as I have purposed, so shall it stand

chapters.n: He will crush Assyria in His own land and on His mountains. This happened when Sennacherib’s army was destroyed outside Jerusalem (701 BC). 2 Nephi 24:25 reads “bring the Assyrian.”
This is God’s plan for the whole earth, and His hand is stretched out over every nation.
Who can cancel what the Lord has decided? Who can turn back His outstretched hand? No one.

f.g: Cancel or annul.

chapters.n: This prophecy came in the year King Ahaz died, about 715 BC.
Don’t celebrate, Philistia, that the rod that struck you is broken. From the snake’s root will come a worse viper — a fiery, flying serpent. A new oppressor will rise.

f.g: Philistia, the coastal land of the Philistines.
A venomous snake.
Perhaps a swift, deadly snake; an image of a fierce enemy.

chapters.n: The poorest of God’s people will graze safely, but Philistia’s root will die by famine and its survivors be killed.

f.g: The poorest of the poor.

chapters.n: Wail, Philistine city gates! Smoke rises from the north — an invading army whose soldiers march in perfect order, no straggler among them.

f.g: Melted in fear.

f.w: none shall be alone in his appointed times
f.g: No soldier falls out of the ranks.

chapters.n: What answer should be given to foreign messengers? That the Lord has founded Zion, and His humble people will find refuge there. 2 Nephi 24 ends Nephi’s long Isaiah quotation here.
A prophecy about Moab, Israel’s neighbor east of the Dead Sea, descended from Abraham’s nephew Lot. Its major cities, Ar and Kir, are destroyed overnight and fall silent.

f.g: A main city near the Arnon River (Numbers 21:28).
Probably Kir-hareseth, Moab’s fortified capital (modern Kerak).

chapters.n: Moabites go up to their temples and high places at Dibon to weep, and wail over Nebo and Medeba. Shaved heads and cut beards were signs of deep mourning.

f.g: “The house” — likely a temple of Chemosh, Moab’s god.
A Moabite city where the famous Mesha Stele was found.
A town near the mountain where Moses viewed the promised land (Deuteronomy 34:1).

chapters.n: People wear sackcloth in the streets and wail on their flat rooftops, weeping uncontrollably.

f.g: Rough goat-hair cloth worn in mourning.
Flat roofs, used as living and worship spaces.

chapters.n: Cries from Heshbon and Elealeh are heard as far as Jahaz. Even Moab’s soldiers cry out, their spirits broken.

f.g: A city north of Moab, once the Amorite capital (Numbers 21:26).

f.w: his life shall be grievous unto him
f.g: His soul trembles within him.

chapters.n: Isaiah himself grieves for Moab, showing God’s compassion even for Israel’s enemies. Refugees flee south toward Zoar, weeping up the slope of Luhith and crying along the road to Horonaim.

f.w: My heart shall cry out for Moab

f.g: A town at the south end of the Dead Sea (Genesis 19:22).

f.w: an heifer of three years old
f.g: Possibly a place name, Eglath-shelishiyah.

chapters.n: The springs of Nimrim have dried up; grass withers and nothing green remains. Even the land mourns.

f.g: A stream or oasis in southern Moab.

chapters.n: Fleeing families carry whatever wealth they can across the Brook of the Willows, Moab’s southern border.

f.g: Probably the Zered valley, Moab’s border with Edom.

chapters.n: The wailing spreads to every border of Moab, reaching Eglaim and Beer-elim.

f.g: “Well of the mighty ones” (compare Numbers 21:16-18).

chapters.n: The waters of Dimon run red with blood, and even more trouble is coming — lions will attack those who escape. “Dimon” sounds like the Hebrew word for blood (dam).

f.g: Likely Dibon, spelled to make a wordplay with dam, “blood.”

chapters.n: Moab is urged to send lambs as tribute to Judah’s king in Zion, as Moab once paid Israel in lambs. Submitting to David’s throne is Moab’s path to safety.

f.g: “Rock” — a stronghold in Edom, possibly later Petra.

chapters.n: Moab’s women, like baby birds pushed from the nest, flutter helplessly at the river crossings of the Arnon.

f.g: Crossings of the Arnon River, Moab’s northern border.

chapters.n: Moab’s refugees plead with Judah: give us advice and fairness; shelter us like shade at noon; hide the fugitives and don’t betray them.

f.g: Betray, reveal.

f.w: make thy shadow as the night
f.g: Provide deep shade — protection.

chapters.n: Let Moab’s outcasts stay with you; shelter them from the destroyer. When the oppressor is gone, peace will come.

f.g: Hiding place, shelter.
Oppressor.

chapters.n: Then a throne will be set up in mercy. A faithful ruler from David’s house will judge justly and quickly do what is right — a picture fully realized in the Messiah.

f.w: in mercy shall the throne be established

chapters.n: But Judah has heard of Moab’s great pride, arrogance, and anger. Its boasting is empty.

f.w: his lies shall not be so
f.g: His idle boasts amount to nothing.

chapters.n: So Moab will wail for itself, mourning the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth, now gone.

f.g: Possibly “raisin cakes,” a delicacy of the region.
Moab’s capital city.

chapters.n: The fields of Heshbon and the famous vines of Sibmah, which once spread to Jazer and the desert and even toward the sea, have been trampled by foreign rulers.

f.g: A town famed for its vineyards.
Rulers of the nations — the invaders.

chapters.n: Isaiah weeps with the people of Jazer for the vines of Sibmah and drenches Heshbon and Elealeh with his tears. The joyful shouts of harvest have stopped.

f.w: I will water thee with my tears

chapters.n: Joy and gladness are gone from the orchards; no one sings in the vineyards or treads grapes in the winepress. God has silenced the harvest songs.

f.g: People who crushed grapes with their feet.

chapters.n: Isaiah’s heart throbs like a harp’s strings with grief for Moab. Even in judgment, God’s prophet feels compassion.

f.g: The inner self — seat of the emotions.
Another form of Kir-hareseth.

chapters.n: Moab will wear itself out at its pagan high places and go to its temple to pray, but its idols cannot help.

f.g: A hilltop shrine for worship.

chapters.n: This is what the Lord has said about Moab in the past.

But now He says: within three years, counted exactly as a hired worker counts his contract, Moab’s glory will be despised and few will survive. Assyria campaigned through the region in the following years.

f.w: as the years of an hireling
f.g: Precisely counted — a hired laborer works not a day more than agreed.
Despised.

chapters.n: A prophecy against Damascus, capital of Syria (Aram), which had allied with Israel against Judah. It will be reduced to a heap of ruins. Assyria captured Damascus in 732 BC.

f.g: A pile of rubble.

chapters.n: The towns of Aroer will be abandoned and become pastures where flocks rest undisturbed.

f.g: Here likely a region of towns east of the Jordan controlled by Damascus.

chapters.n: Ephraim (northern Israel) will lose its fortresses, and Damascus its kingdom. Syria’s survivors will share the same faded glory as Israel — the two allies fall together.
Israel’s glory will shrink and its strength waste away, like a well-fed body becoming thin.

f.g: Brought low; diminished.
Grow thin.

chapters.n: Israel will be harvested like grain cut by a reaper in the fertile valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem. Most of the people will be taken.

f.g: Grain, such as wheat or barley.
A fertile valley southwest of Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:18).

chapters.n: Yet a few will be left, like the last olives at the top of a tree after it is shaken. God always preserves a remnant.

f.g: Gathering what is left after harvest (Leviticus 19:10).

f.w: two or three berries in the top

chapters.n: In that day people will look to their Maker and turn their eyes to the Holy One of Israel. Judgment will bring them back to God.
They will stop trusting altars and idols made with their own hands, including the Asherah poles and incense altars.

f.g: Asherah poles — wooden symbols of a Canaanite goddess.
Probably incense altars or sun pillars.

chapters.n: Israel’s strong cities will be abandoned like the forsaken towns of the Canaanites that fled before Israel long ago.

f.g: The Greek Septuagint reads “the deserted places of the Amorites and Hivites.”

chapters.n: Because Israel forgot God its Savior and its Rock, it planted “pleasant plants” and foreign cuttings — likely gardens for pagan fertility gods.

f.g: Possibly gardens of Adonis, a pagan fertility cult.
Foreign cuttings — idolatry imported from other nations.

chapters.n: Though they make these gardens sprout quickly, the harvest will vanish in a day of grief and incurable pain.

f.g: Incurable pain.

chapters.n: Isaiah hears the roar of many nations crashing like ocean waves — the armies of Assyria, made up of many peoples.
Though they surge like mighty waters, God will rebuke them, and they will flee like chaff on a hilltop or tumbleweed in a storm.

f.g: Husks blown away on high threshing floors.
Tumbleweed or whirling dust.

chapters.n: At evening, terror; by morning, they are gone. This foreshadows the sudden overnight destruction of Sennacherib’s Assyrian army outside Jerusalem.

f.w: before the morning he is not

f.g: Plunder us.

chapters.n: Isaiah addresses a land “beyond the rivers of Ethiopia” — most scholars think of Cush (Nubia), whose kings then ruled Egypt and sought allies against Assyria. Some Latter-day Saint readers have also seen a latter-day land in this verse, but its meaning is debated.

f.g: Possibly “Ho!” or “Ah!” — a call for attention rather than a curse.
Possibly “whirring wings,” referring to insects of the Nile region, or to the land’s protecting outreach.
Hebrew Cush — the region south of Egypt (modern Sudan).

chapters.n: This land sends envoys by sea in papyrus boats. Isaiah tells the swift messengers to return to their tall, smooth-skinned people, feared far and wide, a strong nation whose land is divided by rivers.

f.g: Light papyrus boats used on the Nile.
Better “tall and smooth-skinned.”
Possibly “mighty and conquering.”

chapters.n: All people of the world are told to watch for God’s banner raised on the mountains and listen for His trumpet. The Lord, not human alliances, controls events.
The Lord says He will quietly watch from His dwelling, like shimmering heat in sunshine or a cloud of dew in harvest time — calm, patient, and in control.

f.g: I will stay quiet and watch.
Glowing heat in sunlight.

chapters.n: Then, just before harvest, when the grapes are forming, He will cut off the shoots and branches. He will strike at the right moment — likely referring to Assyria’s sudden defeat.

f.g: Shoots of a vine.

chapters.n: The pruned branches — fallen enemy soldiers — will be left for birds and wild animals through summer and winter.

f.g: Birds of prey.

chapters.n: Then this same distant, mighty people will bring gifts to the Lord at Mount Zion. Even far nations will one day honor Israel’s God.

f.w: the present be brought unto the LORD of hosts
the place of the name of the LORD

chapters.n: A prophecy about Egypt. The Lord rides a swift cloud into Egypt, and its idols tremble before Him. Many in Judah wanted to trust Egypt against Assyria; Isaiah shows Egypt is weak before God.
God will turn Egyptians against each other in civil war — brother against brother, city against city. Egypt was in fact divided among rival rulers during this era.

f.g: Egypt was split among competing dynasties in the 700s BC.

chapters.n: Egypt will lose heart and its plans will fail. Its people will turn to idols, spiritists, and mediums for help, but find none.

f.g: Those who mutter spells.

chapters.n: God will hand Egypt over to a harsh master and fierce king — possibly the Assyrian conquerors who later invaded Egypt, or a cruel native ruler.

f.g: Assyrian kings Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal invaded Egypt in the 600s BC.

chapters.n: The Nile will dry up. Since all of Egypt’s life depended on the Nile, this was the worst disaster imaginable.

f.g: Here the Nile itself, called a “sea” for its size.

chapters.n: Canals will stink and dwindle, and reeds and rushes will rot.

f.g: The channels or canals of Egypt.
Rushes.

chapters.n: The papyrus by the Nile and all the crops planted along its banks will wither and blow away.

f.g: Papyrus plants, used to make writing material.

chapters.n: Fishermen who throw hooks or spread nets in the Nile will mourn and lose heart.

f.g: Throw fishing hooks.

chapters.n: Workers in linen, made from flax, and weavers of fine cloth will be in despair. Egyptian linen was famous throughout the ancient world.

f.g: Flax used for Egypt’s prized linen.
White cloth.

chapters.n: Everyone who works for wages, including those who build fish ponds, will be crushed in spirit.

f.g: Channels for controlling water.

chapters.n: Pharaoh’s wise advisers in Zoan are fools. How can they claim to be descended from wise men and ancient kings?

f.g: Tanis, a major city in the Nile Delta.
Stupid, senseless.

chapters.n: Where are your wise men now? Let them tell what the Lord of hosts has planned for Egypt — if they can.
The leaders of Zoan and Memphis are deceived and have led Egypt astray — even the “cornerstones” of its tribes.

f.g: Memphis, the ancient capital of Egypt.
Cornerstone, support.

chapters.n: The Lord has poured a spirit of confusion on them, so Egypt staggers in everything it does, like a drunk stumbling in his own vomit.

f.g: Spirit of confusion or dizziness.

chapters.n: No one in Egypt — leaders or common people — will be able to do anything useful.

f.w: head or tail, branch or rush

chapters.n: In that day Egypt will tremble in fear when the Lord raises His hand against it.

f.g: An ancient idiom for being terrified and helpless.

chapters.n: Even the name of little Judah will terrify Egypt, because of what the Lord has planned against it.
The prophecy turns hopeful. Five cities in Egypt will speak Canaan’s language (Hebrew) and swear loyalty to the Lord. Later, Jewish communities did flourish in Egypt.

f.g: Hebrew.
Some manuscripts read “city of the sun” — Heliopolis.

chapters.n: An altar to the Lord will stand in the middle of Egypt, and a pillar to Him at its border — signs that Egypt will worship Israel’s God.

f.g: A Jewish temple was later built at Leontopolis in Egypt (2nd century BC).
A standing stone marking a sacred place (Genesis 28:18).

chapters.n: When Egyptians cry to the Lord because of oppression, He will send them a Savior who will deliver them — just as He did for Israel.

f.w: a saviour, and a great one

chapters.n: The Lord will make Himself known to Egypt, and Egyptians will know Him, worship Him with offerings, and keep their vows to Him.

f.w: the Egyptians shall know the LORD

f.g: Offering.

chapters.n: The Lord will strike Egypt and then heal it. When they turn to Him, He will hear their prayers. His discipline aims at healing.

f.w: he shall smite and heal it

f.g: Moved by their prayers.

chapters.n: In that day a highway will run from Egypt to Assyria. The two great enemies will travel freely and worship God together.
Israel will be the third partner with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing in the middle of the earth — fulfilling God’s promise to Abraham.

f.w: a blessing in the midst of the land

chapters.n: The Lord will bless all three: “Egypt my people, Assyria the work of my hands, Israel mine inheritance.” Titles once reserved for Israel are shared with former enemies — a remarkable vision of God’s love for all nations.
In 711 BC the Assyrian commander-in-chief, sent by King Sargon II, captured the Philistine city of Ashdod, which had rebelled with hopes of Egyptian help. Sargon’s own records describe this campaign.

f.g: An Assyrian title for the commander-in-chief, not a personal name (2 Kings 18:17).
Sargon II, king of Assyria about 722–705 BC; named only here in the Bible.
One of the five main Philistine cities.

chapters.n: The Lord told Isaiah to remove his sackcloth and sandals. Isaiah obeyed and went about stripped down and barefoot — likely in just a loincloth, like a captive.

f.g: Coarse garment, perhaps a prophet’s typical clothing.
Probably meaning stripped of his outer garment, as prisoners were.

chapters.n: The Lord explains: Isaiah’s three years of going like this were a living sign about what would happen to Egypt and Cush (Ethiopia).

f.g: Cush — Nubia, whose kings then ruled Egypt.

chapters.n: So Assyria would lead away Egyptian and Cushite captives, young and old, stripped and barefoot, to their deep shame. Assyrian carvings show such lines of prisoners.

f.g: Assyria invaded Egypt in the 670s–660s BC.

chapters.n: Those who had placed their hopes in Cush and boasted of Egypt would be dismayed and ashamed.

f.g: What they looked to for help.

chapters.n: People of the coastland — Philistia and Judah — will say, “If even Egypt, whom we trusted, is captured, how can we escape Assyria?” The lesson: trust God, not political powers.

f.g: This coastland — the Mediterranean coast of Palestine.

chapters.n: A prophecy titled “the desert of the sea,” a cryptic name for Babylon, which lay in flat marshland near the Persian Gulf. Disaster sweeps in like desert whirlwinds.

f.g: Southern Mesopotamia — Babylon’s region, once called “the Sealand.”
Fierce storms from the Negev desert.

chapters.n: Isaiah receives a harsh vision: betrayers betray and destroyers destroy. Elam and Media are called to attack. Media and Persia (whose homeland included Elam) conquered Babylon in 539 BC, ending the groaning it had caused.

f.g: A land east of Babylon, in southwest Iran; part of the Persian empire.

chapters.n: The vision is so terrible that Isaiah feels pain like a woman in labor. He is staggered by what he hears and sees.

f.g: The midsection — the body’s core.
Doubled over in distress.

chapters.n: His heart pounds with terror. The evening he hoped would be peaceful has become a night of dread.

f.g: The twilight he longed for.

chapters.n: Isaiah pictures Babylon’s leaders feasting while danger approaches — then the alarm: “Get up, officers, oil your shields!” Daniel 5 describes Belshazzar’s feast on the night Babylon fell.

f.g: Oil leather shields to prepare for battle.

chapters.n: The Lord tells Isaiah to post a lookout who will report what he sees.
The lookout sees riders — pairs of horsemen, and riders on donkeys and camels — and watches closely.

f.g: Here a troop of riders.

chapters.n: Then he cries out like a lion: “My lord, day and night I have stood at my post!”

f.g: The Dead Sea Isaiah scroll reads “the seer” — “Then the seer cried.”
Guard post.

chapters.n: Here comes a rider with news: “Babylon has fallen, has fallen! Her idols lie shattered.” Revelation repeats this cry for the fall of spiritual Babylon.

f.g: Carved idols.

chapters.n: Isaiah addresses his own people, crushed like grain on a threshing floor: what he has heard from the Lord, he has told them. Babylon’s fall would mean freedom for exiled Judah.

f.g: My people who have been threshed — beaten down by oppression.
Grain of my threshing floor.

chapters.n: A short prophecy about Dumah, an oasis in Arabia (also meaning “silence”). Someone calls from Seir (Edom): “Watchman, how much of the night is left?” They long for the end of oppression.

f.g: An oasis in northern Arabia; the name means “silence.”
The mountain region of Edom, south of the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: The watchman answers: “Morning is coming — but also night.” Relief will be brief, and more darkness follows. If you want to ask, come back and ask again.

f.w: The morning cometh, and also the night
f.g: A short relief, then more trouble.
Or “turn” — perhaps an invitation to repent.

chapters.n: A prophecy about Arabia: traveling caravans of Dedan will have to camp in the thickets instead of on open trade routes, hiding from danger.

f.g: Dedanites, an Arabian trading tribe.
Thickets or scrubland.

chapters.n: The people of Tema bring water and bread to refugees fleeing the war — a picture of hospitality in hard times.

f.g: An oasis city in northwest Arabia.
Met, came to meet.

chapters.n: These refugees are fleeing swords, drawn bows, and the horrors of war.

f.g: A bow drawn and ready to shoot.

chapters.n: Within one year, counted exactly as a hired worker counts, the glory of Kedar will end. Assyria campaigned against Arabian tribes in this period.

f.g: A powerful nomadic Arabian tribe descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:13).

chapters.n: Only a few of Kedar’s mighty archers will survive. The Lord God of Israel has spoken it.

f.g: Remainder.

chapters.n: Surprisingly, this “burden” is against Jerusalem itself, called “the valley of vision” — the place of revelation, surrounded by valleys. Why are its people up on the rooftops celebrating?

f.g: Jerusalem, where God gave visions — now blind to its danger.
Flat roofs, where people gathered to celebrate or watch.

chapters.n: The city is noisy and partying, but its dead did not even die bravely in battle — perhaps they died of famine or were caught fleeing.

f.g: Full of noise and commotion.

chapters.n: Jerusalem’s leaders ran away together and were captured without a single arrow being shot. This may recall the army that fled when Babylon broke in (586 BC), or events in Sennacherib’s invasion (701 BC).

f.w: All thy rulers are fled together

f.g: Captured without the bow — without a fight.

chapters.n: Isaiah refuses comfort and weeps bitterly for the destruction of his people.

f.g: A tender name for the nation.

chapters.n: It is a day of panic, trampling, and confusion sent by the Lord. Walls are broken down, and cries echo off the mountains.

f.g: Confusion, bewilderment.

chapters.n: Elam brings its archers and chariots, and Kir uncovers its shields — foreign troops in the Assyrian army.

f.g: A region in Mesopotamia linked with Aram (Amos 9:7).
Took off the leather cover to prepare for battle.

chapters.n: Jerusalem’s best valleys fill with enemy chariots, and horsemen take position at the city gates.
Judah’s defenses are stripped away. In that day the people looked to the weapons stored in the “House of the Forest,” a royal armory built by Solomon.

f.g: Removed the protection.

chapters.n: They noticed the many cracks in the walls of David’s city and collected water from the lower pool to survive a siege.
