f.g: Breaks or gaps in the wall.

chapters.n: They counted the houses of Jerusalem and tore some down to use the stones to strengthen the wall. Archaeologists have found such a wall in Jerusalem built over houses from this period.
They built a reservoir between the walls for water — likely connected with Hezekiah’s famous tunnel — but they never looked to the God who made it all and planned it long ago.

f.w: a ditch between the two walls
f.g: A reservoir; compare Hezekiah’s tunnel and pool (2 Kings 20:20).

f.w: ye have not looked unto the maker thereof

chapters.n: On that day the Lord called them to weep, mourn, shave their heads, and wear sackcloth — that is, to repent.

f.g: Shaving the head as a sign of mourning.

chapters.n: Instead they partied — slaughtering cattle, eating meat, drinking wine, and saying, “Let’s eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!” Paul and the Book of Mormon both warn against this attitude.

f.w: let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die

chapters.n: The Lord revealed to Isaiah that this sin will not be forgiven until they die. Their refusal to repent seals their fate.

f.g: Atoned for, covered.

chapters.n: Now the Lord sends Isaiah to Shebna, the palace administrator — a powerful royal official.

f.g: The steward of the palace — the king’s chief official.

chapters.n: Isaiah challenges him: “What right do you have to carve yourself a grand tomb high in the rock here?” Shebna was building a monument to himself while the nation was in danger. An ancient tomb inscription found near Jerusalem may be his.

f.g: Tomb.

f.w: graveth an habitation for himself in a rock
f.g: Carves a resting place in the cliffside.

chapters.n: The Lord will grab hold of him and hurl him away.

f.g: Or “grip you firmly.”

chapters.n: God will wad him up like a ball and throw him into a wide land, where he will die far from his fancy tomb. His splendid chariots will become a disgrace to his master’s house.

f.g: A vivid image of being thrown away.

chapters.n: God will remove Shebna from his office and position.

f.g: Office, post.

chapters.n: Then the Lord will call His servant Eliakim son of Hilkiah to replace him.

f.g: “God establishes.”

chapters.n: Eliakim will receive Shebna’s official robe, sash, and authority, and will be like a father to Jerusalem and Judah — a caring, faithful leader.

f.g: Sash of office.

f.w: a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem

chapters.n: He will carry the key of David’s house on his shoulder: what he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open. Revelation applies this to Christ, who holds all keys; Latter-day Saints also think of priesthood keys.

f.w: the key of the house of David

chapters.n: God will fasten him like a peg driven firmly into a solid wall, and he will bring honor to his family.

f.g: A tent peg or wall peg for hanging things.
A firm, secure spot.

chapters.n: His whole family will hang on him like pots and cups hung on a peg — relatives seeking favors and positions.

f.g: Descendants and relatives.
Jars.

chapters.n: But eventually even that firm peg will give way under the weight, and everything hanging on it will fall. No human leader can carry everything forever — a warning against nepotism and reliance on mortals.

f.w: the nail that is fastened in the sure place be removed
f.g: Many think this refers to Eliakim’s family overburdening him; others to Shebna.

chapters.n: A prophecy against Tyre, the great Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast (modern Lebanon), the hub of ancient sea trade. Sailors on the great trading ships hear in Cyprus that their home port is destroyed.

f.g: Large ocean-going merchant ships.
Kittim — Cyprus.

chapters.n: Be silent, people of the coast, enriched by the merchants of Sidon who sailed the seas.

f.g: Sidon, Tyre’s sister city to the north.
Coastland; Tyre was partly built on an island.

chapters.n: Across the great waters came grain from the Nile, the harvest of Egypt. Tyre grew rich trading it and became the marketplace of nations.

f.g: A branch of the Nile, or the Nile itself.
Market, trading center.

chapters.n: Sidon is shamed, for the sea itself mourns as though childless — it no longer raises sons and daughters. The sea-based trading empire has lost its people.

f.g: I have not been in labor — I am bereaved.

chapters.n: When news of Tyre’s fall reaches Egypt, Egyptians will be in anguish, since much of their trade went through Tyre.
Flee to Tarshish, the farthest port! Wail, you people of the coast!

f.g: A distant port in the west, possibly in Spain.

chapters.n: Is this your celebrated city, so ancient? Now its people will wander as exiles to distant lands.

f.w: whose antiquity is of ancient days
f.g: Tyre was very old, founded perhaps before 2000 BC.
Live as a foreigner.

chapters.n: Who planned this against Tyre, the city that crowned kings, whose merchants were princes and whose traders were honored worldwide?

f.g: The city that set up kings in its colonies.
Traders.

chapters.n: The Lord of hosts planned it, to humble all pride and bring down the honored of the earth. Wealth and fame cannot shield anyone from God.

f.w: to stain the pride of all glory

chapters.n: Colonists of Tarshish are now free to spread through their land like the Nile, for Tyre’s controlling power is gone.

f.g: No more harbor or restraint.

chapters.n: The Lord stretched His hand over the sea and shook kingdoms. He commanded the destruction of the strongholds of Canaan’s merchant city.

f.g: Literally “Canaan” — the Phoenicians were Canaanites, and the word came to mean “trader.”

chapters.n: Tyre and Sidon, once proud and untouched, will no longer celebrate. Even if they flee to Cyprus, they will find no rest.

f.g: Once-unconquered city now crushed.

chapters.n: Look at the land of the Chaldeans (Babylonia): Assyria turned it into a wilderness, built siege towers, and ruined its palaces. If Babylon could fall, so can Tyre.

f.g: Babylonia; Assyria’s Sennacherib devastated Babylon in 689 BC.

chapters.n: Wail, great trading ships, for your fortress harbor is destroyed! The chapter’s opening cry is repeated.
Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years — a normal lifespan — then will return to its trade like a forgotten prostitute singing to win back customers.

f.g: A lifetime; compare Psalms 90:10 and Jeremiah 25:11.
A picture of trading purely for profit.

chapters.n: A mocking song: “Take your harp, forgotten one, walk the city, and sing sweetly so people remember you.”
After seventy years the Lord will restore Tyre, and it will return to doing business with every kingdom on earth.

f.g: Here, restore or take notice of.
Wages, earnings.

chapters.n: But in the end, Tyre’s profits will be set apart as holy to the Lord — used to feed and clothe His people. Wealth once used selfishly will be consecrated to God.

f.g: Fine, lasting clothes.

chapters.n: Chapters 24–27 are often called Isaiah’s “little apocalypse,” describing God’s judgment on the whole earth before His reign. The Lord will empty the earth, turn it upside down, and scatter its people.

f.g: Literally “twists its surface” — overturns everything.

chapters.n: No one will be spared because of status: priest and people, master and servant, buyer and seller, lender and borrower — all face the same judgment.

f.g: Interest on loans.

f.w: as with the people, so with the priest

chapters.n: The land will be completely emptied and plundered, because the Lord has spoken.

f.g: Plundered.

chapters.n: The earth dries up and withers; the whole world wastes away, and even the proud powers of the earth weaken.

f.g: Wastes away; droops.

chapters.n: The earth is polluted by its people because they have broken God’s laws, twisted His ordinances, and broken the everlasting covenant. The Lord quotes this in D&C 1 to describe the latter-day apostasy.
So a curse consumes the earth; its people bear their guilt, are burned, and few remain. Latter-day scripture describes the earth being cleansed by fire at the Second Coming.
The new wine dries up, the vines wither, and those who were cheerful groan.

f.g: Freshly pressed grape juice.

chapters.n: The happy sound of tambourines and harps stops; party noise falls silent.

f.g: Tambourines.

chapters.n: People no longer drink with singing; even strong drink tastes bitter.
The “city of chaos” — a picture of the world’s organized wickedness — is broken down, and every house is barred shut.

f.g: Hebrew tohu — the same word for “without form” in Genesis 1:2; a city returned to chaos.

chapters.n: People cry in the streets for wine; all joy has turned to gloom and gladness is banished from the land.
Only ruin remains in the city, and its gate is battered to pieces.

f.g: The city gate — center of public life and defense.

chapters.n: Yet like the few olives left after a tree is beaten or grapes left after harvest, a remnant will survive.

f.w: the shaking of an olive tree

f.g: What is left after harvest.

chapters.n: The survivors raise their voices and sing for joy about the Lord’s majesty, shouting from the west, across the sea.

f.g: From the west (the Mediterranean).

chapters.n: So glorify the Lord in the east and honor His name in the islands of the sea. Latter-day Saints note that Israel was scattered to the “isles of the sea,” and praise will rise from there too.

f.g: Better “in the east” (the regions of light/dawn).

chapters.n: From the ends of the earth come songs praising the Righteous One. But Isaiah feels sick at heart: betrayers keep betraying. Joy and grief exist side by side until the end.

f.g: “I waste away!” — an expression of grief.
Or “glory to the Righteous One.”

chapters.n: Terror, pit, and trap await the people of the earth. In Hebrew, the three words sound alike: pachad, pachat, pach.

f.w: Fear, and the pit, and the snare

chapters.n: Whoever escapes one danger falls into the next. The floodgates of heaven open, as in Noah’s day, and earth’s foundations shake.

f.w: the windows from on high are open
the foundations of the earth do shake

chapters.n: The earth is shattered, split apart, and violently shaken. The threefold repetition emphasizes total upheaval.

f.g: Completely split apart.

chapters.n: The earth staggers like a drunk and sways like a flimsy shelter. Its sin weighs it down; it falls and won’t rise again — the old world order ends.

f.w: reel to and fro like a drunkard

f.g: A flimsy hut or watchman’s shelter.

chapters.n: In that day the Lord will punish rebellious powers in heaven and the proud kings on earth — both spiritual and political evil.

f.w: the host of the high ones
f.g: Rebellious heavenly powers — spiritual forces of evil.

chapters.n: They will be gathered like prisoners in a pit and locked up, and after many days they will be “visited.” Latter-day Saints see in this the spirit prison and the gospel later being preached to the dead.

f.w: after many days shall they be visited

chapters.n: Then the moon will blush and the sun be ashamed, for the Lord’s glory will outshine them when He reigns gloriously in Mount Zion and Jerusalem before His elders. This points to Christ’s millennial reign.

f.w: the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion

f.g: His elders — perhaps like the seventy elders who saw God at Sinai (Exodus 24:9-11).

chapters.n: Isaiah bursts into praise: the Lord is his God, who has done wonders and carried out long-planned purposes with perfect faithfulness.

f.g: Plans made long ago.

chapters.n: God has turned a proud, fortified city into a heap of rubble, never to be rebuilt. This “city” stands for all the world’s organized wickedness.

f.g: Fortress of foreigners.

chapters.n: So even strong and ruthless nations will honor and revere God.

f.g: Ruthless, fearsome nations.

chapters.n: God has been a fortress for the poor and needy in distress, a shelter from storms and shade from scorching heat, when the ruthless rage like a storm against a wall.

f.g: Breath or fury.

chapters.n: As a cloud’s shadow cools desert heat, God silences the uproar of foreigners and the song of tyrants.

f.g: Better “the song of the ruthless.”

chapters.n: On this mountain — Zion — the Lord will prepare a rich banquet for all peoples, with the finest food and aged wine. This anticipates the messianic feast; Latter-day scripture speaks of the “supper of the Lord” prepared for all nations.

f.g: Aged wine, left to mature on its sediment.

chapters.n: On this mountain He will remove the shroud of mourning and the veil of spiritual blindness covering all nations.

f.w: the veil that is spread over all nations

f.g: A burial shroud or veil of grief.

chapters.n: He will swallow up death forever and wipe away tears from every face, removing His people’s disgrace. Paul and John quote this; it is fulfilled through Christ’s Resurrection.

f.w: He will swallow up death in victory
wipe away tears from off all faces

f.g: Reproach, disgrace.

chapters.n: In that day people will say: “This is our God! We waited for Him, and He saved us. Let us rejoice in His salvation.”

f.g: Hebrew yeshu‘ah.

chapters.n: The Lord’s hand will rest protectively on Zion, but Moab — here a symbol of proud enemies — will be trampled like straw in a manure pit.

f.g: Manure pile.

chapters.n: Moab will flail like a drowning swimmer trying to stay afloat, but God will bring down its pride and its skillful schemes.

f.g: Moab struggles helplessly in the dung pit.
Their clever works or tricks.

chapters.n: God will bring down Moab’s high fortified walls and level them to the dust.

f.w: bring to the ground, even to the dust

chapters.n: In that day Judah will sing a new song: “We have a strong city, and God makes salvation its walls and ramparts.” Zion’s security is God Himself, not stone walls.

f.g: Ramparts, fortifications.

chapters.n: Open the gates so that the righteous nation that keeps faith may enter. This resembles ancient temple-entrance songs.

f.g: Keeps faith; stays loyal.

chapters.n: A beloved promise: God will keep in perfect peace the person whose mind is fixed on Him, because that person trusts Him.

f.g: Hebrew shalom shalom — peace doubled, complete peace.

f.w: whose mind is stayed on thee

chapters.n: Trust the Lord forever, because Jehovah is an everlasting Rock.

f.g: Hebrew Yah YHWH — a doubled form of God’s name for emphasis.
Literally “Rock of ages.”

chapters.n: He humbles those who live in lofty pride and levels the proud city to the dust.
The poor and needy, once trampled, will now walk over the ruins of their oppressors. God reverses fortunes.
The path of the righteous is level; God, the Upright One, makes it smooth.

f.g: Make level or smooth.

chapters.n: Walking in the way of God’s judgments, we wait for Him. Our deepest desire is His name and remembering Him.
Isaiah longs for God through the night and seeks Him early. When God’s judgments are on the earth, people learn righteousness.

f.w: when thy judgments are in the earth

chapters.n: Even when shown kindness, the wicked won’t learn righteousness. In a land of goodness they still do wrong and never see God’s majesty.

f.w: Let favour be shewed to the wicked

chapters.n: Lord, Your hand is raised, but they don’t see it. They will see Your zeal for Your people and be ashamed, and the fire reserved for Your enemies will consume them.

f.g: Better “zeal for the people” — God’s passion for His own.

chapters.n: Lord, You give us peace; everything we have achieved, You have done for us.

f.w: thou also hast wrought all our works in us

chapters.n: Other masters have ruled over us — foreign kings and false gods — but we honor Your name alone.
Those tyrants are dead and will not rise again. God has wiped out even the memory of them.

f.g: The oppressors have no future; contrast verse 19.

chapters.n: Lord, You have enlarged the nation and extended its borders; You have won glory.
In distress they sought You, Lord, whispering prayers when You disciplined them.

f.g: Or “whispered a prayer.”

chapters.n: Like a woman in hard labor crying out in pain, so were we before You, Lord.

f.w: Like as a woman with child

chapters.n: We labored and writhed but gave birth only to wind. We could not bring salvation to the earth by our own efforts. Only God can save.

f.g: All that pain produced nothing.

f.w: we have not wrought any deliverance

chapters.n: A glorious promise of resurrection: “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust!” As dew revives plants, God will bring the dead out of the earth.

f.w: together with my dead body shall they arise

f.g: Dew of light — life-giving morning dew.

chapters.n: Come, my people, go into your rooms and shut the doors; hide for a little while until God’s wrath has passed — like Israel sheltering at the first Passover.
For the Lord is coming out of His dwelling to punish the earth’s people for their sins. The earth will expose the blood shed on it and no longer hide its slain. Hidden crimes will be revealed.

f.w: the LORD cometh out of his place

chapters.n: In that day the Lord will slay Leviathan, the twisting sea serpent and dragon. In ancient stories this monster stood for chaos; here it symbolizes evil powers and, ultimately, Satan.

f.g: A legendary sea monster representing chaos and evil (Job 41; Psalms 74:14).
Fleeing or gliding.

chapters.n: In that day sing about a delightful vineyard! This new song reverses Isaiah’s sad vineyard song in chapter 5.
The Lord Himself tends this vineyard, watering it constantly and guarding it day and night so nothing harms it.

f.w: I the LORD do keep it

chapters.n: God is not angry with His vineyard now. If briers and thorns (enemies) attacked, He would march against them and burn them up.
Better yet, let enemies take hold of God’s protection and make peace with Him. The repetition shows God’s eager invitation.

f.g: Grasp my refuge — seek safety in me.

chapters.n: In days to come Jacob will take root, Israel will blossom and bud, and fill the whole world with fruit. Latter-day Saints see Israel’s gathering and missionary work as part of this fulfillment.

f.w: fill the face of the world with fruit

chapters.n: Has God struck Israel as hard as He struck Israel’s attackers? No — His discipline of His people is measured and merciful.
God dealt with Israel in measured ways, sending them into exile, removing them with His fierce wind as on a day of the hot east wind — but holding back His harshest blast.

f.g: With moderation; possibly “by driving her away.”
A scorching desert wind.

chapters.n: This is how Jacob’s sin will be removed: when Israel smashes its pagan altars like crushed chalk, and no Asherah poles or incense altars remain standing.

f.g: Limestone, easily crushed.
Asherah poles.
Atoned for.

chapters.n: The fortified city of the proud will be desolate and empty like a wilderness, where calves graze and strip the branches.
When its branches dry up, women will break them off for firewood. These are people without understanding, so their Maker will not show them favor.
In that day the Lord will thresh His harvest from the Euphrates to the brook of Egypt, and gather His people one by one. Each person matters to Him.

f.g: The Euphrates.
The Wadi of Egypt, Israel’s southwestern border.

chapters.n: A great trumpet will sound, and those lost in Assyria and outcasts in Egypt will come and worship the Lord on the holy mountain at Jerusalem — a picture of the great latter-day gathering.

f.w: the great trumpet shall be blown

chapters.n: Woe to Samaria, capital of Ephraim (northern Israel), sitting proudly on its hill above fertile valleys like a garland on the head of drunken partygoers. Its beauty is a fading flower.

f.g: Samaria, set on a hill like a wreath on a reveler’s head.
Rich, fertile valleys.

chapters.n: The Lord has a mighty one — Assyria — ready like a hailstorm, a destroying tempest, or a flood, to throw Samaria to the ground.

f.g: Assyria, which conquered Samaria in 722 BC.

chapters.n: Ephraim’s proud crown will be trampled underfoot.
Samaria’s fading glory will be like the first ripe fig of the season, snatched and eaten the moment someone sees it. Assyria will devour it just as eagerly.

f.g: The first-ripe fig, a prized early treat.

chapters.n: In that day the Lord Himself will be a glorious crown and beautiful diadem for the faithful remnant — a far better crown than Samaria’s.

f.g: Remnant.

chapters.n: He will give a spirit of justice to judges and strength to soldiers who drive enemies back at the gate.

f.w: turn the battle to the gate
f.g: Push attackers back to the city gate.

chapters.n: Now Isaiah turns to Judah: even its priests and prophets reel from wine and beer. They stagger when seeing visions and stumble when making judgments.

f.g: Off course; staggering.

chapters.n: Their tables are covered with vomit; there is no clean place. A shocking image of spiritual and physical corruption.
The drunken leaders mock Isaiah: “Who does he think he’s teaching? Babies just weaned?” They resent being taught.
They mock his message as baby talk: “tsav la-tsav, kav la-kav” — sounds like a child’s singsong. Yet Latter-day Saints treasure the principle that God reveals truth line upon line.

f.g: In Hebrew, tsav la-tsav, tsav la-tsav, kav la-kav — possibly mocking nonsense syllables.

chapters.n: So be it, says Isaiah: God will speak to them with stammering lips and a foreign tongue — the Assyrian invaders. Paul applies this verse to speaking in tongues.
God had offered them rest and refreshment through trusting Him, but they would not listen.
So the word of the Lord will become to them just what they mocked — meaningless syllables — so that they stumble backward, are broken, trapped, and captured.
Listen, you scoffers who rule Jerusalem!

f.g: Mockers, scoffers.

chapters.n: Judah’s leaders boasted that they had a “covenant with death” — likely a secret alliance with Egypt — and felt safe from the coming flood of Assyria. But they had hidden behind lies.

f.g: Possibly a jab at Egypt’s death-obsessed religion, or a treaty that only brings death.
Hebrew Sheol.

chapters.n: God instead lays in Zion a tested, precious cornerstone, a sure foundation. Whoever trusts it will not panic. The New Testament and Book of Mormon identify this stone as Jesus Christ.

f.g: Will not flee in panic; Romans 9:33 reads “shall not be ashamed.”

chapters.n: God will use justice as His measuring line and righteousness as His plumb line. Hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and floods will wash out the hiding place.

f.g: Plumb line — a weighted cord used to check that walls are straight.

chapters.n: Their “covenant with death” will be canceled. When the overwhelming flood passes through, they will be beaten down by it.

f.g: Canceled, wiped out.

chapters.n: Every time it passes it will catch them, morning after morning, day and night. Just understanding the message will bring terror.

f.g: Terror, dread.

chapters.n: A proverb: the bed is too short to stretch out on and the blanket too narrow to wrap up in. Their plans for safety won’t cover them.

The Lord will rise as He did at Mount Perazim and the valley of Gibeon, where He fought for David and Joshua. But now He will act against His own people — His “strange work.” Latter-day revelation also uses this phrase.
So stop mocking, or your chains will get tighter. Isaiah has heard from God that destruction is decreed for the whole land.

f.g: Chains, bonds.

chapters.n: Isaiah now teaches with a farming parable: listen carefully to what I say.
Does a farmer plow forever? No — he plows and breaks up the soil only as long as needed.

f.g: Lumps of earth.

chapters.n: Once the ground is leveled, he plants each seed in its proper place — dill, cumin, wheat in rows, barley, and spelt at the edges.

f.g: Black cumin or dill, a spice plant.
An aromatic seed spice.
Spelt, a type of wheat.

chapters.n: The farmer knows how to do this because God teaches him wisdom.

f.g: Good judgment.

chapters.n: He doesn’t thresh delicate spices with a heavy sledge or cart wheel; he beats them gently with a stick.

f.g: A heavy sledge with sharp stones underneath.

chapters.n: Grain must be threshed to make bread, but not endlessly or so hard that it is crushed. Likewise, God’s judgments are measured — enough to refine, not to destroy.

f.g: Grain for bread.
Threshed.

chapters.n: This wisdom also comes from the Lord of hosts, whose counsel is wonderful and whose wisdom is great. He knows how much discipline each person needs.

f.g: Great in wisdom; abundant in success.

chapters.n: Woe to Ariel — a poetic name for Jerusalem, David’s city. Its people go through their yearly festivals and sacrifices, but mere routine won’t save them. Nephi applies much of this chapter to the last days in 2 Nephi 26–27.

f.g: Possibly “lion of God” or “altar hearth” — the place where sacrifices burn.
Keep cycling through your festivals.

chapters.n: God will bring distress on Ariel, with mourning and grief; the city will become like an altar hearth — a place of burning.

f.w: it shall be unto me as Ariel
f.g: A wordplay: the city will become like an “altar hearth” of slaughter.

chapters.n: God Himself will encircle Jerusalem with siege camps, towers, and ramps — through Assyria and later Babylon.

f.g: A siege ramp or earthwork.

chapters.n: Brought low, Jerusalem will speak from the ground, its voice whispering from the dust like a ghost. Nephi applies this to his own people, whose record would speak “out of the dust” — the Book of Mormon.

f.w: thy speech shall whisper out of the dust

f.g: Here a faint, low voice, like that of the dead.

chapters.n: But suddenly the hordes of enemies will become like fine dust and blowing chaff — in an instant.
The Lord of hosts will come with thunder, earthquake, a great noise, storm, and devouring fire. Nephi applies this to the destruction among his people before Christ’s visit.
All the nations that attack Ariel and its stronghold will vanish like a dream in the night.

f.g: Stronghold, fortress.

chapters.n: They will be like a hungry man who dreams of eating and wakes up still hungry, or a thirsty man who dreams of drinking and wakes up parched. Their conquest will never satisfy.

f.g: He is still craving.

f.w: all the nations be, that fight against mount Zion

chapters.n: Be astonished and blinded! The people stagger as if drunk — not from wine, but from spiritual stupor.

f.g: Stop and be amazed.

chapters.n: The Lord has poured over them a spirit of deep sleep, closing the eyes of prophets and covering the heads of seers. This describes a time of spiritual blindness or apostasy.

The whole vision has become like a sealed book. When it is given to a learned man to read, he says, “I can’t; it is sealed.” Latter-day Saints see fulfillment when Martin Harris showed characters from the gold plates to scholar Charles Anthon.

f.g: In Latter-day Saint understanding, Professor Charles Anthon of New York (1828).

chapters.n: Then the book is given to someone unlearned, who says, “I am not learned.” Joseph Smith, a farm boy with little schooling, translated the Book of Mormon by the gift and power of God.

The Lord explains why: the people honor Him with their lips but their hearts are far from Him, and their worship is based on human rules. Jesus quoted this; He also used similar words to Joseph Smith in the First Vision.

f.w: with their lips do honour me

chapters.n: So God will do “a marvellous work and a wonder,” confounding the wisdom of the wise. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in the Restoration of the gospel and the coming forth of the Book of Mormon.

f.w: a marvellous work and a wonder
the wisdom of their wise men shall perish

chapters.n: Woe to those who try to hide their plans from the Lord, working in the dark and saying, “Who sees us?” Nephi applies this to secret combinations.
How twisted! They treat the Potter as if He were the clay. Can a thing say of its maker, “He didn’t make me” or “He doesn’t understand”?

f.g: Perversity; reversing the true order.

chapters.n: In a very short time, Lebanon will become a fertile field and the fertile field a forest — a picture of dramatic transformation, including the renewal of the land.

f.w: Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field

chapters.n: In that day the deaf will hear the words of the book and the blind will see out of darkness. The Book of Mormon helps open spiritual eyes and ears.

f.w: the deaf hear the words of the book

f.g: Gloom, darkness.

chapters.n: The humble will find fresh joy in the Lord, and the poor will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.

f.w: The meek also shall increase their joy

chapters.n: The ruthless will disappear, mockers will be finished, and all who look for chances to do evil will be cut off.

f.g: Look for opportunities to do wrong.

chapters.n: These are people who make someone a criminal with a word, set traps for the one who defends justice at the city gate, and deny justice to the innocent with lies.

f.w: make a man an offender for a word

f.g: Speaks up for justice in court (held at the city gate).

chapters.n: The Lord, who redeemed Abraham, says Jacob will no longer be ashamed or turn pale with fear. Israel’s long disgrace will end.

f.g: Grow pale with fear or shame.

chapters.n: When Jacob sees his children — the work of God’s hands — gathered around him, they will honor God’s name and stand in awe of the Holy One of Jacob.

f.w: his children, the work of mine hands

f.g: Treat God’s name as holy.

chapters.n: Those who wandered in spirit will gain understanding, and complainers will accept instruction. Nephi links this to the Book of Mormon’s power to teach true doctrine.

f.w: they that murmured shall learn doctrine

chapters.n: The Lord condemns His “rebellious children” in Judah who make plans and alliances without consulting Him, piling sin on sin. In Hezekiah’s day, Judah sought Egypt’s help against Assyria.

f.g: Make an alliance — literally “pour out a libation,” sealing a treaty.

chapters.n: They go down to Egypt for protection without asking the Lord, trusting Pharaoh’s strength and Egypt’s “shade.”

f.w: have not asked at my mouth

f.g: Egypt’s protection, pictured as shade.

chapters.n: But Pharaoh’s protection will bring them shame, and Egypt’s shade will bring disgrace.

f.g: Humiliation, disgrace.

chapters.n: Judah’s officials have traveled to Zoan and Hanes, important Egyptian cities, seeking an alliance.

f.g: Tanis, in the Nile Delta.
An Egyptian city, probably Heracleopolis.

chapters.n: Everyone will be ashamed of a nation that cannot help them — Egypt will be useless, bringing only disgrace.

f.g: Disgrace.

chapters.n: Isaiah pictures envoys hauling treasures on donkeys and camels through the dangerous Negev desert, home of lions and snakes, to buy help from a nation that cannot help.

f.g: Animals of the Negev desert.
Camels’ humps.

chapters.n: Egypt’s help is worthless. That’s why God calls it “Rahab who sits still” — a big name that does nothing.

f.w: Their strength is to sit still
f.g: Better “Rahab who sits still”; Rahab was a poetic name for Egypt as a chaos monster (Psalms 87:4).

chapters.n: God tells Isaiah to write this on a tablet and in a scroll as a lasting witness for future generations.

f.g: Tablet.

chapters.n: Write that they are a rebellious, lying people who refuse to hear the Lord’s instruction.

f.g: Faithless, deceitful children.

chapters.n: They tell the seers, “Stop seeing visions,” and the prophets, “Don’t tell us what’s right; tell us pleasant things — even illusions.”
“Get out of our way! Stop confronting us with the Holy One of Israel!” They want religion without God’s demands.

f.w: cause the Holy One of Israel to cease
f.g: Stop talking to us about God.

chapters.n: Because they reject God’s word and rely on oppression and deceit instead…

f.g: Crookedness, deceit.
Lean on it.

chapters.n: …their sin will be like a cracked, bulging wall that suddenly collapses all at once.

f.g: A crack in a wall about to give way.

chapters.n: It will shatter like a clay pot smashed so thoroughly that no piece is big enough to scoop a coal from a fire or water from a cistern.

f.g: A fragment of broken pottery.

chapters.n: God had offered a better way: “In returning and rest you will be saved; in quietness and trust is your strength.” But they refused.

f.w: In returning and rest shall ye be saved
in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength

chapters.n: They said, “No, we’ll escape on horses!” — so they will flee. “We’ll ride swift horses!” — so their pursuers will be swifter.
A thousand will flee from one attacker, and from five they will all run, until only a lonely flagpole is left on a hilltop. This reverses God’s promise to the faithful.

f.w: One thousand shall flee at the rebuke of one

f.g: A flagpole.

chapters.n: Yet the Lord is waiting to be gracious to them and rises to show mercy. He is a God of justice; blessed are all who wait for Him.

f.w: the LORD wait, that he may be gracious
blessed are all they that wait for him

chapters.n: People of Zion in Jerusalem, you will weep no more. When He hears your cry, He will answer graciously.
Though the Lord gives you the bread of hardship and water of affliction, your Teacher will no longer hide; you will see Him with your own eyes.

f.g: The Hebrew may be singular: “thy Teacher” — God Himself.

chapters.n: You will hear a voice behind you saying, “This is the way; walk in it,” whenever you turn right or left. Latter-day Saints often connect this with the guidance of the Holy Ghost.

f.w: This is the way, walk ye in it

chapters.n: Then you will treat your silver and gold idols as unclean, throwing them away like a filthy rag: “Get out of here!”

f.g: A ritually unclean rag.

chapters.n: God will send rain for your seed, and the land will produce rich, abundant food. Your livestock will graze in wide pastures.
Even the oxen and donkeys that plow will eat the best seasoned fodder, carefully winnowed — a sign of overflowing abundance.

f.g: Plow the soil.
Animal feed.
A winnowing fork.

chapters.n: On every high mountain and hill streams will flow, on the day of great slaughter when the towers of the proud fall.
The moon will shine like the sun, and the sun seven times brighter, when the Lord binds up His people’s wounds and heals them. This anticipates the glory of the Millennium.

f.w: the light of the sun shall be sevenfold
healeth the stroke of their wound

chapters.n: Look! The Lord comes from afar, burning with anger, His lips full of wrath and His tongue like consuming fire.

f.g: God’s presence and power.
Or “in thick rising smoke.”

chapters.n: His breath is like a flooding torrent rising to the neck. He will shake the nations in a sieve of destruction and put a bridle in their jaws to lead them astray.

f.w: to the midst of the neck

f.g: A sieve that leaves nothing — sifting to destruction.

chapters.n: Meanwhile, God’s people will sing as on a holy festival night, with glad hearts like pilgrims going up with flutes to the Lord’s mountain.

f.g: A sacred festival, likely Passover.
Flute.

chapters.n: The Lord will make His majestic voice heard and show His mighty arm coming down with fierce anger, consuming fire, cloudburst, storm, and hail.

f.w: the lighting down of his arm
f.g: The descending blow of His arm.

chapters.n: At the Lord’s voice Assyria, who struck others with a rod, will be shattered.
Every blow of the Lord’s punishing rod on Assyria will be accompanied by tambourines and harps — Judah celebrating as God fights for them.

f.g: The appointed rod of punishment.
Tambourines.

chapters.n: Long ago a burning place, Topheth, was prepared — deep and wide, piled with wood — for the king. The Lord’s breath, like a stream of burning sulfur, will set it ablaze.

f.g: A site in the Hinnom Valley near Jerusalem where children were burned to Molech (Jeremiah 7:31); later a symbol of hell.
Burning sulfur.

chapters.n: Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, trusting its many chariots and strong cavalry, but who do not look to the Holy One of Israel or seek the Lord.

f.g: Rely on horses.

chapters.n: But God is wise too! He will bring disaster and will not take back His words. He will rise against the wicked and those who help them.

f.g: An ironic jab at Judah’s “wise” politicians.

chapters.n: The Egyptians are mere humans, not God; their horses are flesh, not spirit. When the Lord stretches out His hand, both helper and helped will fall together.

f.w: the Egyptians are men, and not God

f.g: Helped.

chapters.n: Like a lion growling over its prey, unafraid of a crowd of shouting shepherds, the Lord of hosts will come down to fight for Mount Zion.

f.g: Cower or be intimidated.

chapters.n: Like birds hovering over their nest, the Lord of hosts will shield Jerusalem; He will defend, deliver, “pass over,” and rescue it. The word recalls the first Passover.

chapters.n: So return, people of Israel, to the One you have so deeply rebelled against.

f.g: Rebelled.

chapters.n: In that day everyone will throw away the silver and gold idols their own sinful hands made.

f.w: the sword, not of a mighty man

f.g: Routed; put to forced labor.

chapters.n: Assyria’s stronghold will crumble in terror and its officers flee in panic from the Lord’s banner. The Lord’s fire burns in Zion and His furnace is in Jerusalem — His presence protects His people and consumes His enemies.

f.g: Battle standard or flag.

chapters.n: A king will reign with righteousness and his officials will govern with justice. This may first describe a good king like Hezekiah, but it reaches its fullness in the Messiah’s reign.

f.w: a king shall reign in righteousness

chapters.n: Each such leader will be like a shelter from wind and storm, streams in the desert, and the shade of a great rock in a weary land. True leaders protect and refresh.

the shadow of a great rock

chapters.n: Then eyes will no longer be closed and ears will listen — reversing the spiritual blindness of Isaiah 6.

f.w: the eyes of them that see shall not be dim

chapters.n: The hasty will gain understanding, and those who stammered will speak clearly.

f.g: The hasty or impulsive.

chapters.n: Fools will no longer be called noble, and scoundrels will no longer be respected. Society will see people as they truly are.

f.g: Noble, generous.
A miser or scoundrel.

chapters.n: For the fool speaks foolishness and plots evil, acts godlessly, spreads error about the Lord, and leaves the hungry empty and the thirsty without drink.

f.g: Folly, wickedness.

f.w: make empty the soul of the hungry

chapters.n: The scoundrel’s methods are evil; he schemes to ruin the poor with lies, even when the needy person’s cause is just.

f.g: Methods, tools.

chapters.n: But the noble person plans noble things, and by generous deeds he stands firm.
Isaiah calls on the complacent, carefree women of Jerusalem to wake up and listen.
In a little over a year, you careless ones will tremble, because the grape harvest will fail and the fruit won’t come in.

f.g: Literally “days upon a year” — in a little more than a year.

chapters.n: Tremble and shudder! Strip off your fine clothes and wear sackcloth in mourning.
They will beat their breasts in grief for the pleasant fields and fruitful vines that are lost.

f.g: Beat their breasts in mourning.

chapters.n: Thorns and briers will cover the land of God’s people, even the happy homes of the once-joyful city.
The palace will be deserted, the busy city abandoned, and its forts and watchtowers will become dens for wild donkeys and pastures for flocks.

f.g: Possibly “Ophel and watchtower” — Ophel was a hill in Jerusalem.

chapters.n: This will last until the Spirit is poured out on us from on high. Then the wilderness will become fertile and the fertile field like a forest — spiritual renewal transforms everything.

f.w: the spirit be poured upon us from on high
the wilderness be a fruitful field

f.w: the work of righteousness shall be peace

f.g: Security, confidence.

chapters.n: God’s people will live in peaceful homes, secure dwellings, and undisturbed resting places.
Even if hail flattens the forest and the city is laid low, God’s people will be safe. The proud “forest” and “city” of the world will fall.
Blessed are you who sow by every stream and let your ox and donkey roam freely — a picture of peaceful, abundant life.

Woe to you, destroyer, who have never been destroyed; betrayer, who have never been betrayed! When you finish destroying, you’ll be destroyed. This is aimed at Assyria, which broke its agreement with Hezekiah.

f.g: You destroyer — likely Assyria under Sennacherib.

chapters.n: The people pray: Lord, be gracious to us; we have waited for You. Be our strength every morning and our salvation in trouble.

f.w: be thou their arm every morning

chapters.n: At the thunder of God’s voice, peoples flee; when He rises up, nations scatter.

f.g: Roar, uproar.

chapters.n: The enemy’s plunder will be stripped as if by swarming caterpillars and leaping locusts.

f.g: Young locusts.

chapters.n: The Lord is exalted, dwelling on high; He fills Zion with justice and righteousness.

f.w: he hath filled Zion with judgment and righteousness

chapters.n: He will be the stability of your times, a rich store of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge. Reverence for the Lord is Zion’s treasure.

f.w: the fear of the LORD is his treasure

f.g: Firm foundation.

chapters.n: Isaiah describes the crisis: Judah’s brave men cry in the streets, and the envoys who sought peace weep bitterly — their negotiations with Assyria failed.
The highways are empty and travelers have stopped. The enemy has broken the treaty, despised the cities, and respects no one.

f.g: Traveler.

chapters.n: The land mourns and withers. Lebanon is ashamed, Sharon is a desert, and Bashan and Carmel lose their leaves — even the most fertile regions suffer.

f.g: The fertile coastal plain.
Famously lush regions.

chapters.n: “Now I will rise,” says the Lord. “Now I will be exalted; now I will lift Myself up.” God steps in at the darkest moment.
The enemy’s plans are like being pregnant with chaff and giving birth to straw; their own fiery breath will consume them.
The peoples will be burned like lime in a kiln, like cut thornbushes set ablaze.

f.g: Limestone was burned to make lime — reduced to white ash.

chapters.n: You who are far away, hear what God has done; you who are near, recognize His might.
The sinners in Zion are terrified, and trembling grips the godless: “Who among us can live with the consuming fire? Who can dwell with everlasting burnings?” God’s glorious presence is like fire.

f.g: The godless.

chapters.n: The answer: the one who lives righteously and speaks honestly, rejects profit from oppression, refuses bribes, won’t listen to plots of violence, and shuts his eyes to evil. Compare the temple-entrance questions in the Psalms.

f.w: shaketh his hands from holding of bribes
f.g: Refuses to accept bribes.

f.w: shutteth his eyes from seeing evil

chapters.n: That person will dwell on the heights; his refuge will be a mountain fortress, and he will always have bread and water.

f.g: Rocky fortresses.

chapters.n: Your eyes will see the King in His beauty and behold a land stretching far away. The righteous will one day see the Lord.

f.w: Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty
the land that is very far off
f.g: A wide, expansive land — no longer hemmed in by enemies.

chapters.n: You will remember past terror and ask, “Where is the official who counted, who weighed the tribute, who counted the towers?” The Assyrian officials will be gone.

f.g: Recall, think back on.
The one who weighed tribute money.

chapters.n: You will no longer see the fierce invaders with their strange, unintelligible language.

f.g: Obscure, foreign speech.

chapters.n: Look at Zion, city of our festivals! Jerusalem will be a peaceful home, a tent never moved, whose stakes and cords will never break. Latter-day Saints draw the term “stake” from this image.

f.w: a tabernacle that shall not be taken down

f.g: Tent pegs that hold a tent firmly in place.

chapters.n: There the glorious Lord will be for us a place of broad rivers and streams, but no enemy warships will sail on them. God is both supply and protection.

f.g: A warship powered by oars.

chapters.n: The Lord is our Judge, our Lawgiver, and our King; He will save us. He fills every role of government perfectly.
The enemy is like a ship with loose rigging that cannot hold its mast or spread its sail. Its treasure will be divided so abundantly that even the lame will carry off plunder.

f.g: Ship’s ropes and rigging.

chapters.n: No one in Zion will say, “I am sick,” and the people there will be forgiven their sins. Physical and spiritual healing go together.
Isaiah summons all nations and the whole earth to listen. Chapters 34 and 35 form a pair: judgment on the wicked world, then joy for the redeemed.

f.w: Come near, ye nations, to hear

chapters.n: The Lord is angry with all nations and their armies; He has devoted them to destruction and handed them over to slaughter.

f.g: Hebrew ḥerem — devoted completely to destruction.

chapters.n: Their dead will lie unburied, the stench will rise, and the mountains will flow with their blood. The imagery is meant to shock, showing the seriousness of rebellion against God.
The stars will dissolve and the sky roll up like a scroll; the heavenly bodies will fall like withered leaves. Latter-day scripture uses this imagery for the Second Coming.

f.w: the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll

f.g: The stars and heavenly bodies.

chapters.n: God’s sword, prepared in heaven, comes down in judgment on Edom (Idumea), the people He has condemned. In latter-day revelation Idumea stands for the wicked world.

f.g: The Greek name for Edom, Israel’s neighbor and long-time enemy.
Drenched; filled.

chapters.n: The Lord’s sword drips with blood and fat like a sacrificial knife. He holds a “sacrifice” in Bozrah, Edom’s capital — a grim image of judgment.

f.g: A major city of Edom.
Parts offered on the altar in sacrifices (Leviticus 3:4).

chapters.n: Wild oxen, bulls, and steers will fall with them — the powerful leaders of the nation. The land will be soaked with blood.

f.g: Wild oxen — not the mythical one-horned creature.

chapters.n: It is the Lord’s day of vengeance, a year of repayment to defend Zion’s cause. God will set right the wrongs done to His people.

f.w: the day of the LORD's vengeance

f.g: Repayment, retribution.

chapters.n: Edom’s streams will turn to tar, its soil to burning sulfur, and its land to blazing pitch — like Sodom’s destruction.

f.g: Tar.

chapters.n: The fire will burn day and night, its smoke rising forever. The land will lie desolate for generations, and no one will travel through it.

f.w: the smoke thereof shall go up for ever

chapters.n: Desert birds and wild animals will take over. God will measure Edom with the line of chaos and the plumb line of emptiness — undoing creation.

f.g: Measuring line of tohu — chaos (Genesis 1:2).
Plumb stones of bohu — emptiness.
A desert bird, perhaps a pelican or owl.

chapters.n: Its nobles will have no kingdom to rule, and all its princes will vanish.

f.g: Edom’s nobles chose their kings (Genesis 36:31-39).

chapters.n: Thorns will grow in its palaces and nettles in its fortresses. It will become a haunt for jackals and a home for owls.

f.g: Jackals.
Stinging weeds.

chapters.n: Desert creatures and hyenas will meet there; wild goats will call to each other; night creatures will settle there to rest.

f.g: Wild goat, or goat-demon of folklore.
Hebrew lilit — a night creature.

chapters.n: Owls will nest and raise young there, and vultures will gather in pairs. Edom becomes home only to wild birds.

f.g: Perhaps an arrow-snake or owl; uncertain.

chapters.n: Search the Lord’s book and read: none of these creatures will be missing, each with its mate, because the Lord commanded it and His Spirit gathered them. His word is completely reliable.

f.w: no one of these shall fail

chapters.n: God has assigned the land to them by lot and measured it out with His line. They will possess it forever — a solemn reversal of how Israel once received its inheritance.

f.w: he hath cast the lot for them

chapters.n: After judgment comes joy. The wilderness and dry land will be glad, and the desert will bloom like a flower. Latter-day Saints have seen a fulfillment in the gathering to the western American deserts and in Israel’s restoration.

f.w: the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose

f.g: Probably a crocus or similar desert flower.

chapters.n: It will bloom abundantly and sing for joy. The beauty of Lebanon, Carmel, and Sharon — Israel’s greenest places — will be given to it, and people will see the Lord’s glory.

f.g: Lush, fertile regions of Israel.

chapters.n: Strengthen weak hands and steady shaky knees. The prophetic message is meant to encourage the discouraged.
Tell the frightened, “Be strong; don’t be afraid! Your God is coming to set things right — He will come and save you.”

f.w: he will come and save you

chapters.n: Then the blind will see and the deaf will hear. Jesus pointed to such miracles as evidence of who He was.

f.w: the eyes of the blind shall be opened

chapters.n: The lame will leap like deer and the mute will sing for joy, because water will burst out in the wilderness and streams in the desert.

f.w: the lame man leap as an hart

f.g: Unable to speak.

f.w: in the wilderness shall waters break out

chapters.n: Scorching sand will become a pool and thirsty ground bubbling springs. Where jackals once lived, grass, reeds, and rushes will grow.

f.g: Burning sand, or a mirage.
Jackals.

chapters.n: A highway will be there, called the Way of Holiness. The unclean will not travel on it, and it will be so clear that even the simple won’t get lost. Latter-day Saints may think of the covenant path.

f.w: though fools, shall not err therein
f.g: Even the simple will not stray.

chapters.n: No lion or dangerous beast will be on that road. Only the redeemed will walk there, safe from harm.

f.w: the ransomed of the LORD shall return
sorrow and sighing shall flee away

chapters.n: Isaiah 36–39 shifts from poetry to history, closely matching 2 Kings 18–20. In 701 BC, Assyria’s King Sennacherib invaded Judah and captured its fortified cities. His own records boast of taking 46 walled towns and shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem “like a bird in a cage.”

f.g: King of Assyria about 705–681 BC.

f.w: the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah

chapters.n: From Lachish, a major Judean city he was besieging, Sennacherib sent his field commander with a large army to Jerusalem. He stood at the same water channel where Isaiah had once met King Ahaz.

f.g: An Assyrian title — “chief cupbearer” or chief officer — not a personal name.
Judah’s second city; Assyrian palace carvings in Nineveh depict its siege.

f.w: the conduit of the upper pool

chapters.n: Three of Hezekiah’s officials came out to meet him: Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the secretary, and Joah the record keeper.

f.g: Royal herald or chronicler.

chapters.n: The Rabshakeh began his speech: “Tell Hezekiah that the great king of Assyria asks: what are you trusting in?” The question of trust is the theme of the whole confrontation.

f.g: A standard title of Assyrian emperors.

chapters.n: “You claim to have strategy and military strength, but those are empty words. Whom are you relying on, that you dare rebel against me?” Hezekiah had stopped paying tribute to Assyria.
“You’re relying on Egypt, that splintered reed! Lean on it and it will pierce your hand.” Ironically, Isaiah had given the same warning about Egypt.

f.w: the staff of this broken reed

chapters.n: “And if you say you trust the Lord — didn’t Hezekiah tear down His shrines and altars?” The Assyrian misunderstood: Hezekiah’s reforms removed unlawful hilltop shrines to center worship at the temple.

f.w: whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah hath taken away

chapters.n: He mocks: “Make a bet with my master — I’ll give you two thousand horses if you can even find riders for them!” Judah’s army was tiny compared to Assyria’s.

f.g: Make a wager or deal.

chapters.n: “How can you repel even the lowest of my master’s officers, relying on Egypt for chariots and horsemen?”

f.g: Repel, drive back.

chapters.n: Then a bold claim: “Have I come without the Lord’s approval? The Lord told me to attack this land!” It was propaganda, though Isaiah had said God would use Assyria as His rod (10:5).
Hezekiah’s officials asked him to speak in Aramaic, the diplomatic language they understood, not in Hebrew where the people on the wall could hear and lose heart.

f.g: Aramaic — the international language of diplomacy in that era.
Hebrew, the people’s own language.

chapters.n: He refused crudely: his message was for the ordinary people on the wall, who would soon be reduced to eating and drinking their own waste in a siege. He wanted to break their morale.

f.w: the men that sit upon the wall
f.g: The ordinary soldiers and citizens on the city wall.

chapters.n: So the Rabshakeh stood and shouted in Hebrew: “Hear the words of the great king, the king of Assyria!”
“Don’t let Hezekiah deceive you; he can’t save you.”
“Don’t let him persuade you to trust the Lord, promising that the city won’t fall to Assyria.” The enemy attacks faith itself.

f.w: The LORD will surely deliver us

chapters.n: “Don’t listen to Hezekiah. Make peace with me and surrender; then each of you can enjoy your own vine, fig tree, and well.” He uses Israel’s traditional picture of peace as bait.

f.w: every one of his vine, and every one of his fig tree
Make an agreement with me by a present
f.g: Make peace with me; surrender.

chapters.n: “Until I come and deport you to a land like your own, full of grain, wine, bread, and vineyards.” He makes exile — Assyria’s standard policy — sound pleasant.

f.w: take you away to a land like your own land

chapters.n: “Don’t believe Hezekiah when he says the Lord will rescue you. Has any nation’s god saved its land from Assyria?” He puts the Lord on the same level as idols — a fatal mistake.

f.w: Hath any of the gods of the nations delivered his land

chapters.n: “Where are the gods of Hamath, Arpad, and Sepharvaim? Did they save Samaria from me?” All these cities had fallen to Assyria.

f.g: A city whose people Assyria resettled in Samaria (2 Kings 17:24).

chapters.n: “Which god of all these lands has ever saved his country from me? So how could the Lord save Jerusalem?” His boast sets up the Lord’s dramatic answer in chapter 37.

f.w: that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem

chapters.n: The people stayed silent and didn’t answer, because King Hezekiah had ordered, “Do not answer him.” Silence was wiser than arguing with a mocker.
Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah returned to Hezekiah with their clothes torn in grief and reported the Rabshakeh’s words. Chapter 37 tells how Hezekiah turned to the Lord and Isaiah.

f.g: Tearing one’s clothes was a sign of grief or horror at blasphemy.

f.w: told him the words of Rabshakeh

chapters.n: When Hezekiah hears the Assyrian officer’s insulting threats (chapter 36), he tears his clothes and puts on sackcloth—signs of grief and humility—and goes straight to the temple. His first move in a crisis is to turn to God.

f.g: rent = tore; tearing one’s garments was a public sign of mourning or distress.

chapters.n: The king sends his top officials and the senior priests, all dressed in mourning, to ask the prophet Isaiah for help. This chapter closely parallels 2 Kings 19.

f.g: A royal secretary; Isaiah had earlier rebuked a Shebna for pride (Isaiah 22:15-19).

chapters.n: Hezekiah’s message uses a painful image: Jerusalem is like a woman in labor whose baby is ready to be born, but she has no strength left to deliver. The nation is at the critical moment and feels helpless.

f.w: the children are come to the birth
f.g: A proverb for a crisis at its peak with no power to see it through.

chapters.n: The king hopes God has heard the Assyrian’s mockery of the “living God” and will answer it. He asks Isaiah to pray for the small remnant of Judah still standing, since Assyria had already captured most of the country’s cities.

f.g: An Assyrian title (roughly “chief officer”), not a personal name.

chapters.n: A simple transition: the king’s messengers arrive at Isaiah’s home with their request.
Isaiah’s answer begins with comfort: “Don’t be afraid.” The insults were really aimed at the Lord, and the Lord will deal with them.

f.g: Spoken with contempt against God.

chapters.n: The Lord promises to put a “spirit” or impulse in the Assyrian king so that a report will send him home, where he will die by the sword. Verses 37–38 record exactly that.

f.g: Hebrew ruach—wind or spirit; here an impulse God puts in the king’s mind.

f.w: fall by the sword in his own land

chapters.n: The Assyrian officer returns to his king, who has moved from Lachish to attack Libnah, another fortified town in Judah’s lowlands.

f.g: A major Judean fortress southwest of Jerusalem; Assyrian palace reliefs famously show its siege.

chapters.n: News arrives that an Egyptian-Cushite army under Tirhakah is marching against Assyria. Sennacherib, worried about a second front, sends a letter to pressure Hezekiah into surrender.

f.g: Taharqa, of the Cushite (Nubian) dynasty that ruled Egypt; “Ethiopia” here means Cush, south of Egypt.

chapters.n: The letter tries to drive a wedge between Hezekiah and his God: don’t let your God fool you into thinking Jerusalem is safe. It is the same tactic the Rabshakeh used in chapter 36.
Sennacherib boasts of Assyria’s record: they have utterly destroyed every land they attacked, so why would Judah be different?
He lists conquered places in Mesopotamia and Syria whose gods failed to save them. His mistake is treating the Lord as just one more local idol.
More examples of fallen cities and kings, especially in Syria, recently crushed by Assyria. The point: your king will join this list.
Hezekiah does something beautifully simple: he takes the threatening letter to the temple and spreads it open before the Lord, as if to say, “Look at this—it’s Yours to answer.”
Introduces Hezekiah’s prayer, one of the great prayers of the Old Testament.
Hezekiah begins with worship, not panic. He addresses God as enthroned above the cherubim of the ark, the only true God over all nations, and the Creator of heaven and earth.

f.g: The cherubim were the golden figures on the ark of the covenant, symbolizing God’s throne.

f.w: thou art the God, even thou alone

chapters.n: He asks God to listen and look—human language for asking God to act. The real issue is that Sennacherib has insulted “the living God,” unlike the lifeless idols of other nations.
Hezekiah is honest: the Assyrian boasts are true. Assyria really has devastated many nations.
But those nations’ gods were only carved wood and stone, so of course they burned. Hezekiah sees the difference between man-made idols and the real God.
His request aims beyond Judah’s safety: save us so that every kingdom will know You alone are the Lord. Hezekiah prays for God’s name to be honored.

f.w: that all the kingdoms of the earth may know

chapters.n: Because Hezekiah prayed, the Lord answers through Isaiah. The phrasing stresses that the prayer itself made a difference.
The answer opens with a taunt-song against Sennacherib. Jerusalem, pictured as a young unconquered woman, shakes her head and laughs at the would-be conqueror.

f.w: The virgin, the daughter of Zion
f.g: A poetic name for Jerusalem, pictured as an unconquered young woman.
A gesture of scorn in the ancient Near East.

chapters.n: The Lord asks Sennacherib whom he has really insulted. Not a small city or its king, but the Holy One of Israel—Isaiah’s favorite title for God.

God quotes Sennacherib’s arrogant boasts: with his countless chariots he has conquered even the mountains and cut down Lebanon’s famous cedars. Assyrian kings really did brag about felling Lebanon’s trees.

f.g: Carmel means “garden-land” or fruitful forest; a symbol of the land’s richest places.

chapters.n: More boasting: he has dug wells in foreign lands and dried up rivers with his feet, as though nothing in nature could stop him.

f.w: the rivers of the besieged places
f.g: Hebrew may mean “the streams of Egypt” (matsor); many translations read it that way.

chapters.n: Now God answers: Sennacherib succeeded only because the Lord planned and allowed it long ago. Assyria was a tool in God’s hand, not the master of history.
The conquered peoples were weak like grass sprouting on a flat rooftop—it springs up quickly and withers before it can grow.

f.g: Shallow-rooted grass on mud-plaster roofs that dries up fast.
Grain of any kind (wheat or barley), not American maize.

chapters.n: God knows everything about Sennacherib—where he sits, where he goes, and his rage. Nothing the king does is hidden.

f.w: thy going out, and thy coming in

chapters.n: Assyrians sometimes led captives with hooks through their noses. Now God will do that to Assyria’s king—lead him back home like a controlled animal.

f.g: Assyrian reliefs show captives led by rings or hooks; the punishment fits the crime.

chapters.n: Isaiah gives Hezekiah a sign: for two years the people will eat what grows on its own, since the invasion ruined planting, but in the third year normal farming will return.

f.g: Grain that sprouts from seed spilled at the previous harvest.

chapters.n: The surviving remnant of Judah will be like a healthy plant again—roots going down, fruit growing up.

f.w: take root downward, and bear fruit upward

chapters.n: A remnant will go out from Jerusalem and survive, not by their own strength but by the Lord’s zeal—His passionate commitment to His people.

f.w: the zeal of the LORD of hosts shall do this

chapters.n: A very specific promise: the Assyrian king won’t enter Jerusalem, won’t shoot even one arrow at it, and won’t build siege ramps against it. Sennacherib’s own records boast of shutting Hezekiah up “like a bird in a cage” but never claim to take the city.

f.g: Build a siege ramp of earth against a city wall.

chapters.n: The promise repeated for emphasis: he will go back the way he came.
God will defend Jerusalem for His own name and because of His covenant with David—the line through which the Messiah would come.
That very night the angel of the Lord strikes the Assyrian camp, and 185,000 die. The deliverance comes from heaven, not from Judah’s army.

f.w: a hundred and fourscore and five thousand

chapters.n: Sennacherib goes home to Nineveh, his capital, just as Isaiah prophesied in verse 34.

Years later (about 681 BC) Sennacherib is murdered by two of his sons while worshipping his god, and another son, Esarhaddon, takes the throne. The god who could not protect him in his own temple contrasts with the Lord who protected Jerusalem.

f.g: Hebrew Ararat—the region of Urartu, north of Assyria.

chapters.n: Around the time of the Assyrian crisis, Hezekiah becomes deathly ill. Isaiah brings a hard message: get your affairs in order, because you are going to die. The account parallels 2 Kings 20:1-11.

f.g: Give final instructions to your family and household—make your will, so to speak.

chapters.n: Hezekiah turns to the wall—away from everyone in the room—to pour out a private prayer to God.

f.w: turned his face toward the wall
f.g: A gesture of turning away from people to be alone with God.

chapters.n: He reminds the Lord of his faithful life and weeps bitterly. A “perfect heart” means a whole, undivided heart—sincere devotion, not flawlessness.

f.g: Hebrew shalem—whole, complete, wholehearted.
sore = intensely, bitterly.

chapters.n: God responds quickly; 2 Kings 20:4 says Isaiah had not even left the palace courtyard when the new word came.
The Lord, “the God of David thy father,” says He has heard the prayer and seen the tears, and grants fifteen more years. It is a tender witness that sincere prayer can matter to God’s decisions.
The healing is tied to a larger promise: God will also rescue Jerusalem from Assyria. This suggests the illness came during or just before Sennacherib’s invasion in 701 BC.
The Lord offers a sign to confirm His promise, as He had offered Hezekiah’s father Ahaz (who refused one).

The sign: the shadow on the “steps of Ahaz” moves backward ten steps. This was likely a staircase used to tell time by the sun’s shadow. How this happened isn’t explained—scripture simply records it as a miracle.

f.g: Literally “the steps (degrees) of Ahaz”—probably a stairway whose shadow marked the hours.

chapters.n: A heading introduces a psalm Hezekiah wrote after recovering. It appears only in Isaiah, not in 2 Kings.
Hezekiah recalls his despair: in the prime of life he thought he was headed to the gates of the grave, robbed of the years he expected.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol—the realm of the dead, pictured as a city with gates.

chapters.n: He feared he would never again worship the Lord among the living or see other people. For him, death meant losing the chance to praise God on earth.
Two vivid images: his life is folded up like a shepherd’s tent being taken down, and cut off like cloth a weaver trims from the loom.

f.g: Quickly packed up and moved—an image of life’s impermanence.
Or “from the thrum”—the loose threads that tie cloth to the loom.

chapters.n: Through the night he waited, feeling as if God were crushing him like a lion breaks bones. The repeated line “from day even to night” shows how relentless the suffering felt.

f.g: Here likely “waited quietly” or “calmed myself.”

chapters.n: Too weak to speak clearly, he could only chirp like a bird and moan like a dove. He cries, “Lord, be my security”—a plea for God to stand in for him like a guarantor.

f.g: Be my surety; take responsibility for me, as one guarantees another’s debt.

chapters.n: What can he say? God both spoke the word and did it. Hezekiah vows to walk humbly the rest of his life because of what he went through.

f.g: Walk carefully or humbly, sobered by the experience.

chapters.n: He realizes that real life comes from God’s words and acts. He pleads—and rejoices—that God has restored him.
His bitterness turned out to be for his good. In love God pulled him from the pit and threw his sins behind His back—a beautiful image of forgiveness, of God choosing not to look at them anymore.

f.w: cast all my sins behind thy back

f.g: The grave or place of decay.

chapters.n: The dead cannot sing praises in mortal life. This reflects the limited Old Testament view of the afterlife at that time; later revelation teaches much more about the spirit world.
Only the living can praise God now, and Hezekiah intends to do so. Parents passing on God’s faithfulness to their children is a key way that praise continues.

f.w: the father to the children shall make known thy truth

chapters.n: The psalm closes with a vow of lifelong worship and music in the temple because the Lord was ready to save.

f.g: Hebrew neginoth—instruments played with strings, as in many psalm titles.

chapters.n: This and the next verse seem to be added details (found earlier in 2 Kings 20:7-8). Isaiah prescribed a poultice of pressed figs for Hezekiah’s boil—God’s healing came alongside a practical remedy.

f.g: A cake of pressed figs, a known ancient remedy for sores.
A medicinal paste or poultice spread on the skin.

chapters.n: Hezekiah had asked for a sign that he would be well enough to go up to the temple—the place where he most wanted to worship again.
Merodach-baladan, a Chaldean leader who repeatedly rebelled against Assyria, sends a get-well gift to Hezekiah. The gesture was likely political too—he wanted allies against Assyria.

f.g: Babylonian Marduk-apla-iddina II; he ruled Babylon twice (about 721–710 and 703 BC).

chapters.n: Flattered, Hezekiah gives the envoys a full tour of his treasury and armory—everything. It was a proud display, and perhaps a quiet bid to join an anti-Assyrian alliance.

f.g: Fine oil, a valuable trade item.
His armory or weapons storehouse.

chapters.n: Isaiah arrives and questions the king. Hezekiah answers proudly that they came from far-off Babylon—as if that proved his importance.

f.g: Babylon lay about 500 miles (800 km) east of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Isaiah asks what they saw. Hezekiah admits: everything. Earlier he had trusted God alone; here he seems to rely on impressing foreign powers.

f.w: there is nothing among my treasures that I have not shewed them

chapters.n: Isaiah prepares to deliver the Lord’s response.

A stunning prophecy: the day will come when everything in the palace will be carried to Babylon. At the time Babylon was a minor power under Assyria’s thumb; about a century later (586 BC) Babylon did exactly this.
Some of Hezekiah’s descendants will be taken as captives to serve in the Babylonian court. Daniel and his friends were among the young men of royal and noble Judah later taken there.

f.g: Court officials; the Hebrew word can mean high officers as well as castrated servants.

f.w: in the palace of the king of Babylon

chapters.n: Hezekiah accepts the word as good, relieved that peace will last in his lifetime. Some read this as humble submission; others see a hint of shortsightedness. This chapter bridges to Isaiah 40, which speaks comfort to those later exiled in Babylon.

f.w: Good is the word of the LORD
f.g: An acceptance of God’s judgment as just.

f.w: peace and truth in my days

chapters.n: A new section of Isaiah begins with tenderness. After warning of exile to Babylon (chapter 39), the Lord looks ahead to His captive people and says, twice for emphasis, “Comfort My people.” Many scholars think chapters 40–66 address the exiles; Latter-day Saints accept them as Isaiah’s prophetic words.

f.w: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people
f.g: The doubled command shows urgency and deep compassion.

chapters.n: Speak to Jerusalem’s heart: her hard service is over, her sin is forgiven. “Double” may mean she has suffered fully, or that God’s pardon now matches her suffering in full measure.

f.g: Literally “speak to the heart”—tender, persuasive words.
Hebrew tsaba—hard service or term of enlistment, here the time of exile.

chapters.n: A herald calls out to build a road through the desert for the Lord, as servants prepared roads for a king’s arrival. All four Gospels apply this verse to John the Baptist preparing the way for Jesus.

f.w: The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness
Prepare ye the way of the LORD

chapters.n: Valleys raised, mountains leveled, crooked paths straightened—a picture of removing every obstacle. Spiritually, it suggests preparing hearts by humbling the proud and lifting the lowly.
When the way is ready, the Lord’s glory will be revealed and all people will see it together. Latter-day Saints also see a future fulfillment at the Second Coming.

f.w: all flesh shall see it together

chapters.n: A voice tells the prophet to cry out; he asks what message to give. The answer: human beings are like grass and wildflowers—beautiful but brief.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed here—beauty, constancy, or loyalty; human faithfulness doesn’t last.

chapters.n: Grass dries up when the hot desert wind blows. So human life and power fade quickly under God’s breath.

f.g: Hebrew ruach—breath or wind; the scorching east wind that withers plants.

chapters.n: The contrast that matters: people fade, but God’s word stands forever. His promises of comfort and redemption can be trusted.

f.w: the word of our God shall stand for ever

chapters.n: Zion is told to climb a high mountain and shout the good news without fear: “Here is your God!” This is gospel language—the joyful announcement that God is coming to save.

f.g: The Greek Old Testament uses the word family behind “gospel” (euangelion) here.

chapters.n: The Lord comes as a mighty ruler, His arm representing His power. He brings His reward with Him—the people He has redeemed, and justice for all.
The same powerful King is also a gentle Shepherd: He gathers lambs in His arms, carries them close, and leads nursing ewes carefully. Jesus later called Himself the Good Shepherd.

f.w: He shall feed his flock like a shepherd

f.g: Ewes that are nursing lambs.

chapters.n: A series of questions shows God’s greatness: who can hold the oceans in a palm, measure the sky with a hand’s width, and weigh mountains on a scale? Only the Creator.

f.g: The distance from thumb to little finger with the hand spread—about 9 inches.

chapters.n: No one advised God or gave Him directions. He needs no counselor.

f.w: Who hath directed the Spirit of the LORD

chapters.n: The questions continue: from whom did God learn justice or wisdom? The implied answer is no one—He is the source of all understanding.

f.g: The way of justice, right order.

chapters.n: Compared to God, the great nations are like a drop falling from a bucket or a speck of dust on a scale—too small to matter in the weighing.

f.g: Coastlands and islands—distant lands, often around the Mediterranean.

chapters.n: Even all of Lebanon’s forests as firewood and its animals as offerings would not be enough sacrifice to honor God properly.
Before God all nations are as nothing. This is not contempt for people but a reminder that no empire can rival Him.

f.g: Hebrew tohu—emptiness, chaos, nothingness.

chapters.n: So to whom could God be compared? The question sets up a satire of idol-making.

f.w: To whom then will ye liken God

chapters.n: A craftsman casts an idol, a goldsmith covers it in gold and adds silver chains. The “god” is entirely a human product.

f.g: A carved or cast idol.

chapters.n: A poor man who can’t afford gold picks wood that won’t rot and hires a skilled carpenter so his idol won’t topple over. Isaiah’s irony: a god that has to be kept from falling down.

f.g: An offering; here the costly material for an idol.
cunning = skilled.

chapters.n: Haven’t you known this from the very beginning? Creation itself testifies who God is.

f.w: from the foundations of the earth

chapters.n: God sits enthroned above the earth’s horizon; people look like grasshoppers from there. He spreads the sky like a tent curtain for people to live under.

f.g: The vault or horizon; Hebrew ḥug, the circle of sky over the earth.

f.w: stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain

chapters.n: He can bring the most powerful rulers to nothing.
Proud rulers are like seedlings that barely take root—one breath from God and they wither and blow away like straw.

f.g: The dry stalks left after harvest.

chapters.n: The Holy One Himself repeats the challenge: is anyone equal to Me?
Look at the stars: God created them, leads them out like an army in order, and calls each by name. Not one is missing. If He knows every star, He knows each of us.

f.w: he calleth them all by names

f.g: The “army” of stars.

chapters.n: God addresses discouraged Israel, who complain that He doesn’t see their trouble or care about their rights. Many exiles likely felt forgotten.

f.w: My way is hid from the LORD

chapters.n: The answer: the eternal God, Creator of the whole earth, never gets tired, and His understanding is beyond measure. He hasn’t lost track of you.
He gives strength to the worn out and power to the powerless.

f.w: He giveth power to the faint

chapters.n: Even young, fit people get exhausted and stumble. Human strength alone isn’t enough.

But those who wait on the Lord—trusting and hoping in Him—gain new strength. They soar like eagles, run without weariness, and walk without fainting. The Word of Wisdom promise in D&C 89 echoes this verse.

f.g: Hebrew qavah—to wait with hopeful expectation, like a cord being twisted tight.

f.w: they shall run, and not be weary

chapters.n: The Lord calls the distant nations into a courtroom: be quiet, gather your strength, then come and argue your case. The trial will show who is truly God.

f.g: Coastlands—distant nations, especially in the west.

f.w: let us come near together to judgment

chapters.n: Who stirred up a conqueror from the east who crushes kings like dust? Most readers see Cyrus of Persia, named in Isaiah 44:28–45:1, who conquered Babylon in 539 BC.

f.w: the righteous man from the east
f.g: Or “one whom righteousness calls”; often identified with Cyrus the Great.

f.w: as driven stubble to his bow

chapters.n: The conqueror moves so fast he hardly seems to touch the ground, passing safely through unfamiliar territory.
The answer: the Lord did it. He is “the first, and with the last”—present from the beginning to the end of history. Latter-day Saints recognize Jesus Christ as Jehovah, the First and the Last.

f.w: the first, and with the last

chapters.n: The far-off nations tremble at the conqueror’s rise and huddle together in fear.
Their response is to encourage one another—not to turn to God, but to make more idols.
Isaiah mocks the scene: craftsmen cheer each other on, solder the idol, and nail it down so it won’t tip over. They trust a god they have to fasten in place.

f.g: Soldering—joining metal pieces.

f.w: that it should not be moved

chapters.n: In contrast, Israel is God’s servant, chosen, descended from Abraham, whom God called His friend. Israel’s identity rests on God’s covenant, not on idols.
God reminds Israel that He called Abraham from a far country and chose his family—and He has not thrown them away, even in exile.

f.w: I have chosen thee, and not cast thee away

chapters.n: One of scripture’s most comforting verses: don’t be afraid, I am with you; I am your God; I will strengthen, help, and hold you up with My righteous right hand.

f.w: Fear thou not; for I am with thee
the right hand of my righteousness
f.g: The right hand symbolizes power and covenant faithfulness.

chapters.n: Those who rage against Israel will end up ashamed; those who fight against them will disappear.
Israel will look for their enemies and not even find them—they will have vanished.
The Lord takes Israel by the right hand, like a parent holding a child’s hand, and repeats: don’t fear, I will help you.

f.w: I the LORD thy God will hold thy right hand

chapters.n: Israel is small and weak as a worm, yet the Holy One is their Redeemer—the kinsman who buys back a relative from slavery. Christ is the great Redeemer.

f.g: A picture of helplessness, not contempt.
Hebrew go’el—the near relative who rescues or buys back family members.

chapters.n: The weak worm becomes a powerful threshing sledge with sharp teeth that grinds mountains to dust. God will turn weakness into strength.

f.g: A heavy board studded with stones or iron, dragged over grain to break it.

chapters.n: Like winnowed chaff, the obstacles blow away, and Israel rejoices in the Lord—giving Him, not themselves, the credit.

f.g: Winnow—toss grain in the air so the wind blows away chaff.

chapters.n: When the poor and thirsty search for water and find none, the Lord will answer them. He never abandons the needy.

f.w: I the LORD will hear them

chapters.n: God will make rivers flow on bare hills and springs in dry valleys—a new Exodus with miraculous water in the desert.

f.w: I will make the wilderness a pool of water

chapters.n: He will plant a forest of fine trees in the desert. The barren land blooms—a symbol of the restoration of His people.

f.g: The acacia, whose wood was used for the tabernacle.
Probably a cypress or similar evergreen.

chapters.n: The purpose: so everyone will see and understand that the Lord’s hand did it. Restoration testifies of God.
Back in court, the Lord challenges the idols: present your case and your best arguments.

f.g: A title of the Lord as Israel’s true king.
