chapters.n: The test: let the idols explain the past or predict the future. A true God knows history from beginning to end.

f.w: declare us things for to come

chapters.n: Do anything at all—good or bad—just prove you are real! The idols are silent.
The verdict: the idols are nothing, and choosing them is detestable.

f.g: Something morally disgusting to God.

chapters.n: God again speaks of the conqueror He has raised—coming from the north and the east (Persia lay east, and its armies came down from the north). He will trample rulers like a potter treads clay.

f.w: from the rising of the sun
f.g: From the east.

f.w: shall he call upon my name

chapters.n: Which idol announced this ahead of time so we could say it was right? None.
The Lord was first to announce good news to Zion and give Jerusalem a herald of hope.
God looked among the idols and their worshippers for anyone to answer, but no one could say a word.
Final judgment: the idols are empty, their works worthless, their metal images just wind.

f.g: Empty air and chaos (tohu).

chapters.n: The first of Isaiah’s “Servant Songs.” God presents His chosen Servant, whom He supports and delights in, filled with His Spirit, who will bring justice to the nations. Matthew applies this passage directly to Jesus.

f.w: I have put my spirit upon him

chapters.n: The Servant won’t shout or campaign in the streets like a conqueror. His power works quietly.
He won’t snap a bent reed or snuff out a wick that’s barely smoldering. He is gentle with the weak and nearly broken, nurturing them rather than discarding them—yet He faithfully brings justice.

f.w: A bruised reed shall he not break

f.g: A lamp wick that is dimly smoldering, about to go out.

chapters.n: He won’t grow faint or be crushed until He establishes justice on earth, and distant lands will long for His teaching.

f.w: He shall not fail nor be discouraged
f.g: A wordplay: “He will not burn dimly nor be bruised,” echoing the wick and reed of verse 3.

f.w: the isles shall wait for his law

chapters.n: The speaker is the Creator who stretched out the sky, spread out the earth, and gives breath and spirit to every person. The One who made all life commissions the Servant.
God holds the Servant’s hand and makes Him a covenant for the people and a light to the Gentiles. Simeon quoted this when he held the infant Jesus.

f.w: for a covenant of the people

chapters.n: His mission: open blind eyes and free prisoners from dark dungeons. Jesus healed the blind, and Latter-day Saints also see this fulfilled in Christ’s ministry to spirits in prison.

f.w: to bring out the prisoners from the prison

chapters.n: “I am the LORD”—Jehovah—that is My name. God will not share His glory with idols.

f.w: I am the LORD: that is my name
f.g: LORD in small capitals stands for the divine name YHWH (Jehovah).

f.w: my glory will I not give to another

chapters.n: Earlier prophecies have come true; now God announces new things before they happen. Prophecy fulfilled is evidence He is God.
A call for the whole world—sailors, sea creatures, island peoples—to sing a new song of praise because of the Servant’s saving work.

f.w: Sing unto the LORD a new song

chapters.n: Even desert towns and nomads join the song. Kedar was an Arabian tribe; Sela (“the rock”) was a city in Edom.

f.g: Nomadic Arab tribes of the Syrian–Arabian desert, descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:13).
Possibly Sela in Edom, a city carved in rock.

chapters.n: Everyone everywhere should give glory to the Lord.
The Lord goes out like a warrior, roaring a battle cry, and defeats His enemies. The gentle Servant and the mighty warrior are both pictures of the same God.

f.g: Zeal—passionate commitment to protect His people.

chapters.n: God has held back a long time, but now He cries out like a woman in labor—an image of intense effort as something new is born.

f.w: I have long time holden my peace

f.g: In labor, giving birth.

chapters.n: He will dry up the land and waters that stand in the way—a reversal of the blessings in 41:18, aimed at His enemies.
He will lead the blind along unfamiliar roads, turning darkness to light and crooked paths straight. He promises never to forsake them.

f.w: I will make darkness light before them

chapters.n: Those who call idols “our gods” will be shamed and turned back.
God calls to spiritually deaf and blind Israel: listen and look!

Ironically, God’s own servant Israel is the blindest of all. The Joseph Smith Translation rewrites verses 19–22: the Lord will send His servant to the blind as a messenger to open their eyes, and they can be made perfect despite their blindness if they hearken.

f.w: Who is blind, but my servant?
f.g: JST: “For I will send my servant unto you who are blind; yea, a messenger to open the eyes of the blind.”

chapters.n: Israel has seen and heard much but taken none of it to heart.

f.w: Seeing many things, but thou observest not

chapters.n: The Lord was pleased, for the sake of His righteousness, to make His law great and glorious. Israel’s failure is not God’s failure.

f.g: Make the law great, honoring it by fulfilling it.

chapters.n: Yet Israel is plundered and trapped—hidden in pits and prisons, with no one to rescue them or demand their return. This describes the exile.

f.g: No one demands that they be given back.

chapters.n: Who will finally listen and pay attention for the future?
Who handed Israel over to plunderers? The Lord Himself, because they wouldn’t follow His ways. The exile was not Babylon’s triumph over God but God’s discipline.
God’s anger burned around Israel like fire, yet they still didn’t understand or take it to heart. Trials teach only when we let them.

f.w: yet he laid it not to heart

chapters.n: After rebuking Israel, God turns with surprising tenderness: the One who created you says don’t be afraid—I have redeemed you, I have called you by name, you are Mine. Each person belongs to God personally.

f.w: I have called thee by thy name

chapters.n: God doesn’t promise to keep us out of floods and fire, but to be with us in them. It recalls crossing the Red Sea and the Jordan, and the three young men in the fiery furnace.

f.w: When thou passest through the waters
when thou walkest through the fire

chapters.n: As Savior, God paid a ransom for Israel, giving up Egypt, Cush, and Seba—lands Persia later conquered after freeing the Jews. The point is how much Israel is worth to Him.

f.g: A people of the Nile region south of Egypt, or southern Arabia.

chapters.n: Because you are precious, honored, and loved by Me, I would give nations in exchange for you. Few verses express God’s love more directly.

f.w: thou wast precious in my sight

chapters.n: The promise of gathering: God will bring Israel’s descendants from east and west. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled both in the return from Babylon and in the latter-day gathering of Israel.

f.w: I will bring thy seed from the east

chapters.n: God commands north and south to release His sons and daughters from the ends of the earth.

f.w: bring my sons from far, and my daughters

chapters.n: Everyone called by God’s name—His covenant people—was created for His glory. Taking His name brings identity and purpose.

f.w: every one that is called by my name

chapters.n: Bring out the people who have eyes and ears but haven’t used them—Israel, called again as witnesses despite their blindness.

f.w: the blind people that have eyes

chapters.n: Another courtroom scene: let the nations gather and produce witnesses that their gods predicted history. If they can’t, let them admit the truth.
Israel is God’s witness. No god was formed before Him or will be after Him—He alone is God for Israel. Latter-day Saints also understand Jehovah here to be the premortal Christ.

f.w: before me there was no God formed

chapters.n: There is no Savior but the Lord. Latter-day Saints read this as a witness that Jehovah is Jesus Christ, the only source of salvation.

f.w: beside me there is no saviour

chapters.n: God announced, saved, and revealed when no foreign god was among them. Israel’s own history testifies that He is God.

f.g: A foreign god.

chapters.n: From before time began He is the same. No one can snatch anything from His hand, and no one can stop what He does.

f.g: let = hinder or prevent (archaic).

f.w: none that can deliver out of my hand

chapters.n: For Israel’s sake God will send against Babylon and bring down the Chaldeans, whose ships were their pride. The empire that captured Judah will itself fall.

f.g: The ruling people of the Neo-Babylonian empire.

f.w: whose cry is in the ships
f.g: Babylon was proud of river and sea trade; the phrase may also picture them fleeing by boat.

chapters.n: God names Himself: your Holy One, Israel’s Creator, your King.
He reminds them He once opened a path through the sea—the Exodus.

f.w: maketh a way in the sea

chapters.n: Pharaoh’s chariots and army lay down and never got up, snuffed out like a wick.

f.g: Flax fibers used as a lamp wick.

chapters.n: Surprisingly, God says: don’t dwell on the past. What He is about to do will be even greater than the Exodus.

f.w: Remember ye not the former things

chapters.n: “I am doing a new thing; can’t you see it sprouting?” A new Exodus is coming—a road in the wilderness and rivers in the desert as God brings His people home.

f.w: I will do a new thing

chapters.n: Even wild animals will honor God for the water He provides His chosen people in the desert.

f.g: Hebrew tannim—probably jackals.
Probably ostriches.

chapters.n: God formed this people for Himself so they would declare His praise.

f.w: they shall shew forth my praise

chapters.n: The tone turns: yet Israel hasn’t called on Him; they have grown weary of Him.
God says He didn’t burden them with demands, yet they failed to honor Him even in the worship He asked. Perhaps their offerings had become empty or were impossible in exile.

f.g: Sheep and goats.

chapters.n: They didn’t buy Him fragrant cane or bring rich offerings. Instead they turned things around—they burdened Him with their sins. Here is a hint of the Savior bearing the weight of sin.

f.g: Calamus, a fragrant reed used in the holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:23).

f.w: thou hast made me to serve with thy sins

chapters.n: And yet—God Himself wipes out their sins for His own sake and chooses not to remember them. Forgiveness flows from His nature, not from Israel’s merit.
God invites Israel to court: remind Me of your case; argue it, if you think you are in the right.
Israel’s sin goes far back—to its “first father” (probably Jacob) and to its own spokesmen or leaders.

f.g: Likely Jacob, whose early life included deceit (Genesis 27).
Literally “interpreters” or spokesmen—priests and prophets meant to guide Israel.

chapters.n: So God disgraced the temple leaders and gave Israel over to destruction and scorn—a reference to the fall of Jerusalem and exile.

f.g: Leading priests of the temple.
Hebrew ḥerem—devoted to destruction.

chapters.n: Right after describing Israel’s judgment (43:28), God says, “But now listen.” Judgment is not His last word; His chosen servant still has a future.
The Lord who formed Israel from the womb promises help and says again, “Fear not.” He uses the affectionate name Jeshurun, “upright one”—a name expressing what Israel was meant to be.

f.g: Jeshurun, “the upright one,” a poetic pet name for Israel.

chapters.n: Like rain on parched ground, God will pour out His Spirit on Israel’s children. Joel later uses similar language, and Latter-day Saints see it fulfilled in the Restoration.

f.w: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed

chapters.n: Their descendants will flourish like grass and like willows along streams—fresh, green, and growing.

f.w: as willows by the water courses

chapters.n: People will proudly claim the Lord: one says “I belong to the Lord,” another writes “the Lord’s” on his hand. Even outsiders may join Israel by covenant—a picture of conversion and adoption.

f.w: subscribe with his hand unto the LORD
f.g: Write on his hand “belonging to the Lord,” like a mark of ownership or loyalty.

f.w: surname himself by the name of Israel

chapters.n: The Lord is Israel’s King and Redeemer, the First and the Last; there is no other God. The resurrected Christ uses this title for Himself in Revelation.

f.w: I am the first, and I am the last

chapters.n: Who else can announce the future and lay it out in order as God has done since ancient times? Let the idols try.

f.g: Literally “the everlasting people”—the people of long ago.

chapters.n: Don’t be afraid—God told you long ago, and you are His witnesses. Is there any other God? He knows of no other Rock.

f.g: The Hebrew adds “no Rock”—God as the stable foundation.

chapters.n: A long satire begins. Idol makers are empty, and the treasured idols they love are useless. Their gods can’t see or know anything—an embarrassing witness for them.

f.g: Things they delight in—their prized idols.

chapters.n: Who would make a god that profits nothing?

f.g: Cast in melted metal.

chapters.n: Everyone involved will be ashamed. The craftsmen are only humans; let them gather and see how they tremble together.
The blacksmith sweats at the forge, hammering the idol with all his strength until he’s hungry, thirsty, and exhausted. The god he makes can’t even give him a drink of water.

f.g: Or a cutting tool used in metalwork.

chapters.n: The carpenter measures, marks, and planes wood into a handsome human shape—to sit in a house. The idol is shaped like a man and can do even less than one.

f.g: Stretches a measuring line.
A tool for drawing curves and circles.

chapters.n: He cuts down cedar, cypress, or oak, or plants a tree and waits for rain to grow it. Notice: it is God’s rain that grows the wood for the idol.

f.g: Probably a laurel or pine; the exact tree is uncertain.

chapters.n: The same wood is firewood: he warms himself and bakes bread with it—then makes a god from it and bows down to it.
Half of it he burns, cooks meat over it, eats his fill, and says, “Ah, I’m warm!”
And from the leftover piece he makes a god, bows down, and prays, “Save me, you are my god!” Isaiah’s humor exposes how absurd it is to worship what we make.

f.w: Deliver me; for thou art my god

chapters.n: They don’t understand because their eyes are smeared shut and their hearts closed. Idolatry blinds.
No one stops to think, “I baked bread on half of this—should I bow down to the other half, a block of wood?”

f.g: A block or chunk of wood.

chapters.n: Such a person feeds on ashes. A deceived heart leads him astray so he can’t save himself or admit, “This thing in my hand is a lie.” Modern idols—money, status, pleasure—can blind in the same way.

f.w: Is there not a lie in my right hand?

chapters.n: Remember this, Israel: you are My servant whom I formed. I will never forget you.

f.w: thou shalt not be forgotten of me

chapters.n: God has swept away Israel’s sins like a morning mist that the sun burns off. Forgiveness is already offered; the invitation is “Return to Me.”

f.w: I have blotted out, as a thick cloud, thy transgressions
return unto me; for I have redeemed thee

chapters.n: All creation is invited to sing—heavens, depths, mountains, forests—because the Lord has redeemed Jacob and shown His glory in Israel.
The Redeemer who formed Israel is also the Maker of everything, who alone stretched out the heavens and spread out the earth.

f.w: I am the LORD that maketh all things

chapters.n: He frustrates false prophets and fortune-tellers and turns the “wisdom” of the world into foolishness.

f.g: Omens or signs used by diviners.

chapters.n: But He fulfills the words of His true servants and messengers. He declares that Jerusalem will be lived in again and Judah’s ruined towns rebuilt.

f.w: confirmeth the word of his servant

chapters.n: He can command even the deep waters to dry up—recalling the Red Sea, and perhaps hinting at Babylon’s river defenses.

f.w: I will dry up thy rivers

chapters.n: Remarkably, God names Cyrus as His shepherd who will order Jerusalem and the temple rebuilt. Cyrus of Persia did issue such a decree in 538 BC. Many scholars date this passage to the exile; Latter-day Saints see it as genuine prophecy by Isaiah long before Cyrus lived.

f.g: “Shepherd” was a common ancient title for a king.

chapters.n: God calls Cyrus His “anointed”—the only non-Israelite given this title. Cyrus wasn’t a believer, but God would use him to defeat kings and swing open city gates, as Babylon fell to him in 539 BC with little resistance.

f.g: Hebrew mashiaḥ (messiah)—one set apart for a special task.
Strip kings of their belts, i.e., disarm them.
Double-doored city gates.

chapters.n: God promises to go ahead of Cyrus, leveling obstacles and smashing gates of bronze and iron bars.

f.g: brass = bronze in the KJV.

chapters.n: He will give Cyrus hidden treasures stored in dark vaults—Babylon and Lydia were famous for wealth. The purpose: so Cyrus would know the Lord who called him by name.

f.g: Riches hidden away in storerooms and vaults.

f.w: which call thee by thy name

chapters.n: All this is for Israel’s sake. God called Cyrus by name and gave him a title of honor, even though Cyrus didn’t know Him.

f.g: Given you an honorable title.

chapters.n: There is no God besides the Lord. He equipped Cyrus for battle even though Cyrus didn’t know Him—God works through people who don’t yet recognize Him.

f.g: Fastened your belt—prepared you for action.

chapters.n: The goal is for everyone from east to west to know there is no other God.
God is sovereign over everything—light and darkness, peace and calamity. Here “evil” means disaster or hardship, not moral wickedness. Even the rise and fall of empires is under His control.

f.g: Hebrew ra‘—trouble or calamity, the opposite of “peace” (shalom) in this line.

f.w: I form the light, and create darkness

chapters.n: A lovely image: let righteousness rain down from heaven and salvation sprout up from the earth. Latter-day Saints have linked this verse to the restoration—truth from heaven and the Book of Mormon from the earth.

f.w: let the earth open, and let them bring forth salvation

chapters.n: Woe to anyone who argues with his Maker—like a broken piece of pottery criticizing the potter, or clay saying, “What are you making?” or “You have no hands!”

f.g: A fragment of broken pottery.

f.w: Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it

chapters.n: Or like a child scolding his parents for having him. Some Israelites may have resented God for using a pagan king to save them.
God, Israel’s Maker, says in effect: Do you question Me about My children, or tell Me how to do My work?

f.g: Probably ironic: “Would you give Me orders about My own work?”

chapters.n: He made the earth, created humanity, stretched out the heavens, and commands the stars. He has every right to direct history.
God raised Cyrus to rebuild His city and release His captives—not for a bribe or payment. Cyrus’s decree let exiles return and even funded the temple.

f.w: he shall let go my captives

chapters.n: A vision of nations coming to Israel—Egyptians, Cushites, and the tall Sabeans—acknowledging, “God is truly with you; there is no other.” The “chains” may suggest humble submission. Ultimately the nations turn to Israel’s God.

f.g: Tall people from Seba, probably in the Nile region or southern Arabia.

chapters.n: A cry of wonder: truly You are a God who hides Himself—working in hidden ways, even through a foreign king—yet You are Israel’s Savior.
Idol makers will all end in shame and confusion together.
But Israel will be saved by the Lord with an everlasting salvation and never be ashamed—forever.

f.g: Forever (literally “unto ages of eternity”).

chapters.n: God created the earth with a purpose—not to be empty, but to be inhabited. Latter-day Saints connect this to the plan of salvation: the earth was made as a home for God’s children.

f.w: he formed it to be inhabited

f.g: Hebrew tohu—empty, formless (as in Genesis 1:2).

chapters.n: Unlike pagan oracles muttered in secret places, God has spoken openly. He never told Israel to seek Him for nothing; His words are true and right.

f.w: I have not spoken in secret

chapters.n: God invites survivors among the nations to gather and see: those who carry wooden idols and pray to gods that can’t save have no understanding.

f.w: ye that are escaped of the nations
f.g: Survivors from the nations, perhaps those left after Cyrus’s conquests.

chapters.n: Who predicted all this long ago? The Lord alone—a righteous God and a Savior. There is no one else.

f.w: a just God and a Saviour

chapters.n: One of the great gospel invitations: “Look to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth.” Salvation is offered to every nation, not only Israel.

f.w: Look unto me, and be ye saved

chapters.n: God swears by Himself, since there is no one greater: every knee will bow and every tongue will confess Him. Paul applies this to Jesus Christ.
People will say, “Only in the Lord do I have righteousness and strength.” All will come to Him, and those who raged against Him will be ashamed.

f.w: in the LORD have I righteousness and strength

chapters.n: All Israel’s descendants will be justified—made right—in the Lord and will boast in Him, not in themselves.

f.g: Declared righteous, put right with God.

chapters.n: Babylon’s chief gods, Bel and Nebo, are pictured loaded onto pack animals as the city falls—heavy cargo weighing down tired beasts. Idols have to be carried; they can’t carry anyone.

f.g: A title (“lord”) of Marduk, Babylon’s chief god.
Nabu, god of writing and wisdom, son of Marduk; his name appears in kings’ names like Nebuchadnezzar.
Things carried—loads or baggage (not wheeled vehicles).

chapters.n: The idols bow and stoop together; they can’t rescue the load—they themselves go into captivity. Ancient conquerors often carried off a defeated people’s gods.
The contrast: Israel doesn’t carry God—God has carried Israel since birth, like a parent carries a baby.

f.w: borne by me from the belly

chapters.n: Even into old age and gray hair, God will still carry and rescue His people. “I have made, and I will bear”—He takes responsibility for those He created.

f.g: Gray or white hair.

f.w: I will carry, and will deliver you

chapters.n: Who could possibly compare to God?

f.w: To whom will ye liken me

chapters.n: People pour out gold and weigh silver, pay a goldsmith to make a god, then fall down and worship it—spending their wealth on something they own rather than something that owns them.

f.w: lavish gold out of the bag
f.g: Pour gold freely from their purses.

chapters.n: They hoist it on their shoulders, set it in place, and there it stands—it can’t move. People cry to it, but it can’t answer or save. Compare this with the God who carries us (verse 4).
Remember this and act like grown men; take it to heart, you rebels.

f.g: Be firm, stand strong; the Hebrew may mean “take courage” or “be ashamed.”

chapters.n: Remember what God has done in the past: He alone is God, and no one is like Him.

f.w: I am God, and there is none else

chapters.n: God announces the end from the beginning—what hasn’t happened yet. His plan will stand and He will do all He intends. Latter-day Saints see in this God’s foreknowledge and His eternal plan.

f.w: Declaring the end from the beginning

chapters.n: He calls a bird of prey from the east—Cyrus, swooping down on Babylon. What God has planned, He will carry out.

f.w: a ravenous bird from the east
f.g: A bird of prey such as an eagle; a picture of Cyrus’s swift conquest (Isaiah 41:2; 44:28).

chapters.n: God speaks to the stubborn-hearted who are far from doing right.

f.g: Stubborn, hard-hearted.

chapters.n: Yet He brings His righteousness near—salvation won’t be delayed. He will place salvation in Zion for Israel, His glory. Grace reaches even the stubborn.
A taunt-song against Babylon, pictured as a pampered princess who will be pulled off her throne to sit in the dust. Her days of luxury are over. Babylon fell to Cyrus in 539 BC.

f.g: A poetic personification: Babylon as a young, never-conquered princess.
The dynasty ruling Babylon in Nebuchadnezzar’s time.

chapters.n: The princess becomes a slave: grinding grain, hitching up her skirt to wade rivers into exile. This is what Babylon had done to captives; now it happens to her.

f.w: Take the millstones, and grind meal
f.g: Grinding grain was the work of the lowest servants and captives.
Remove your veil—a sign of humiliation for a noblewoman.

chapters.n: Her shame will be exposed. God will take vengeance and spare no one.

f.w: I will not meet thee as a man
f.g: Possibly “I will spare no one,” or “no one will intercede.”

chapters.n: A burst of praise from God’s people: our Redeemer is the Lord of Hosts, the Holy One of Israel. Babylon’s fall is His work.
Babylon must sit silent in darkness—no longer called “queen of kingdoms.”

f.g: Mistress or queen of the nations.

chapters.n: God explains: He was angry with Israel and let Babylon conquer them as discipline. But Babylon went too far—showing no mercy, crushing even the elderly with heavy burdens.

f.g: Profaned My own heritage—let My people be treated as common.

f.w: thou didst shew them no mercy

chapters.n: Babylon thought she would be queen forever and never considered how it would all end.

f.w: I shall be a lady for ever

chapters.n: She lives for pleasure, feels secure, and says, “I am, and there is no one else”—claiming the very words God uses of Himself. She thinks she will never be widowed or lose children.

f.w: I am, and none else beside me

f.g: Lives securely, without worry.

chapters.n: Both disasters will strike in a single day—loss of children and widowhood—despite all her sorceries and spells.

f.w: in a moment in one day

f.g: Magic spells.

chapters.n: She trusted her own wickedness and thought, “No one sees me.” Her wisdom and knowledge led her astray. Pride in human cleverness without God leads to ruin.

f.w: Thy wisdom and thy knowledge, it hath perverted thee

chapters.n: Disaster will come that she can’t charm away or buy off, and ruin will fall suddenly from where she doesn’t expect.

f.w: thou shalt not know from whence it riseth
f.g: Or “you won’t know how to charm it away.”
Avert it, perhaps by paying a ransom or performing a ritual.

chapters.n: A sarcastic challenge: go ahead, keep using all the spells you’ve practiced since your youth—maybe they’ll help!
Babylon was famous for astrology. Isaiah mocks it: let your star-gazers and monthly forecasters stand up and save you. They’ll wear you out but won’t rescue you.

f.g: Those who made predictions at each new moon.

chapters.n: They will burn like straw—not a cozy fire to warm yourself by, but a blaze that consumes them.
All the advisers and merchants Babylon relied on will scatter, each going his own way. No one will save her. Revelation 18 reuses this imagery for the spiritual “Babylon” of the last days.

God addresses Israel, descended from Judah, who use His name in oaths and worship but without sincerity. Nephi quotes this chapter as 1 Nephi 20 and adds the phrase “or out of the waters of baptism,” linking covenant birth to baptism.

f.w: come forth out of the waters of Judah
f.g: Descended from Judah, as from a spring; the Book of Mormon adds “or out of the waters of baptism.”

f.w: but not in truth, nor in righteousness

chapters.n: They claim the holy city as home and say they lean on God, yet their hearts aren’t in it. Nephi’s version begins, “Nevertheless, they call themselves of the holy city,” but adds that they do not stay themselves on God.

f.g: Lean on, rely on.

f.w: they call themselves of the holy city

chapters.n: God announced past events long before they happened, then suddenly brought them to pass.

f.w: I have declared the former things from the beginning

chapters.n: Why announce things ahead of time? Because God knew Israel was stubborn—a neck like iron that wouldn’t bow, a forehead hard as bronze.

f.w: thy neck is an iron sinew
f.g: An unbending neck—stubbornness, like an ox refusing the yoke.
A brazen, shameless forehead.

chapters.n: He told them beforehand so they couldn’t credit their idols when it happened.
You’ve heard and seen it—won’t you admit it? Now God reveals new, hidden things they never knew before.
These new things are being created now, not long ago, so Israel can’t say, “I already knew that.”
Israel never really listened—their ears were closed. God knew they would be treacherous, rebels from birth. Even so, His plan included them.
For the sake of His name and praise, God holds back His anger so as not to wipe Israel out. Mercy flows from His character.
God has refined Israel—not like silver in a smelter, but through the furnace of suffering. Hard trials can purify and prepare a chosen people.

f.g: Some manuscripts read “I have tested you.”

chapters.n: God acts for His own sake so His name won’t be dishonored, and He won’t give His glory to anyone else. 1 Nephi 20:11 reads, “for I will not suffer my name to be polluted.”

f.w: how should my name be polluted?
I will not give my glory unto another

chapters.n: Listen, My called ones: I am He, the First and the Last. These titles belong to Jehovah, whom Latter-day Saints know as Jesus Christ.

f.w: I am the first, I also am the last

chapters.n: His hand laid earth’s foundations and spread the heavens; when He calls, they all stand at attention.

f.w: my right hand hath spanned the heavens

chapters.n: Which idol foretold this? The Lord loves the one He has chosen (Cyrus), who will carry out His will against Babylon. Nephi’s version adds that the Lord “will fulfil his word which he hath declared by them.”
God Himself has spoken and called this deliverer; He will make his mission succeed.

Come close and listen: God has always spoken openly. Then a voice says, “Now the Lord God and His Spirit have sent me.” Many Christians and Latter-day Saints hear the Messiah speaking here, with the Father and the Spirit also present.

f.w: I have not spoken in secret
the Lord GOD, and his Spirit, hath sent me

chapters.n: The Redeemer teaches Israel what is truly good for them and leads them in the path they should take.

f.g: Teaches you what is for your benefit.

f.w: leadeth thee by the way that thou shouldest go

chapters.n: A heartfelt sigh from God: if only you had obeyed! Your peace would have flowed like a river and your righteousness rolled in like ocean waves. Nephi quoted this, and Lehi’s family heard it again in the wilderness.

f.w: then had thy peace been as a river

chapters.n: Their descendants would have been countless as sand—the promise made to Abraham—and their name never cut off.

f.w: Thy seed also had been as the sand

chapters.n: Get out of Babylon! Flee the Chaldeans and shout to the ends of the earth that the Lord has redeemed Jacob. Latter-day scripture repeats this call to leave spiritual Babylon—worldliness.
Just as God gave Israel water from the rock in the Sinai desert, He will care for them on the journey home.

f.w: he caused the waters to flow out of the rock

chapters.n: A sobering close: there is no peace for the wicked. Nephi’s version begins, “And notwithstanding he hath done all this, and greater also,” stressing that even great blessings can’t give peace to those who refuse God.

f.w: There is no peace, saith the LORD, unto the wicked

chapters.n: The second Servant Song. The Servant speaks to distant peoples: God called him before birth and named him. Nephi quotes this chapter as 1 Nephi 21, adding an opening address to scattered Israel, “broken off” because of wicked pastors—which fits Lehi’s family.

f.g: Nephi taught that his people lived on an “isle of the sea.”

f.w: The LORD hath called me from the womb

chapters.n: God made the Servant’s words sharp like a sword and kept him hidden like a polished arrow in a quiver, ready for the right moment.

f.w: my mouth like a sharp sword

f.g: A smooth, sharpened arrow.

chapters.n: God calls the Servant “Israel,” in whom He will be glorified. The Servant embodies what Israel was meant to be—ultimately fulfilled in Christ, and also in faithful covenant Israel.

f.w: Thou art my servant, O Israel

chapters.n: The Servant feels his work has failed—spent for nothing. Yet he trusts that God will judge and reward him. A comforting verse for anyone who feels their efforts haven’t mattered.

f.w: my judgment is with the LORD
f.g: My cause and my reward are in God’s hands.

chapters.n: God formed the Servant to bring Jacob back to Him. Even if Israel doesn’t gather at first, the Servant is honored by God, who is his strength.

f.g: Some manuscripts read “that Israel might be gathered to him.”

chapters.n: Restoring Israel is too small a task; God will also make the Servant a light to the Gentiles, bringing salvation to the ends of the earth. Paul and Barnabas cited this verse as their mission to the Gentiles.

f.g: The survivors God has kept.

chapters.n: The Servant is despised by people and nations, a servant of rulers—yet kings will rise and princes bow because the faithful Lord has chosen him. This anticipates the rejected yet exalted Messiah of Isaiah 53.

In the time of God’s favor He answered the Servant and will make him a covenant for the people, restoring the land’s desolate inheritances. Paul quotes this: “Now is the day of salvation.” Nephi’s version addresses it to “O isles of the sea.”

f.w: In an acceptable time have I heard thee

chapters.n: He will say to prisoners, “Come out,” and to those in darkness, “Show yourselves.” They’ll be like sheep grazing safely along the way home. Latter-day Saints also connect this to the spirit world and temple work.
They won’t hunger or thirst, nor be struck by desert heat, because the Merciful One leads them to springs of water. John uses this image for the redeemed in heaven.

f.w: They shall not hunger nor thirst

chapters.n: God will turn mountains into roads and raise up highways for the journey home.
They come from far away—north, west, and from Sinim. The location of Sinim is uncertain; many scholars think of Syene (Aswan) in southern Egypt.

f.g: Uncertain; the Dead Sea Isaiah Scroll reads “Syene” (Aswan, Egypt). Some older readers suggested China.

chapters.n: Heavens, earth, and mountains are told to burst into song because the Lord has comforted His people. Nephi’s version adds “for the feet of those who are in the east shall be established” and “they shall be smitten no more.”
But Zion complains, “The Lord has abandoned me and forgotten me.” Nephi’s version adds, “but he will show that he hath not.”
God answers with one of scripture’s tenderest images: can a nursing mother forget her baby? Even if she could, I will never forget you. God’s love is more faithful than a mother’s.

f.w: Can a woman forget her sucking child

f.g: Nursing infant.

chapters.n: God has engraved Zion on the palms of His hands. Christians and Latter-day Saints see here the nail wounds in the Savior’s hands—a permanent reminder of His people.

f.w: I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands
thy walls are continually before me
f.g: Like a builder’s plans always in view; God never stops thinking of rebuilding Zion.

chapters.n: Zion’s children hurry home, while those who destroyed her leave.

f.g: The Dead Sea Scroll and others read “your builders hurry.”

chapters.n: Look around! Your gathered children will adorn you like a bride’s jewelry. Gathered Israel is Zion’s beauty.
Ruined, empty places will become too crowded for all the people, and the oppressors will be far away.
Children born to bereaved Zion will say, “It’s too cramped here—make room for me!” A picture of explosive growth after near-extinction.

f.w: The place is too strait for me
f.g: strait = narrow, cramped.

chapters.n: Zion will wonder, “Where did all these children come from? I was alone, a captive wanderer!” The latter-day gathering surprises even Israel.

f.g: Wandering, driven back and forth.

chapters.n: God will raise a signal to the Gentiles, and they will carry Israel’s sons and daughters home in their arms and on their shoulders. Nephi explained this as Gentile nations in the last days helping restore Israel and bringing them the gospel.

f.w: set up my standard to the people

f.g: A banner or flag raised as a rallying signal.

chapters.n: Kings and queens will care for Israel like foster parents and honor them, and Israel will know that those who wait on the Lord are never put to shame.

f.w: kings shall be thy nursing fathers
they shall not be ashamed that wait for me

chapters.n: A doubtful question: can prey be taken from a warrior, or captives rescued from a tyrant? It seems impossible. Nephi’s version reads “For shall the prey be taken from the mighty...”

f.g: Possibly “the captives of the righteous” or, by a small change, “of the tyrant.”

chapters.n: God’s answer: yes! He will fight against Israel’s enemies and save her children. Jacob, Nephi’s brother, quoted this passage as part of his great covenant sermon.

f.w: I will contend with him that contendeth with thee

chapters.n: Oppressors will turn on each other and destroy themselves. Then all humanity will know that the Lord is Israel’s Savior, Redeemer, and Mighty One of Jacob.

f.w: I the LORD am thy Saviour and thy Redeemer

chapters.n: Israel feels God has divorced her or sold her into slavery to pay a debt. God asks: where are the divorce papers? Which creditor did I sell you to? Exile came from Israel’s sins, not from God abandoning her. Jacob quotes this chapter in 2 Nephi 7, opening with “Have I put thee away, or have I cast thee off forever?”

f.w: the bill of your mother's divorcement
f.g: A legal divorce certificate (Deuteronomy 24:1); none exists—God never formally rejected Israel.

f.w: for your iniquities have ye sold yourselves

chapters.n: When God came and called, no one answered. Is His hand too short to rescue? He who can dry up the sea at a word is not powerless. 2 Nephi 7:2 adds “O house of Israel.”
He can dress the sky in black like mourning clothes. Some connect this to the darkness at Christ’s death.

The third Servant Song. The Servant says God gave him a disciple’s tongue to sustain the weary with a word, and wakes him each morning to listen like a student. Christ spoke as one taught by the Father.

f.g: Literally “the tongue of disciples”—trained by listening.

f.w: a word in season to him that is weary

chapters.n: God opened his ear, and he did not rebel or turn back—perfect obedience.

He offered his back to those who beat him, his cheeks to those who tore out his beard, and didn’t hide from insults and spitting. The Gospels record Jesus enduring exactly this before His crucifixion.

f.w: I gave my back to the smiters
them that plucked off the hair
f.g: Tearing out a man’s beard was a grave insult.

chapters.n: Because God helps him, he won’t be disgraced. He sets his face like flint—firm, unwavering resolve. Luke says Jesus “stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem.”

f.w: I set my face like a flint

f.g: Very hard stone.

chapters.n: The One who declares him innocent is near; who dares bring charges? Let them face him in court. 2 Nephi 7:8 reads, “And the Lord is near, and he justifieth me.”

f.w: He is near that justifieth me

chapters.n: With God helping him, who can condemn him? His accusers will wear out like moth-eaten clothes.
An invitation to every believer: if you fear God and obey His servant but are walking in darkness without light, trust in the Lord’s name and lean on God. Faith holds on even when we can’t see.

f.w: walketh in darkness, and hath no light

f.g: Lean on and rely on God.

chapters.n: A warning: those who light their own fires—relying on their own light instead of God’s—will end up lying down in sorrow.

f.w: walk in the light of your fire

chapters.n: God speaks to those seeking righteousness: remember the rock you were cut from and the quarry you were dug out of—your spiritual ancestors. Jacob quotes this chapter as 2 Nephi 8.

f.w: look unto the rock whence ye are hewn

f.g: Cut, carved out (as stone from a quarry).

chapters.n: Look to Abraham and Sarah. God called Abraham when he was just one man and multiplied him into a nation. If God did that, He can restore a small remnant now.
The Lord will comfort Zion and turn her ruins into a garden like Eden, full of joy, thanksgiving, and music.

f.w: he will make her wilderness like Eden

chapters.n: Listen, My people: law and justice will go out from Me as a light to the nations.

f.w: a law shall proceed from me

chapters.n: God’s righteousness and salvation are near and already on the way. Distant lands will hope in His arm—His saving power.

f.w: on mine arm shall they trust

chapters.n: The sky will vanish like smoke and the earth wear out like clothing, but God’s salvation lasts forever.

f.w: the heavens shall vanish away like smoke

chapters.n: You who have God’s law in your heart: don’t fear people’s scorn or insults. 2 Nephi 8:7 is the same.

f.w: the people in whose heart is my law
fear ye not the reproach of men

chapters.n: Those mockers will be eaten like moth-eaten wool, but God’s righteousness and salvation will last for all generations.
Now the people cry out: wake up, Arm of the Lord, as in ancient days! You defeated Rahab and the sea monster—poetic names for chaos and for Egypt.

f.g: Not Rahab of Jericho; a mythic sea monster symbolizing chaos, used poetically for Egypt.
Hebrew tannin—sea monster.

chapters.n: You dried up the sea and made a road through the depths for the redeemed to cross—the Exodus through the Red Sea.

f.w: made the depths of the sea a way for the ransomed to pass over

chapters.n: So the redeemed will return to Zion singing, crowned with everlasting joy, while sorrow and mourning run away. Nearly identical to Isaiah 35:10.

f.w: the redeemed of the LORD shall return

chapters.n: God answers: I am the One who comforts you. Why fear mortal men who wither like grass?

f.w: I, even I, am he that comforteth you

chapters.n: Why forget your Maker who spread out the heavens, and live in constant fear of the oppressor? Where is his fury now? It is gone.

f.w: where is the fury of the oppressor?

chapters.n: The bowed-down captive will soon be freed—he won’t die in the dungeon or go without bread.

f.g: Literally “the one bent over”—a prisoner stooped under chains.

chapters.n: For I am the Lord your God, who stirs up the sea so its waves roar; the Lord of Hosts is My name.

f.g: Or “who stirs up the sea”; either way, God controls the waters.

chapters.n: God puts His words in His people’s mouth and shelters them in His hand, in order to establish a new heaven and earth and say to Zion, “You are My people.”

f.w: I have put my words in thy mouth

chapters.n: Wake up, Jerusalem! You drank God’s cup of wrath down to the dregs. In scripture, a cup can stand for one’s appointed suffering—Christ later drank the bitter cup for us.

f.g: The bitter sediment at the bottom of a cup.

chapters.n: Like a mother too drunk to stand, Jerusalem has no son to take her hand and guide her home.
Two calamities hit her—ruin and destruction, famine and sword. Who can comfort her? In 2 Nephi 8:19 this reads “These two sons are come unto thee,” suggesting two helpers.

f.w: These two things are come unto thee

chapters.n: Her sons lie collapsed in the streets like an antelope caught in a net, overcome by God’s anger. 2 Nephi 8:20 adds “save these two”—many Latter-day Saints connect these to the two prophets in Jerusalem in Revelation 11.

f.g: Probably an antelope or oryx.

chapters.n: So listen, afflicted Jerusalem, staggering—not from wine but from suffering.
The Lord who defends His people takes the cup of staggering from her hand—she will never drink it again. Judgment gives way to mercy.

f.w: that pleadeth the cause of his people
f.g: Who argues His people’s case like a defense lawyer.

f.w: thou shalt no more drink it again

chapters.n: God will give that cup to her tormentors, who forced her to lie down so they could walk over her back like a road. Ancient conquerors sometimes literally walked on defeated foes. 2 Nephi 8 continues into Isaiah 52:1-2.

f.w: Bow down, that we may go over

chapters.n: Zion is told to wake up and dress in strength and beautiful clothes, because the unclean will no longer invade her. The Lord explained in D&C 113 that putting on strength means putting on the authority of the priesthood. This verse is quoted in 2 Nephi 8:24, 3 Nephi 20:36, and Moroni 10:31.

f.w: put on thy strength, O Zion

f.g: Those outside the covenant and those ritually impure—here, invaders who defiled the city.

chapters.n: Shake off the dust, rise and take your seat (on a throne), and slip off the slave collar from your neck. D&C 113:9-10 explains the bands as the curses of God, and the call as scattered Israel returning to the Lord.

f.w: loose thyself from the bands of thy neck

f.g: Sit enthroned, as a queen—no longer on the ground as a captive.

chapters.n: You sold yourselves for nothing, and you will be redeemed without money. Peter teaches that we were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ.

f.w: ye shall be redeemed without money

chapters.n: History review: Israel once lived in Egypt as foreigners and was later oppressed by Assyria for no good reason.

f.g: Live temporarily as a foreigner.

chapters.n: Now again My people are taken away for nothing; their rulers make them wail, and My name is insulted every day. Paul quotes the last line about God’s name being blasphemed.

f.w: my name continually every day is blasphemed

f.g: Wail in grief.

chapters.n: Therefore My people will come to know My name—that I am the One speaking: “Here I am.” Jesus quoted this to the Nephites.

A beloved verse: how beautiful are the feet of the messenger running over the mountains with good news of peace and salvation, telling Zion, “Your God reigns!” Abinadi explained it as referring to prophets and especially to Christ, the bearer of good tidings.

f.w: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet

f.g: Proclaims, announces publicly.

chapters.n: Zion’s watchmen sing together, seeing “eye to eye”—face to face, unmistakably—the Lord returning to Zion. Latter-day Saints also apply it to watchmen united in testimony.

f.w: they shall see eye to eye
f.g: Literally “eye in eye”—they will see directly, with their own eyes.

chapters.n: Jerusalem’s ruins are invited to burst into song together: the Lord has comforted and redeemed His people.
The Lord rolls up His sleeve, so to speak, baring His holy arm before all nations; the whole earth will see God’s salvation. Book of Mormon prophets quoted this repeatedly.

f.w: The LORD hath made bare his holy arm

chapters.n: Leave, leave! Don’t touch anything unclean. Those who carry the Lord’s holy vessels must be clean. Originally about priests bringing temple vessels back from Babylon, the Lord repeats this command in latter-day revelation.

f.w: be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the LORD

chapters.n: Unlike the first Exodus, which was hurried, this departure won’t be a panicked flight. The Lord goes in front and guards the rear—as with the pillar of cloud and fire.

f.w: ye shall not go out with haste

f.g: Rear guard.

chapters.n: The fourth and greatest Servant Song begins (52:13–53:12). God’s servant will act wisely and succeed, and be lifted up and highly exalted.

f.g: Wisely, with success.

chapters.n: Many were horrified at him—his appearance so disfigured he hardly looked human. Christians see the beaten, crucified Christ. In 3 Nephi 21:10 the Savior also speaks of a latter-day servant who would be “marred,” whom many Latter-day Saints associate with Joseph Smith.

f.g: Astonished, appalled.
Face, appearance.

chapters.n: He will “sprinkle” many nations—as a priest sprinkles blood or water to cleanse—and kings will be speechless, seeing what they had never been told. Paul applies the last part to preaching Christ to the Gentiles.

f.w: So shall he sprinkle many nations
f.g: Sprinkling was a priestly act of purification; some translate “startle.”

f.w: the kings shall shut their mouths at him

chapters.n: The heart of the fourth Servant Song. The speakers marvel: who would have believed what we’ve heard? To whom has God’s saving power been shown? Abinadi quoted this whole chapter to King Noah’s priests (Mosiah 14) and explained it as a prophecy of Christ.
He grows up like a tender shoot from dry, unpromising ground. Nothing about his appearance draws attention or marks him as a king. Jesus grew up in humble Nazareth, unrecognized by most.

f.w: as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground

f.g: Attractiveness, splendor.

chapters.n: He was despised and rejected, a man of sorrows familiar with grief. People turned their faces away and didn’t value him. Jesus experienced rejection from His own people and abandonment by His friends.

f.w: a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief

chapters.n: He carried our griefs and sorrows—yet we assumed God was punishing him. Alma teaches that Christ took upon Himself not only sins but also pains, sicknesses, and infirmities, so He knows how to help us. Matthew links this verse to Jesus’s healings.

f.w: Surely he hath borne our griefs

f.g: Hebrew ḥoli—sicknesses; sorrows here means pains.

chapters.n: He was pierced for our rebellions and crushed for our sins; the punishment that brought us peace fell on him, and by his wounds we are healed. This is the core of the Atonement: Christ suffered in our place.

f.w: he was wounded for our transgressions

f.g: Welts or wounds from a whip.
Punishment or discipline.

chapters.n: We all wandered off like sheep, each choosing our own way, and the Lord laid all our sins on him. No one is excluded from either the problem or the remedy.

f.w: All we like sheep have gone astray
the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all

chapters.n: Mistreated and afflicted, he didn’t say a word in his defense—like a lamb led to slaughter or a sheep silent before shearers. Jesus stayed silent before His accusers; Philip taught the Ethiopian about Jesus from this very verse.

f.w: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter

f.g: Silent, unable or unwilling to speak.

chapters.n: Through oppression and an unjust trial he was taken away. Who even considered his fate? He was cut off from life for his people’s sin. Abinadi explained “his generation” as those who become Christ’s seed (Mosiah 15).

f.w: cut off out of the land of the living

chapters.n: They assigned him a grave with criminals, yet he was with a rich man in his death—though he had done no violence or deceit. Jesus died between two thieves and was buried in the rich Joseph of Arimathea’s tomb.

f.w: he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death
neither was any deceit in his mouth

chapters.n: Startlingly, it was the Lord’s will to let him be crushed. As he becomes an offering for sin, he will see his offspring and live long, and God’s purpose will succeed. The Father’s plan required the Son’s sacrifice; after it comes resurrection and “seed”—those redeemed.

f.w: it pleased the LORD to bruise him

f.g: A hint of life after death—fulfilled in the Resurrection.

chapters.n: After his anguish he will see the result and be satisfied. By knowing him, many will be made righteous, because he bears their sins.

f.g: Travail = intense labor, anguish, as in childbirth.

f.w: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many

chapters.n: God gives him a victor’s share because he poured out his life to death, was counted among criminals, carried many people’s sins, and pleaded for sinners. Jesus prayed for those crucifying Him and still intercedes for us.

f.w: he was numbered with the transgressors

f.g: Share the plunder after a victory—a sign of triumph.

chapters.n: Right after the suffering Servant, Zion is pictured as a childless woman who is told to sing, because she will end up with more children than a married wife. The Savior quoted this entire chapter to the Nephites (3 Nephi 22), saying “great are the words of Isaiah.”

f.g: Labor in childbirth.

chapters.n: Make your tent bigger—stretch the curtains, lengthen the ropes, drive the stakes deeper—so there’s room for all the children. Latter-day Saints took the word “stakes” from this verse for local Church units that strengthen Zion.

f.g: The fabric walls of a tent.

chapters.n: Zion will spread out in every direction; her descendants will possess the nations and fill once-empty cities.

f.w: thy seed shall inherit the Gentiles

chapters.n: Don’t be afraid or ashamed. You will forget the shame of your youth (bondage in Egypt) and of your widowhood (exile).

f.g: The disgrace of seeming abandoned—Israel in exile.

chapters.n: Why? Because your Maker is your Husband—the Lord of Hosts, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, God of all the earth. The covenant is pictured as a marriage, with the Lord as a faithful Husband.

f.w: The God of the whole earth

chapters.n: The Lord calls her back like a young wife who was abandoned and heartbroken.
“For a brief moment I left you, but with great compassion I will bring you back.” The time of separation is short compared to the mercy that follows.
In a flash of anger God hid His face for a moment, but His mercy is everlasting kindness. The Hebrew word ḥesed means loyal, covenant love.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed ‘olam—eternal covenant love and loyalty.

f.w: I hid my face from thee

chapters.n: Just as God swore after Noah’s flood never again to flood the earth, He swears never again to be angry with or rebuke His people this way. His covenant is as sure as the rainbow.

f.g: Angry.

chapters.n: Mountains may move and hills shift, but God’s loving kindness and covenant of peace will never be removed. One of the strongest promises in scripture.

f.w: my kindness shall not depart from thee

chapters.n: To storm-battered, uncomforted Zion, God promises to rebuild her with beautiful stones and sapphire foundations.

f.g: Probably lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone.

chapters.n: Her towers and gates will be made of gems. John’s vision of the New Jerusalem echoes this jeweled city.

f.g: Carbuncles = glittering red stones; the Hebrew word suggests sparkling.
Perhaps “battlements of rubies.”

chapters.n: All her children will be taught by the Lord and enjoy great peace. Jesus quoted this to teach that those who come to Him are taught by God.

f.w: all thy children shall be taught of the LORD
great shall be the peace of thy children

chapters.n: Zion will be firmly established in righteousness, free from oppression and terror.

f.w: In righteousness shalt thou be established

chapters.n: If anyone gathers to attack her, it won’t be by God’s doing, and the attackers will fall.
God created the blacksmith who forges weapons and the destroyer who uses them. Since He is over both, nothing can happen to Zion outside His control.

f.g: The destroyer—the warrior or ravager.

chapters.n: A famous promise: no weapon made against God’s servants will succeed, and every accusation against them will be answered. This is their inheritance, and their righteousness comes from God.

f.w: No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper

chapters.n: Like a street vendor calling customers, God shouts: everyone who is thirsty, come! Even if you have no money, come take water, wine, and milk for free. Salvation is a gift, not a purchase. Jacob echoes this in 2 Nephi 9:50.

f.g: An exclamation calling attention—“Hey!” or “Come!”

chapters.n: Why spend money on what isn’t real food, and work for what never satisfies? Listen to God and feast on what’s truly good. Many of us spend our lives chasing things that can’t fill us.

f.w: spend money for that which is not bread

f.g: Rich food—abundance.

chapters.n: Listen and come to Me so your soul may live. God offers an everlasting covenant—the faithful love promised to David. Paul connects the “sure mercies of David” to Christ’s resurrection.
God made David—and ultimately David’s greater descendant, the Messiah—a witness, leader, and commander for the nations.
Israel will call nations it didn’t know, and they will run to it because of the Lord who has glorified His people—missionary work across the world.

f.w: nations that knew not thee shall run unto thee

chapters.n: Seek the Lord while He can be found; call on Him while He is near. There is urgency—don’t put off turning to God.

f.w: Seek ye the LORD while he may be found

chapters.n: Let the wicked abandon their ways and even their thoughts, and return to the Lord. He will have mercy and pardon generously. Repentance changes both actions and thinking.
God’s thoughts and ways are not like ours. Even His forgiveness is beyond what we would expect or give.

f.w: my thoughts are not your thoughts

chapters.n: As high as the sky is above the earth, so much higher are God’s ways and thoughts. Trusting Him means accepting that He sees far more than we do.

f.w: as the heavens are higher than the earth

chapters.n: Rain and snow don’t return to the sky without first watering the ground, making plants grow, and providing seed and bread.
Just so, God’s word never comes back empty. It always accomplishes His purpose. His promises will be fulfilled.

f.w: it shall not return unto me void

f.g: Empty, without result.

chapters.n: God’s people will leave captivity with joy and be led home in peace; mountains will sing and trees clap their hands. All creation celebrates redemption.

f.w: all the trees of the field shall clap their hands
ye shall go out with joy

chapters.n: Thorns and briers—symbols of the curse on the ground after the Fall—will be replaced by cypress and myrtle. This renewed land will be a lasting monument to the Lord’s name.

f.w: Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree

f.g: A fragrant evergreen shrub, a symbol of joy and peace.

chapters.n: Many see a new section beginning here (chapters 56–66), focused on life in restored Zion. It opens with a practical command: be just and do right, because God’s salvation is about to arrive.

f.w: Keep ye judgment, and do justice
my salvation is near to come

chapters.n: Blessed is the person who holds firmly to this, keeps the Sabbath holy, and keeps his hands from evil. The Sabbath was a sign of the covenant, especially important for exiles without a temple.

f.w: keepeth the sabbath from polluting it

f.g: Here simply “a human being,” in parallel with “the man.”

chapters.n: Two groups who feared exclusion: foreigners who had joined the Lord, and eunuchs, who couldn’t have children and were barred from the assembly under the law of Moses. Neither should think God has shut them out.

f.g: A foreigner, a non-Israelite convert.
A tree that bears no fruit—someone with no descendants to carry on his name.

chapters.n: To eunuchs who keep the Sabbath, choose what pleases God, and hold to His covenant, the Lord makes a special promise.

f.g: Grip firmly—commit to the covenant.

chapters.n: God will give them a memorial and name in His house better than sons and daughters—an everlasting name. The Hebrew for “a place and a name” is yad vashem, now the name of Israel’s Holocaust memorial. Covenant belonging matters more than lineage.

f.g: Hebrew yad va-shem—literally “a hand (monument) and a name.”

chapters.n: Likewise foreigners who join the Lord, love His name, keep the Sabbath, and hold to His covenant are fully welcome.

f.w: the sons of the stranger, that join themselves to the LORD

chapters.n: God will bring them to His holy mountain, make them joyful in His house of prayer, and accept their offerings, because His house will be a house of prayer for all people. Jesus quoted this when He cleansed the temple.

f.w: an house of prayer for all people

chapters.n: The Lord who gathers Israel’s outcasts will gather still others besides them. Jesus spoke of “other sheep” not of this fold—Latter-day Saints include the Nephites and others.

f.w: Yet will I gather others to him

chapters.n: A sudden shift: wild beasts are invited to come and devour. With careless shepherds, the flock is open to attack.

f.w: All ye beasts of the field, come to devour

chapters.n: Israel’s watchmen—its leaders—are blind and clueless, like guard dogs that can’t bark, always lying around and loving to sleep.

f.g: Mute dogs—useless as watchdogs.

chapters.n: They are greedy dogs never satisfied, shepherds without understanding, each looking out only for his own profit.
Their motto: “Let’s get drunk; tomorrow will be just as good, only better!” Self-indulgent leaders who assume nothing will ever change.

f.w: to morrow shall be as this day

chapters.n: The righteous die and no one notices. Devout people are taken away, and no one realizes that God may be sparing them from coming evil. Death can be a mercy for the faithful.

f.w: the righteous is taken away from the evil to come

chapters.n: They enter peace and rest—those who lived uprightly. Latter-day revelation calls the spirit world for the righteous a paradise of rest.

f.g: Rest in their graves—death pictured as sleep.

chapters.n: God turns to the idolaters with harsh words: come here, children of a sorceress and of adultery. In the prophets, adultery is often a metaphor for unfaithfulness to the covenant.

f.g: A sharp insult: their spiritual “mother” is witchcraft.

chapters.n: Whom are you mocking—sticking out your tongues and sneering? You are children of rebellion and lies.

f.g: Make fun of, mock.

chapters.n: They inflame themselves with fertility rites under green trees and sacrifice children in the ravines—horrific practices linked to Molech worship that the law forbade.

f.w: slaying the children in the valleys

f.g: Clefts, crevices.

chapters.n: Their “portion” is the smooth stones of the stream—worshipped as idols—instead of the Lord, who should be their portion. Why would God be pleased with such offerings?

f.w: Among the smooth stones of the stream is thy portion
f.g: A wordplay: the Lord was meant to be Israel’s portion (inheritance), not stones.
A grain offering (meat = food in the KJV).

chapters.n: On high hills they set their “bed”—a picture of spiritual adultery at hilltop shrines.
They hid pagan symbols behind their doorposts—where God’s law was supposed to be written—and made covenants with idols. The image is of an unfaithful spouse.

f.w: Behind the doors also and the posts hast thou set up thy remembrance

f.g: Uncovered yourself—exposed yourself to another lover.

chapters.n: They went to “the king”—perhaps the god Molech, whose name resembles the Hebrew for king, or foreign kings—with oils and perfumes, sending envoys far and sinking even to Sheol.

f.g: Hebrew melek; possibly a play on Molech, the god of child sacrifice.
Hebrew Sheol—the underworld, the realm of the dead.

chapters.n: Worn out from chasing idols, they still wouldn’t admit it was hopeless. They found just enough strength to keep going, so they never felt sorry.

f.g: Renewed strength.

chapters.n: Whom were you so afraid of that you lied and forgot Me? Because God stayed quiet, they stopped fearing Him.

f.w: have not I held my peace even of old

chapters.n: God will expose their so-called righteousness and deeds—none of it will help them.

f.g: Sarcastic: “I’ll show what your ‘righteousness’ really is.”

chapters.n: When you cry for help, let your collection of idols save you—a breath of wind will blow them away. But whoever trusts in the Lord will inherit the land and His holy mountain.

f.w: he that putteth his trust in me shall possess the land

chapters.n: A call goes out: build up the road, prepare the way, and remove every obstacle from the path of God’s people.

f.w: Cast ye up, cast ye up, prepare the way

f.g: Build up a raised roadway.

chapters.n: A treasured verse: the high and lofty One who lives in eternity, whose name is Holy, lives both in the highest heaven and with the humble and repentant, to revive their spirits. God’s greatness doesn’t keep Him distant from the broken-hearted.

f.g: Crushed, deeply sorry for sin.

chapters.n: God won’t accuse forever or stay angry always, or the human spirits He created would faint before Him. He knows our limits.

f.w: I will not contend for ever

chapters.n: Because of Israel’s greed, God was angry, struck them, and hid His face; yet they kept going stubbornly their own way.

f.g: Greed for gain.
Stubbornly, perversely.

chapters.n: Yet God says, “I have seen his ways, and I will heal him.” He will lead and comfort them, including those who mourn. Healing comes even to the undeserving.

f.w: I have seen his ways, and will heal him

chapters.n: God creates praise on people’s lips: “Peace, peace to the far and the near.” Paul applies this to Christ bringing peace to both Gentiles (far) and Jews (near).

f.w: Peace, peace to him that is far off, and to him that is near

chapters.n: But the wicked are like the stormy sea that can never be still, constantly churning up mud and filth.

f.g: Mud.

chapters.n: “There is no peace for the wicked,” says God—echoing Isaiah 48:22 and closing this section.
God tells His prophet to shout like a trumpet blast and not hold back: show My people their sins. Prophets are called to speak plainly even when it’s unwelcome.

f.w: lift up thy voice like a trumpet

f.g: Don’t hold back.

chapters.n: The irony: they look very religious. They seek God daily, seem eager to learn His ways, and enjoy drawing near—as if they were a righteous nation.

f.w: as a nation that did righteousness

chapters.n: They complain: “We fasted—why don’t You notice?” God answers: on your fast day you pursue your own business and drive your workers hard.

f.g: Humbled ourselves—a phrase for fasting (Leviticus 16:29).
Demand full work from your laborers.

chapters.n: Their fasting ends in quarrels and fistfights. Fasting like that won’t get your voice heard in heaven.

f.w: ye fast for strife and debate

chapters.n: Is that the kind of fast I want—just a day of looking miserable, bowing your head like a drooping reed, and sitting on sackcloth and ashes? Outward show isn’t the point.

f.w: bow down his head as a bulrush
f.g: Droop like a reed in the wind—a display of piety.

chapters.n: The fast God chooses: break the chains of injustice, lift heavy burdens, free the oppressed, and smash every yoke. True fasting changes how we treat others.

f.w: Is not this the fast that I have chosen?
to let the oppressed go free

chapters.n: Share your food with the hungry, take in the homeless poor, clothe the naked, and don’t turn away from your own relatives. Latter-day Saints practice this through the monthly fast and fast offerings for the needy.

f.w: deal thy bread to the hungry

f.g: Your own kin—fellow human beings.

chapters.n: Then your light will dawn like morning and your healing will come quickly. Your righteousness will go before you and the Lord’s glory will guard you from behind—like Israel’s pillar of cloud.

f.w: thy light break forth as the morning

f.g: Rear guard.

chapters.n: Then when you call, the Lord will answer, “Here I am.” This requires removing oppression, finger-pointing, and malicious talk from among you.

f.w: he shall say, Here I am
the putting forth of the finger
f.g: Pointing in scorn or accusation.

chapters.n: If you give yourself to the hungry and satisfy the afflicted, your light will rise in the darkness and your gloom become like noon.

f.w: draw out thy soul to the hungry
f.g: Pour yourself out—give generously and with real feeling.

chapters.n: The Lord will guide you always, satisfy you in dry seasons, and strengthen your bones. You’ll be like a well-watered garden and a spring that never runs dry.

f.g: Give strength and vitality.

chapters.n: Your people will rebuild ancient ruins and restore old foundations; you’ll be called “Repairer of the Breach” and “Restorer of Streets to Live In.” Latter-day Saints see in this a call to build Zion and restore what was lost.

f.g: One who rebuilds broken walls—restoring what was broken.

chapters.n: If you stop trampling the Sabbath with your own business, call it a delight, honor it, and set aside your own pursuits and idle talk on God’s holy day...

f.w: turn away thy foot from the sabbath
f.g: Stop treading on it—stop treating it as an ordinary day.

chapters.n: ...then you will find joy in the Lord, ride on the heights of the land, and enjoy the inheritance promised to Jacob. The Lord has spoken it.

f.w: ride upon the high places of the earth
the heritage of Jacob thy father

chapters.n: The problem isn’t God. His arm isn’t too short to save, nor His ear too dull to hear.

f.w: the LORD's hand is not shortened

chapters.n: It’s our sins that have built a wall between us and God and hidden His face. Sin causes separation; the Atonement of Christ is what bridges it.

f.w: your iniquities have separated between you and your God

chapters.n: Their hands are stained with blood, their fingers with wrongdoing; their lips lie and mutter wickedness.

f.w: your hands are defiled with blood

chapters.n: No one sues for justice or argues honestly in court. They trust empty words, plot trouble, and give birth to evil.
Their schemes are like hatching viper eggs or weaving spider webs: eat the eggs and you die; crack one and a snake comes out.

f.g: An old word for a venomous snake, probably a viper.

chapters.n: Spider webs make useless clothing—their deeds can’t cover them. Their hands are full of violence.
Their feet rush to do evil and shed innocent blood; ruin follows them wherever they go. Paul quotes this in describing universal sinfulness.
They don’t know the way of peace; there is no justice in their paths, and anyone who follows them won’t find peace.

f.w: The way of peace they know not

chapters.n: Now the people confess: that is why justice is far from us. We wait for light but see only darkness.

f.w: we wait for light, but behold obscurity

f.g: Darkness, gloom.

chapters.n: We feel our way along the wall like blind people, stumbling at noon as if it were night. Among the living we are like the dead.

f.w: We grope for the wall like the blind

chapters.n: We growl like bears and moan like doves, longing for justice and salvation that never come.
An honest confession: our sins are many and testify against us; we know them well. Recognizing sin is the first step of repentance.
We rebelled, denied the Lord, turned from God, spoke oppression and revolt, and muttered lies from the heart.
Justice is pushed back, righteousness stands far off, truth has stumbled in the public square, and honesty can’t get in.

f.w: truth is fallen in the street
f.g: The street or town square was where courts met; truth has collapsed in public life.
Fairness, uprightness.

chapters.n: Truth is missing, and anyone who turns from evil becomes a target. The Lord saw this and was displeased that there was no justice.

f.w: he that departeth from evil maketh himself a prey

chapters.n: God saw no one to step in and was amazed that no one would intervene. So His own arm brought salvation. Latter-day Saints see Christ as the One who came when no one else could save.

f.w: wondered that there was no intercessor
his arm brought salvation unto him

chapters.n: The Lord dresses for battle: righteousness as a breastplate, salvation as a helmet, vengeance as clothing, and zeal as a cloak. Paul borrows this armor for the believer.

f.w: he put on righteousness as a breastplate

chapters.n: He will repay people according to their deeds—wrath to His enemies, even to distant lands.

f.g: Payment, what is deserved.

chapters.n: From west to east people will fear His name. When the enemy rushes in like a flood, the Spirit of the Lord will raise a banner against him.

f.w: When the enemy shall come in like a flood
f.g: Many translators read: “He will come like a rushing river driven by the wind (Spirit) of the Lord.”

chapters.n: A Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from sin. Paul quotes this as fulfilled in Christ, who will save Israel.

f.w: the Redeemer shall come to Zion

f.g: Those who repent.

chapters.n: God’s covenant: His Spirit and His words will stay in His people’s mouths and their descendants’ forever. Latter-day Saints see this in continuing revelation and in parents teaching children the gospel.

f.w: this is my covenant with them
my words which I have put in thy mouth

chapters.n: A burst of joy: “Arise, shine!” Zion is like a woman lying in darkness who is told to stand up, because the Lord’s glory has risen on her like the sunrise. Latter-day revelation echoes this call to the Church.

f.w: Arise, shine; for thy light is come

chapters.n: Thick darkness covers the earth and its peoples, but the Lord rises on Zion and His glory is seen on her. The contrast makes her light visible to all.

f.g: Thick, deep darkness.

f.w: the darkness shall cover the earth

chapters.n: Gentile nations and kings will be drawn to Zion’s light. The gospel spreading to all nations is part of this fulfillment.

f.w: the Gentiles shall come to thy light

chapters.n: Look around! Your sons and daughters are coming home from far away, carried like children on the hip. A picture of the great gathering of Israel.

f.w: thy sons shall come from far

f.g: Carried on the hip, as mothers carried young children.

chapters.n: Zion will glow with joy and her heart will swell with wonder as the wealth of the seas and the nations streams to her.

f.g: Be radiant, beam with joy.
The wealth or riches of the nations.

chapters.n: Caravans of camels from Midian, Ephah, and Sheba will bring gold and incense and proclaim the Lord’s praise. Christians have long seen a foreshadowing in the wise men’s gifts to the Christ child.

f.w: they shall bring gold and incense

f.g: Young camels used for swift travel.
A wealthy kingdom in southern Arabia (modern Yemen), famous for incense.

chapters.n: Flocks from Kedar and rams from Nebaioth—Arabian tribes descended from Ishmael—will be accepted on God’s altar as He glorifies His temple. Ishmael’s descendants join in worship.

f.g: An Ishmaelite tribe (Genesis 25:13).
Ishmael’s firstborn son and the tribe from him (Genesis 25:13).

chapters.n: Who are these flying like clouds, like doves to their dovecotes? Ships with white sails hurrying God’s people home—or, as some Latter-day Saints have suggested, modern travel by air.

f.w: as the doves to their windows
f.g: Like doves returning to the openings of their nesting houses.

chapters.n: Distant coastlands wait for the Lord, with the ships of Tarshish leading the way, bringing Zion’s children home along with their silver and gold, to honor the Lord.

f.g: Large ocean-going merchant ships; Tarshish was a distant port, perhaps in Spain.

f.w: Surely the isles shall wait for me

chapters.n: Foreigners will rebuild Zion’s walls and their kings will serve her. God struck her in anger, but now shows favor and mercy.

f.w: the sons of strangers shall build up thy walls
in my favour have I had mercy on thee

chapters.n: Zion’s gates will stay open day and night, with no fear of attack, so the wealth of nations and their kings can enter. John sees this in the New Jerusalem.

f.w: thy gates shall be open continually

chapters.n: Nations that refuse to serve Zion will perish—meaning those that fight against God’s kingdom will not last.
Lebanon’s finest trees will come to beautify God’s sanctuary, the place where His feet rest. Solomon’s temple was built with Lebanon’s cedar.
Children of Zion’s oppressors will bow before her and call her “The City of the Lord, Zion of the Holy One of Israel.” Former enemies come to honor her.
Once abandoned and hated, with no one passing through, Zion will become majestic forever, a joy to all generations.

f.g: Everlasting pride, majesty.

chapters.n: Zion will be nourished by nations and kings like a baby at the breast, and will know that the Lord is her Savior, Redeemer, and Mighty One of Jacob.

f.w: suck the milk of the Gentiles
I the LORD am thy Saviour and thy Redeemer

chapters.n: Everything will be upgraded: gold instead of bronze, silver instead of iron. Her rulers will be peace and her overseers righteousness—a government of goodness.

f.g: Exactors = taskmasters or tax collectors; they will be replaced by righteousness.

chapters.n: No more violence, ruin, or destruction. Zion’s walls will be called Salvation and her gates Praise.

f.w: thou shalt call thy walls Salvation

chapters.n: The sun and moon won’t be needed, because the Lord Himself will be Zion’s everlasting light and glory. John uses this image for the celestial city.

f.w: the LORD shall be unto thee an everlasting light

chapters.n: Her sun will never set or her moon wane; the Lord will be her endless light, and her days of mourning will be over.

f.w: the days of thy mourning shall be ended

chapters.n: All her people will be righteous and inherit the land forever—a shoot God planted, the work of His hands, to show His glory.

f.w: they shall inherit the land for ever

chapters.n: The smallest will become a thousand, the weakest a mighty nation. “I the Lord will hasten it in its time.” Latter-day Saints have often applied this to the growth of the Church and the gathering.

f.w: A little one shall become a thousand
I the LORD will hasten it in his time

chapters.n: An anointed messenger speaks: God’s Spirit is on him to bring good news to the humble, heal broken hearts, free captives, and open prison doors. In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus read this and declared, “This day is this scripture fulfilled.”

f.w: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me

f.g: Anointed—Hebrew mashaḥ, the root of “Messiah.”

f.w: the opening of the prison to them that are bound

chapters.n: He announces the year of the Lord’s favor—like the jubilee year when debts were forgiven and slaves freed—and the day of God’s vengeance, and comforts all who mourn. Notably, Jesus stopped reading before “the day of vengeance,” suggesting that part belongs to His Second Coming.

f.w: the acceptable year of the LORD
f.g: The year of God’s favor, recalling the jubilee (Leviticus 25:10).

f.w: the day of vengeance of our God

chapters.n: He gives mourners a crown of beauty instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of grief, and a garment of praise instead of a heavy spirit. They will be called oaks of righteousness, planted by the Lord. In Hebrew “beauty” (pe’er) and “ashes” (efer) rhyme.

f.g: A headdress or garland instead of the ashes mourners put on their heads; a wordplay in Hebrew.
Fragrant oil used at festive occasions instead of mourning.

chapters.n: These healed people will rebuild ancient ruins and restore cities devastated for generations.

f.w: they shall build the old wastes

chapters.n: Foreigners will tend the flocks and fields, freeing Israel for a holy calling.

f.g: Workers who tend grapevines.

chapters.n: Israel will be called “Priests of the Lord” and “Ministers of our God”—fulfilling God’s original intent for them to be a kingdom of priests. Peter applies this to all believers.

f.w: ye shall be named the Priests of the LORD

chapters.n: Instead of shame, they receive a double portion—the firstborn’s inheritance—and everlasting joy.

f.g: A double portion was the firstborn son’s inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17).

chapters.n: The Lord loves justice and hates robbery even when disguised as offerings. He will faithfully reward His people and make an everlasting covenant with them.

f.w: I hate robbery for burnt offering
f.g: Possibly “robbery and wrongdoing”; God despises worship funded by injustice.

chapters.n: Their descendants will be recognized among the nations as a people blessed by the Lord.

f.w: the seed which the LORD hath blessed
