chapters.n: A song of joy: God has dressed me in garments of salvation and a robe of righteousness, like a groom with a festive headdress or a bride wearing her jewels. Nephi prayed for the Lord to encircle him in “the robe of thy righteousness.”

f.w: as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments
f.g: The Hebrew suggests a priestly turban worn like a crown.

chapters.n: As surely as earth makes seeds sprout in a garden, God will make righteousness and praise spring up before all nations.

f.w: as the earth bringeth forth her bud

chapters.n: The speaker—the prophet, or the Lord Himself—vows not to keep quiet or rest until Zion’s righteousness shines like dawn and her salvation blazes like a torch.

f.w: For Zion's sake will I not hold my peace

chapters.n: Nations and kings will see her glory, and the Lord Himself will give her a new name. In scripture a new name marks a new identity and covenant relationship.

f.w: thou shalt be called by a new name

chapters.n: Zion will be a beautiful crown held in God’s hand—His treasured, honored possession.

f.g: A royal headband or crown.

chapters.n: No longer called “Forsaken” or “Desolate,” Zion will be named Hephzibah, “My delight is in her,” and her land Beulah, “Married.” The covenant relationship is restored like a joyful marriage.

f.g: Hebrew: “My delight is in her.” Also the name of Hezekiah’s wife (2 Kings 21:1).
Hebrew: “Married.”

chapters.n: As a young man marries a bride, so Zion’s children will claim her, and as a groom rejoices over his bride, God will rejoice over His people.

f.w: as the bridegroom rejoiceth over the bride

chapters.n: God has posted watchmen on Jerusalem’s walls who pray day and night without stopping. Those who “remind” the Lord in prayer must not be silent.

f.w: I have set watchmen upon thy walls
ye that make mention of the LORD
f.g: Those who call on the Lord or remind Him in prayer—intercessors.

chapters.n: Give the Lord no rest until He establishes Jerusalem and makes her the praise of the earth. A bold invitation to persistent prayer.
God swears by His powerful right arm that enemies will no longer seize Israel’s grain or foreigners drink her wine.

f.w: The LORD hath sworn by his right hand

f.g: Grain.

chapters.n: Those who harvest will eat and praise the Lord, and those who gather grapes will drink in the courts of His sanctuary—celebrating festivals in peace.
Go out through the gates! Build the road for the people, clear the stones, and raise a banner for the nations. The way home for God’s people is being prepared.

f.w: cast up, cast up the highway
lift up a standard for the people

chapters.n: The Lord has announced to the whole world: tell Zion, your salvation is coming, bringing His reward with Him. In Hebrew “salvation” is yeshu‘ah, closely related to the name Jesus (Yeshua).

f.g: Hebrew yesha‘ / yeshu‘ah—close to the name Yeshua (Jesus).

chapters.n: God’s people will be called “The Holy People” and “The Redeemed of the Lord,” and Zion will be called “Sought Out” and “A City Not Forsaken.” She who felt abandoned is now pursued by God’s love.

A watchman sees a majestic warrior approaching from Edom, from its city Bozrah, in crimson-stained clothes. He answers, “It is I, speaking in righteousness, mighty to save.” D&C 133 applies this scene to Christ’s Second Coming in red apparel.

f.w: Who is this that cometh from Edom

f.g: A major city of Edom; “Bozrah” sounds like the Hebrew for grape harvest.
Israel’s longtime enemy; in the prophets it often stands for the world opposed to God (Isaiah 34:5-6; D&C 1:36).

chapters.n: Why are your clothes red, like someone who has been treading grapes in a winepress?

f.g: Wine vat—a stone pit where people stomped grapes barefoot.

f.w: Wherefore art thou red in thine apparel

chapters.n: “I have trodden the winepress alone; no one was with me.” In context it describes judgment on the wicked, but Latter-day Saints also hear the Savior’s solitary suffering in Gethsemane, where He alone bore the full weight of sin.

f.w: I have trodden the winepress alone
of the people there was none with me

chapters.n: The day of vengeance was in His heart, and the year of His redeemed had come. Judgment on evil and redemption of His people come together.

f.w: the year of my redeemed is come

chapters.n: He looked, but no one helped; amazed that no one stepped in, His own arm brought salvation. Only the Savior could accomplish the Atonement.

f.w: mine own arm brought salvation unto me
I wondered that there was none to uphold

chapters.n: He trampled the nations in His wrath and made them drunk with His fury—the cup of judgment.

f.w: make them drunk in my fury

chapters.n: The tone shifts to a beautiful prayer of remembrance. The prophet recalls the Lord’s acts of loving kindness and great goodness toward Israel.

f.g: Hebrew ḥasdei YHWH—the Lord’s acts of faithful covenant love.

chapters.n: God had said, “Surely they are My people, children who will not betray Me,” and so He became their Savior. His trust in His people was moving—and they would test it.

f.g: Children who will not be false or disloyal.

chapters.n: In all their suffering He suffered too, and the angel of His presence saved them. In His love and pity He redeemed them and carried them all along. God is not distant from our pain—He feels it with us. D&C 133:53 quotes this verse.

f.w: In all their affliction he was afflicted
he bare them, and carried them

chapters.n: But they rebelled and grieved His Holy Spirit, so He became like an enemy and fought against them. Paul warns not to grieve the Holy Spirit.

f.g: Grieved, caused sorrow.

chapters.n: Then the people remembered the days of Moses: Where is the God who brought them up through the sea with their shepherd? Where is He who put His Holy Spirit among them?

f.g: Moses (and perhaps Aaron).

f.w: he that put his holy Spirit within him

chapters.n: Who guided Moses’s right hand with His glorious arm and split the sea before them to make an everlasting name?
Who led them through the depths as surefooted as a horse running on open ground, so they didn’t stumble?

f.w: as an horse in the wilderness
f.g: Like a horse on open, level ground—steady and sure.

chapters.n: Like cattle going down into a peaceful valley, the Spirit of the Lord gave them rest. So God led His people and made His name glorious.

f.w: the Spirit of the LORD caused him to rest

chapters.n: A plea: look down from heaven! Where is Your zeal and might? Where is Your deep tender compassion? Why are You holding it back from me?

f.g: The stirring of Your inner feelings—in Hebrew thought the bowels were the seat of deep compassion.

chapters.n: You are our Father, even if Abraham and Jacob wouldn’t recognize us. You, Lord, are our Father and Redeemer; that has always been Your name. A rare and tender Old Testament address to God as Father.

f.w: thou, O LORD, art our father

f.g: Even if our ancestors would disown us, God will not.

chapters.n: Why did You let us wander and harden our hearts? Come back for the sake of Your servants. The question reflects Hebrew thinking that God is ultimately behind all events; it is also an honest cry of grief.

f.w: why hast thou made us to err from thy ways
f.g: Hebrew idiom often credits God with permitting what people choose.

chapters.n: Your holy people held the land only a short time; now enemies have trampled Your sanctuary—likely a reference to the temple’s destruction.

f.w: our adversaries have trodden down thy sanctuary

chapters.n: We have become like people You never ruled, never called by Your name. The plea: claim us again as Your own.

f.w: they were not called by thy name

chapters.n: The prayer from chapter 63 continues with a passionate cry: “Oh, that You would tear open the heavens and come down,” so that mountains would melt before You. D&C 133 quotes this in describing the Second Coming.

f.w: Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens

f.g: Tear open.

chapters.n: Come like a fire that sets brushwood ablaze and makes water boil, so Your enemies know Your name and the nations tremble.

f.g: Fire burning brushwood.

f.w: the nations may tremble at thy presence

chapters.n: Remember when You did awesome things we never expected, came down, and the mountains shook—as at Mount Sinai.

f.w: the mountains flowed down at thy presence

f.g: Awe-inspiring deeds.

chapters.n: Since the world began no one has heard or seen any God besides You who acts for those who wait for Him. Paul adapts this to say no eye has seen what God has prepared for those who love Him; the Lord echoes it in D&C 76.
God meets those who gladly do right and remember His ways. But we sinned and He was angry. The last line is hard to translate; the KJV hopes that by continuing in God’s ways “we shall be saved.”

f.w: Thou meetest him that rejoiceth and worketh righteousness

f.g: In Your ways is permanence; the Hebrew here is difficult.

chapters.n: A famous confession: we have all become unclean, and even our best deeds are like stained rags. We wither like leaves, and our sins blow us away like wind. Without God’s grace, human goodness can’t save us.

f.w: all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags
we all do fade as a leaf

chapters.n: No one calls on God’s name or stirs himself to hold on to Him, because God has hidden His face and let them melt away in their sins.

f.w: stirreth up himself to take hold of thee

chapters.n: “But now, Lord, You are our Father. We are the clay; You are the potter. We are all the work of Your hands.” An appeal to God’s love as Creator and Father, and a humble willingness to be reshaped.

f.w: we are the clay, and thou our potter

chapters.n: Please don’t be angry beyond measure or remember our sins forever. Look—we are all Your people.

f.g: Exceedingly.

chapters.n: Your holy cities have become a desert; Zion is a wilderness and Jerusalem a ruin.
Our holy and beautiful temple, where our ancestors praised You, has been burned, and all our treasures lie in ruins. The Babylonians burned Solomon’s temple in 586 BC.

f.g: Precious, treasured things.

chapters.n: After all this, will You hold back, Lord? Will You stay silent and keep afflicting us so severely? The prayer ends with an open question that chapter 65 answers.
God answers the prayer of chapter 64: He has been ready to be found all along, even by people who didn’t look for Him, calling “Here I am, here I am.” Paul applies this to Gentiles coming to Christ.

f.w: I am found of them that sought me not

f.g: Literally “Here I am, here I am”—God eagerly offering Himself.

chapters.n: All day long God held out His hands to a rebellious people who followed their own ideas. The image is of a parent reaching out with open arms; Jacob uses it in the Book of Mormon.

f.w: I have spread out my hands all the day

chapters.n: They provoke God openly—offering sacrifices in sacred gardens and burning incense on brick altars, practices tied to pagan worship and forbidden by the law.

f.g: God’s law required altars of earth or uncut stone (Exodus 20:24-25).

chapters.n: They sit among tombs and spend nights in secret places—probably trying to contact the dead—and eat pork and unclean broth, things the law of Moses forbade.

f.g: Likely seeking oracles from the dead.

chapters.n: Worst of all, they say, “Keep away—I’m holier than you!” Such smug pride is like smoke in God’s nose—a constant irritation.
It’s all written down before God. He won’t stay silent; He will repay them fully—into their lap, as grain was measured into a fold of one’s robe.

f.g: Pay back into the fold of their garment, like measured grain.

chapters.n: He will repay their sins and their ancestors’ sins, who burned incense on hilltops and insulted Him there.
But not everyone will be destroyed. Just as people say “Don’t destroy that grape cluster—there’s still good juice in it,” God will spare His faithful servants.

f.w: Destroy it not; for a blessing is in it
f.g: Possibly the opening words of a vintage song.

chapters.n: He will bring out descendants from Jacob and heirs from Judah to inherit His mountains; His chosen ones will live there.
From the Plain of Sharon in the west to the Valley of Achor in the east, the land will be peaceful pasture for those who seek the Lord. Achor, once a place of judgment, becomes a place of hope.

f.g: The fertile coastal plain of Israel.
“Valley of Trouble,” near Jericho, where Achan was judged (Joshua 7:24-26).

chapters.n: But those who abandon the Lord and set tables for Gad and Meni—gods of “Fortune” and “Destiny”—are another story.

f.g: Hebrew Gad—a god of good luck.
Hebrew Meni—a god of fate or destiny.

chapters.n: So God will “destine” them for the sword (a wordplay on Meni). When He called, they didn’t answer; they chose what He hated.

f.w: when I called, ye did not answer

chapters.n: Contrast: God’s servants will eat, drink, and rejoice, while the rebellious go hungry, thirsty, and ashamed.
His servants will sing from glad hearts; the rebels will cry from broken hearts and wail in anguish.

f.g: A crushed or tormented spirit.

chapters.n: Their name will become a curse word among God’s chosen, but He will give His servants a different name—a new identity.

f.w: call his servants by another name

chapters.n: Anyone who blesses or takes an oath will do it by “the God of truth”—literally “the God of Amen,” whose word is sure—because past troubles are forgotten.

f.g: Hebrew “God of Amen”—the God who is faithful and reliable.

chapters.n: God announces: “I create new heavens and a new earth,” and the former troubles won’t even come to mind. Latter-day Saints understand the earth will be renewed in the Millennium and ultimately glorified.

f.w: I create new heavens and a new earth
f.r: Isaiah 66:22; 2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1; Articles of Faith 1:10; D&C 101:25

chapters.n: Be glad and rejoice forever in what God creates: He will make Jerusalem a joy and her people a delight.
God Himself will rejoice in Jerusalem, and weeping and crying will never be heard there again.

f.w: the voice of weeping shall be no more heard in her

chapters.n: No more infant deaths or lives cut short; someone who dies at a hundred will be considered young. D&C 101 explains that in the Millennium people will live to the “age of a tree” and then be changed in the twinkling of an eye.

f.w: the child shall die an hundred years old

f.g: A baby who lives only a few days.

chapters.n: People will build houses and live in them, plant vineyards and eat their fruit—enjoying the results of their own work.

f.w: they shall build houses, and inhabit them

chapters.n: No one will lose their home or harvest to invaders. God’s people will live long like trees and enjoy what their hands have made.

f.w: as the days of a tree

chapters.n: Their work won’t be wasted and their children won’t be born into disaster, because they and their children are blessed by the Lord.

f.w: They shall not labour in vain

chapters.n: Before they even call, God will answer; while they’re still speaking, He will hear. Perfect closeness between God and His people.

f.w: before they call, I will answer

chapters.n: Wolf and lamb will graze together, the lion will eat straw like an ox, and the serpent will eat dust. Nothing will hurt or destroy on God’s holy mountain—a picture of millennial peace that echoes Isaiah 11.

f.w: The wolf and the lamb shall feed together
dust shall be the serpent's meat

chapters.n: Isaiah’s final chapter opens with God’s greatness: heaven is His throne and earth His footstool. What house could people build that would contain Him? Stephen quoted this before he was martyred.

f.w: The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool

chapters.n: God made all of it. But the person He looks to with favor is the humble, contrite one who trembles at His word. God values a humble heart more than grand buildings.

f.w: him that is poor and of a contrite spirit

f.g: Reveres God’s word and takes it seriously.

chapters.n: For the hypocritical, sacrifices are no better than murder or pagan offerings—sacrificing an ox is like killing a man; offering incense is like praising an idol. Ritual without a right heart is offensive to God.

f.w: He that killeth an ox is as if he slew a man

f.g: Grain offering.

chapters.n: Since they chose their own ways, God will let them have the consequences they dread. When He called, no one answered.

f.w: I also will choose their delusions
f.g: I will choose their punishments—let their own choices rebound on them.

f.w: when I called, none did answer

chapters.n: A word of comfort to the faithful who tremble at God’s word: your own relatives hated and excluded you because of Me, mocking, “Let the Lord show His glory!” But He will appear to your joy, and they will be put to shame.

f.w: cast you out for my name's sake

chapters.n: Hear that uproar from the city, that voice from the temple! It is the Lord repaying His enemies.
An amazing image: Zion gives birth before her labor even begins—a son delivered before the pains came. Restoration comes with unexpected speed.

f.w: she was delivered of a man child

chapters.n: Who has ever heard of such a thing? Can a land be born in one day, a nation in a moment? Yet as soon as Zion went into labor, her children were born.

f.w: shall a nation be born at once?
f.g: Many have connected this to the sudden rebirth of Israel or to the rapid latter-day gathering.

chapters.n: Would God bring a birth to the very moment of delivery and then not allow it? Of course not. He finishes what He begins.

f.w: shall I cause to bring forth, and shut the womb?

chapters.n: All who love Jerusalem and mourned over her should now rejoice with her.
Zion is pictured as a nursing mother; her children drink deeply from her comfort and abundance.

f.g: The comforting nourishment Zion provides, like a mother’s milk.

chapters.n: God will send peace flowing to Zion like a river and the wealth of nations like an overflowing stream. Her children will be carried on her hip and bounced on her knees.

f.w: I will extend peace to her like a river

f.g: Bounced playfully, as a parent does with a baby.

chapters.n: “As a mother comforts her child, so I will comfort you.” One of the most tender images of God in scripture.

f.w: As one whom his mother comforteth

chapters.n: When you see this, your heart will rejoice and your body will flourish like fresh grass. God’s hand will be clear—blessing His servants and opposing His enemies.

f.w: your bones shall flourish like an herb

chapters.n: The Lord will come in fire, with chariots like a whirlwind, bringing judgment. Scripture repeatedly connects fire with the Second Coming.

f.w: the LORD will come with fire

chapters.n: By fire and sword the Lord will judge all humanity, and many will fall.

f.w: will the LORD plead with all flesh
f.g: Enter into judgment with all people.

chapters.n: Those who “sanctify” themselves for pagan rites in gardens, following a leader in the middle, and eat pork, rodents, and other detestable things will perish together.

f.w: behind one tree in the midst
f.g: Possibly “following one in the middle”—a cult leader or priest of a pagan rite.

chapters.n: God knows their works and thoughts. The time is coming when He will gather all nations and languages to see His glory.

f.w: I will gather all nations and tongues

chapters.n: God will set a sign among them and send survivors as messengers to distant nations—Tarshish, Put, Lud, Tubal, Javan (Greece), and faraway coastlands—to declare His glory to those who never heard. A remarkable picture of worldwide missionary work.

f.g: Far western and African peoples; “Pul” likely means Put (Libya).
Greece (Ionia).

f.w: they shall declare my glory among the Gentiles

chapters.n: They will bring back all your brothers from every nation as an offering to the Lord—on horses, chariots, litters, mules, and camels—to Jerusalem, just as Israelites bring grain offerings in clean vessels to the temple. The gathering itself is an offering.

f.w: they shall bring all your brethren for an offering unto the LORD

f.g: Covered chairs or couches carried on poles.
Probably dromedary camels.

chapters.n: Astonishingly, God will take some of these gathered people—perhaps even from among the Gentiles—to be priests and Levites.

f.w: I will also take of them for priests and for Levites

chapters.n: As permanent as the new heavens and new earth God will make, so permanent will His people’s descendants and name be.

f.w: the new heavens and the new earth

chapters.n: Every new moon and every Sabbath, all people will come to worship the Lord. Worship becomes universal and regular.

f.w: shall all flesh come to worship before me

chapters.n: A sobering final image: outside the city lie the bodies of those who rebelled, where the worm doesn’t die and the fire isn’t quenched. Jesus used this language for the fate of the unrepentant. Isaiah ends with both hope and warning: choose the Lord.

f.w: their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched

f.g: Something repulsive, looked on with horror.
